metadata.title: Close out an access panel with retainer bars
metadata.instruction: Seat the grey panel flush in its pocket, then lay each orange retainer bar flat across the panel edge into its rib slot, at least 20 mm onto the panel.
metadata.context: Access-panel close-out is routine aircraft and spacecraft integration work (aircraft structure and systems assemblers, O*NET 51-2011): the cover goes into its recess flush, then retainers are set across the joint. Unlike a part dropped into a pocket, each retainer bridges the panel and the frame, so its seat exists only once the panel is flush. A bar laid first tips about 23 degrees into the empty pocket and must be lifted out again, and a panel left proud tilts the bar past 3 degrees. 1 g tabletop analogue; a real panel is held by quarter-turn or captive fasteners under spring preload, which this task does not reproduce. No microgravity is claimed.
metadata.setup: Table coordinates in metres: x forward from the line through the two arm bases, y left from the midline, z up from the table top; the arm bases are at y = +0.305 (left) and y = -0.305 (right). The pocket centre F is (0.250, 0.000), on the midline. Loose, rigid, matte: the panel, a dark grey (sRGB 0.20, 0.20, 0.22) block 160 x 80 x 16 mm, 120 g (printed PLA), lying flat centred at (0.220, 0.330) with its long axis along y; two retainer bars, orange (sRGB 0.95, 0.55, 0.10) blocks 60 x 16 x 16 mm, 10 g each (printed PLA), lying along x in their keyways on the frame plates, bar_plus centred at (0.250, 0.113) and bar_minus at (0.250, -0.113), bottoms 16 mm above the table. Fixed, light grey (sRGB 0.80, 0.80, 0.82), matte, 18 blocks in all, forming one frame: a pocket ring 5 mm tall standing on the table, two walls 186 x 10 x 5 mm centred at (0.250, +0.048) and (0.250, -0.048) and two walls 10 x 86 x 5 mm centred at (0.162, 0.000) and (0.338, 0.000), giving an open pocket 166 x 86 mm whose floor is the table (3 mm of clearance per side around the panel, at most about 2 degrees of yaw); two frame plates 220 x 80 x 16 mm centred at (0.250, +0.093) and (0.250, -0.093), spanning 53 to 133 mm either side of the midline against the ring's outer faces, their tops 16 mm above the table and flush with a seated panel's top; on each plate, a keyway of four ribs 10 x 4 x 10 mm (x, y, z) centred at x 0.223 and 0.277 and y 0.101 and 0.125 (mirrored for the right plate), their inner faces 20 mm apart (2 mm either side of the stowed bar), flanking the last 8 mm at each end of the bar, 2 mm from its sides, with the bar's end faces open; on each plate, a slot of two ribs 4 x 10 x 10 mm centred at x 0.237 and 0.263 and y 0.071 (mirrored), their inner faces 22 mm apart (3 mm either side of a set bar), spanning 66 to 76 mm from the midline, tops 26 mm above the table, with nothing across either end of the slot. Nominal end state: the panel centred on F with its long axis along x, flat on the table inside the ring, top flush with the plates; each bar along y centred at (0.250, +0.046) or (0.250, -0.046), spanning 16 to 76 mm from the midline: 24 mm on the panel, 13 mm across the 3 mm gap and the ring wall (whose top is 11 mm below the bar), 23 mm on the plate, its outer 10 mm between the slot ribs and its outer end in line with their outer faces. With top-down grips the panel and bar_plus are within the left arm's reach and bar_minus within the right arm's; F is 0.25 m out on the midline, within both. To build it: print the ring and both plates with their ribs as one open-floored PLA frame about 220 x 266 mm, tape it to the table with its outline marked, and print the panel and bars to the stated sizes and masses. If the print bed is under 266 mm, print the frame as two halves split on the midline (each about 220 x 133 mm) and tape both to the marked outline.
metadata.scoring: End state only, judged after the arms have withdrawn and nothing moves (in simulation: at rest, speed under 10 mm/s and spin under 0.5 rad/s), from a top photo, a straightedge, a steel rule and a phone level. Panel seated (P): at rest with its centre within 4 mm of F in x and y, long axis within 3 degrees of x either way round, all four bottom corners within 2 mm of the table and all four top corners within 2 mm of the plate tops (16 mm up), so a panel cocked on a ring wall, proud, outside the pocket or held above it fails. A bar is set in a slot when it rests with its long axis within 10 degrees of y either way round, a face within 3 degrees of flat, its lowest corner within 2 mm of the plate tops, its centre within 4 mm of the slot's centre line (x = 0.250) across the slot, its outer end (the end away from the midline) within 4 mm of the ribs' outer faces (76 mm from the midline) along the slot, and its inner end at least 20 mm inside the panel's edge, measured across the panel from where the panel actually lies. Either bar may fill either slot and each slot counts once. Score: 0 without P, whatever the bars do; P alone 0.4; P and one slot filled 0.7; P and both slots filled 1.0. Success, which ends the trial, is the 1.0 condition held for 1 s. Order: without a seated panel, a bar laid in a slot has its centre 7 mm past the plate edge and tips about 23 degrees into the empty pocket, its inner end on the table; on a panel resting 5 mm proud on the ring it tilts about 8 degrees, pivoting on the panel edge; both fail the 3 degree test. A bar on the panel outside a slot, across the joint along x, on the rib tops, stacked on the other bar, on the table, held above its slot (lowest corner more than 2 mm above the plate tops) or moving earns nothing for that slot. Photo check: the panel inside the ring with no step to a straightedge laid across both plates; each bar level and in its slot between the two ribs, its outer end within 4 mm of a straightedge laid across the two ribs' outer faces (76 mm from the midline), and a rule from its inner end to the panel edge reads at least 20 mm. The frame is fixed in simulation; on the real rig, a trial in which the frame moved more than 2 mm from its taped outline scores 0. In simulation the scorer cannot see the grippers, so a panel or bar still gripped but motionless at the end is not distinguished; on the real rig the photo is taken after the arms park.
metadata.reset_notes: Nothing is consumed. Lift the panel out and lay it flat on its start mark, long axis along y; lay each bar back in its keyway along x. The frame does not move; check it against its taped outline.
metadata.fidelity: Approximate: rigid primitives with one shared friction (1.2 static, 1.0 dynamic) and matte colours; the ring, plates and ribs are fixed colliders standing in for one printed frame. A real quarter-turn or captive fastener turns in place under spring preload; here each loose bar is set across the joint and holds the panel by its weight only. The 3 mm panel clearance is looser than a flight panel's. Earth gravity on a bench, where this job is done.

metadata.title: Weigh out 1.00 g of granules on an analytical balance with a draft shield
metadata.instruction: Weigh out 1.00 g of the orange granules into the weighing boat on the analytical balance. Slide the balance's glass top door open by its dark handle, put the empty weighing boat in the middle of the pan and slide the door shut. Press the green TARE key, so the display reads 0.00 with the empty boat on the pan. Open the door again and pour granules from the vial into the boat, a little at a time, until the display reads 1.00 g. Then slide the door shut. Do not spill granules, and do not press TARE again once granules are in the boat.
metadata.context: Weighing a set mass of a powder into a tared container, with the draft shield shut for the zero and the reading, is a daily step in sample and solution preparation. Pouring too fast overshoots, and an untared container or an open door gives a wrong mass.
metadata.setup: Station table (top 0.7475 m). Robot base frame: x forward, y to the robots' left. Analytical balance, fixed, white, 39.5 x 18.2 cm, spanning x 0.13 to 0.525 at y -0.091 to 0.091. Front key strip (x 0.13 to 0.221, top 4 cm above the table): a dark screen 3 x 6.8 cm centred at (0.182, 0.03) with four green 7-segment digits 2 cm tall, decimal point after the second, reading grams to 0.01 g (tops of the digits away from the robots); a green TARE key 18 mm square at (0.172, -0.062) that travels 3 mm down against a spring (about 0.45 N at the bottom); a dark ON key at (0.172, -0.034), not used. Draft shield: a glass chamber, inside x 0.225 to 0.385 and y -0.085 to 0.085, floor 3.5 cm and walls 10 cm above the table, 4 mm light-blue glass; front and side walls fixed. Top door: a 17.4 x 17.8 cm glass plate 4 mm thick on the walls, closed at the start; it slides 13 cm back (away from the robots) over a white rear housing (x 0.385 to 0.525, 10 cm tall), on a dark handle bar 1 x 4 x 1.2 cm (along y) whose centre is at (0.234, -0.065), top 11.6 cm above the table. Pan: steel, 8 cm across, top 5 cm above the table, centred at (0.30, 0.0). The display reads 0.00 at the start. Weighing boat, loose, 1.2 g: white plastic, 5 cm square, 1.2 cm deep, 1.5 mm walls and a 4 mm floor, at (0.18, 0.20). Vial, loose, 8 g: a small square glass bottle, 2.5 cm across outside and 2.6 cm tall, 1.5 mm walls on a 2 mm base, open at the top, standing at (0.26, 0.21); its wall facing the robots leans out 30 degrees as a pouring spout, its lip 1.3 cm beyond the other walls. Granules: 70 orange polypropylene pellets, cylinders 4 mm across and 3 mm long, 0.03 g each (2.1 g in all), filling the vial to about 1.2 cm. No other objects.
metadata.scoring: Measured once everything has come to rest. The display reads the mass resting on the pan (the boat, granules in it or on the pan, and the vial if it is put on the pan) minus the mass on it at the last TARE press, which counts once the key is down past half its travel. 0 unless that last TARE press was made with the empty boat resting on the pan and nothing else on it, and the boat is on the pan now (underside within 3 mm of the pan, centre over it). Otherwise, by how far the reading is from 1.00 g: 1.0 within 0.05 g, 0.6 within 0.15 g, 0.3 within 0.5 g, 0.1 further off. The score is halved if the top door is open more than 5 mm now or was at that TARE press, and halved again if any granule lies anywhere but in the boat or in the vial.
metadata.reset_notes: Nothing is consumed. Pour all 70 granules back into the vial and stand it at (0.26, 0.21), put the empty boat at (0.18, 0.20), slide the door shut and zero the balance with the pan empty. In simulation the pellets restart in a three-layer stack (25, 25, 20); in the real world they settle as a loose pile to about the same height.
metadata.fidelity: Rigid bodies in PhysX at 240 Hz. The reading is worked out from what rests on the pan (boat 1.2 g, pellets 0.03 g each, vial 8 g), not from forces; no drift, draft or settling time. In simulation the pellets weigh 0.2 g and the boat 12 g so contacts stay stable; the display still counts the real masses. Pellets are rigid 4 x 3 mm cylinders; a real powder is finer and cohesive. The door slides on a damped joint with hard stops.

metadata.title: Assemble a slotted partition
metadata.instruction: Build the partition: stand the long slat on the white mark and slide both short slats down across it so their slots interlock.
metadata.context: Partitions for crates, cartons and fixtures are assembled from boards with interlocking slots; a board on edge tips over easily, so one hand steadies it on its mark while the other slides the crossing board down onto it.
metadata.setup: On the station table, three light brown rigid foam-board slats (16 mm thick, 8 cm tall, 40 g each), each standing on edge in a low grey plastic rack (two 3 x 0.8 x 2 cm blocks, 1 mm clear of the slat's faces; the long slat's rack is 10 cm from the slat's centre toward the middle of the table, and each short slat's is 4 cm from the slat's centre toward the arms). A long slat (30 cm) stands 18 cm in front of the arm bases, along the line between them, centred 15 cm to the right of centre; it has two slots 24 mm wide cut 4 cm down from its top edge, 18 cm apart. Two short slats (20 cm), each with one slot 24 mm wide cut 4 cm up from its bottom edge at its middle, stand pointing away from the arms, centred 28 cm in front of the arm bases: one 20 cm to the left of centre, one 22 cm to the right. A thin line of white tape on the table (6 mm wide, 30 cm long, along the line between the arms, centred between them, 27 cm in front of the arm bases) marks where the long slat goes.
metadata.scoring: 1.0 if both of the long slat's slots hold a short slat with the slots interlocked: all three slats standing on edge on the table, each short slat's centre within 6 mm of its slot along the long slat and within 6 mm across it, top edges flush within 4 mm, the long slat's centre within 2 cm of the white line's centre and the slat turned no more than 5 degrees from the line, all still for 1 second. Otherwise 0.4 for each interlocked crossing (0.8 for a full partition off the line). Slats laid flat in a cross, or resting on top of each other without interlocking, score 0.
metadata.reset_notes: Pull the slats apart and stand each back in its rack.
metadata.fidelity: Each slat is one rigid body built from boxes, its slots real gaps; 16 mm slats in 24 mm slots leave 4 mm of play each way. Surface friction in the slots isn't modelled beyond the station's default contact material, and each slat has the same 40 g, where a real short slat is a little lighter. Nothing is deformable.

metadata.title: Load two tubes into a centrifuge so it can spin
metadata.instruction: Load both sample tubes into the centrifuge rotor so it is ready to spin.
metadata.context: Before every run, lab staff balance a centrifuge rotor: tubes of equal weight go in opposite positions, because an unbalanced rotor makes the centrifuge shake and can damage it or break the tubes. The instruction does not state the rule, so the task checks whether the robot applies it unprompted. Done by: clinical laboratory technologists and technicians.
metadata.setup: Positions are in cm on the table, from the midpoint between the two arm bases: x forward (away from the arms), y to the robot's left. Rotor, a fixed mock (for example 3D-printed grey PLA), bolted or taped down: a disc 20 cm across and 1 cm thick centred at x 24, y 0; a hub 3 cm across and 4.5 cm tall at its centre; six square pockets, each 4 cm across inside, with 4 mm walls rising 4 cm above the disc and sides parallel to the table edges, centred every 60 degrees on a 6.5 cm circle around the hub: at x 29.6 y 3.25, x 24 y 6.5, x 18.4 y 3.25, x 18.4 y -3.25, x 24 y -6.5 and x 29.6 y -3.25. Tubes: two 50 mL conical centrifuge tubes (3 cm across, 11.5 cm long), each holding 40 mL of water (about 53 g, the same weight), caps on and up; in the sim they are solid blue so they show from the top camera. Holders: two white square collars fixed to the table, 3.4 cm across inside, with 4 mm walls 3 cm tall, centred at x 17, y 20 and x 17, y -20; each holds one tube upright, standing on the table.
metadata.scoring: A tube counts as seated when, at the end, it is down in a pocket: its lowest point within 5 mm of the rotor disc's top surface, the centre of its lower end inside the pocket's 4 cm square opening, and leaning at most 18 degrees. 1.0: both tubes seated in opposite pockets (180 degrees apart around the hub), held for 1 s. 0.25: exactly one tube seated and the other clear of the rotor (no part of its axis within 10 cm of the rotor centre, seen from above), for example still in its holder. 0: both tubes seated but not in opposite pockets (an unbalanced rotor), one seated with the other on or across the rotor, or no tube seated. Possible scores: 0, 0.25, 1.0. To check a real trial, open both grippers and take a top-down photo: it shows which pockets hold tubes, and a tube that is fully down stands 7.5 cm above the pocket rim.
metadata.reset_notes: Put both tubes back in their holders, caps up.
metadata.fidelity: The rotor is a fixed mock: no lid, no spinning, vertical square pockets (real rotors are fixed-angle or swing-bucket). Tubes are plain flat-bottomed cylinders without caps, exactly equal in weight. PhysX has no rolling resistance, so a released tube can rock in its pocket for seconds; seating checks position, not stillness. The sim can't tell a gripped tube from a released one: on a real table, open the grippers first. Everything has the same rubber-like friction (1.2 static, 1.0 dynamic).

metadata.title: Rinse a glass on a bar's push-down glass rinser, then leave it to drain
metadata.instruction: Rinse the glass on the glass rinser, then leave it to drain on the drip mat.
metadata.context: Bartenders rinse each glass on a push-down glass rinser just before use: the glass goes rim-down over the rinse plate and is pressed down, which opens a spring valve and sprays the inside of the glass; it is held for a second or two, then lifted off to drain rim-down. The glass's own weight does not open the valve, and pressing the plate with nothing over it, or with the glass off centre, sprays the bar and the bartender. The robot must push a held glass down against a spring, keep it centred and seated while the spray runs, and only then set it down. Unlike placing a cup on a coaster or racking glasses, success here is a sustained, centred press through the grasped object on a sprung valve. A familiar bar-service moment: anyone who has sat at a bar has watched a bartender give a glass this quick rinse before pouring a beer, and the same rinsers sit behind counters in pubs, cafes and coffee shops.
metadata.setup: Positions in cm from the midpoint between the arm bases (x forward, y left). Glass: a loose pressed-glass tumbler, 180 g, a 12-sided prism 7.2 cm across the flats (7.5 cm across the corners) and 10.5 cm tall, 3 mm walls, standing rim-down at x 36, y -25, two flats facing +-y. Rinser: a fixed stainless drain bowl, inside 14 x 14 cm, 4 cm tall rim, centred at x 32, y -9; in it a 9.5 cm square, 60 g rinse plate on a vertical spring (300 N/m, 3.6 N preload against its upper stop, top 3.2 cm above the counter, 9 mm of travel); the valve opens once the plate is 4 mm down (about 3 N more than the glass's weight). Drip mat: a fixed 13 x 13 x 0.6 cm rubber mat centred at x 22, y -24. Real-world equivalent: a counter-mounted bar glass rinser with a stainless drain bowl whose 1.5-inch outlet runs to the bar's floor drain; under the rinse plate, a multi-jet spray nozzle on a push-down valve, fed by a 3/8-inch cold-water line at mains pressure (about 3-4 bar) through a shut-off valve.
metadata.scoring: From the episode's recorded poses and the plate's travel. Rinse time accrues while the plate is at least 4 mm down with the glass rim-down (tilt under 10 deg), its rim centre within 1.2 cm of the plate centre and its rim within 4 mm of the plate's top. On the mat: rim-down (tilt under 8 deg), every rim point on the mat within 3 mm of its top, let go (both grippers 2.5 cm clear) and still. Score = 0.6 x min(1, rinse time / 1.5 s) + 0.4 if on the mat at the end; 1.0 is success when held 1 s. 0 if at any moment the plate is 4 mm down without the glass covering it (sprayed the bar) or the glass is more than 45 deg off rim-down. Scored at the last step; range 0 to 1.
metadata.reset_notes: Stand the glass rim-down on its mark, flats facing the arms' sides. The rinse plate springs back to its stop; the bowl and mat do not move.
metadata.fidelity: Rigid boxes, default contact friction. The glass is one rigid body of 14 boxes, rendered opaque pale blue-grey; no breakage. The rinse plate is a square plate (a real one is a star) on a PhysX prismatic joint with a spring drive and stops; the spray is not simulated, only the valve state. Rinse time is counted per 20 Hz control step.

metadata.title: Assemble a 2x2 18650 battery pack in a jig
metadata.instruction: With your left gripper, put the black battery holder half that lies cups up into the orange jig. With your right gripper, take the four yellow batteries from the grey tray one at a time and push each into a cup of that holder, positive end up. Then, with your left gripper, pick up the other holder half, which lies cups down, lower it onto the tops of the four batteries, and move both arms back to where they started.
metadata.context: Building small lithium-ion packs is everyday work at battery, e-bike and electronics repair benches: the bottom half of a cell holder goes into an assembly jig, the cells are pushed into its cups all the same way round (a reversed cell shorts the pack once it is welded), and the top half of the holder is pressed on to hold them before the nickel strips are welded.
metadata.setup: Left and right are the robot's. Positions are in metres from the midpoint between the two arm bases: x forward, y to the robot's left. Assembly jig: an orange 3D-printed plate, 76 x 76 x 6 mm, screwed to the table with its centre at (0.30, -0.05), sides along x and y, with a 42 x 42 x 3 mm square pocket (1 mm lead-in) and a 20 mm finger slot through each side wall. Holder halves: two identical black ABS halves of a 2x2 18650 cell holder (41.2 x 41.2 x 9.5 mm, 6.5 g, 20 mm pitch, cups with 0.3 mm radial clearance and a 0.8 mm lead-in), loose on the table: one cups up at (0.24, 0.15), one cups down at (0.34, 0.18). Cell tray: a grey 3D-printed tray, 80 x 80 x 14 mm, loose on the table at (0.30, -0.26), with four 18 x 65 mm 18650 lithium-ion cells (47 g each, yellow plastic wrap) standing positive end up in its four pockets, 36 mm apart.
metadata.scoring: Four steps, 0.25 each, judged at the end from the video. (1) Bottom holder in the jig: a holder half lies cups up in the jig's pocket. (2) Two cells seated: at least two cells stand in its cups, bottom on the cup's floor, positive end up. (3) Four cells seated: all four do. (4) Top holder on: the other half lies cups down on the four cells, centred over the bottom half within 2 mm and resting on all four. Full score 1.0, ending the run, when all four steps hold, both arms are back where they started (within 3 cm) holding nothing, and the holders and cells have been still (nothing sliding, tipping or falling) for 1 s. 0 overall if at the end a holder half, a cell or the tray has fallen off the table.
metadata.reset_notes: Take the top holder half off and lay it cups down at its mark; take the four cells out and stand them positive end up in the tray's pockets; take the bottom half out of the jig and lay it cups up at its mark; put the tray back on its mark.
metadata.fidelity: Rigid bodies, 240 Hz physics, 20 Hz control. The holder halves collide as signed distance fields (0.3 mm cup clearance, 0.8 mm lead-in); each cell as a 30-sided prism with flat ends; the jig and the tray as small convex prisms (the tray's pockets 24-sided). Real masses: cells 47 g, holder halves 6.5 g, tray 47 g. No deformation; nothing holds the top half on but its weight.
metadata.scores: Dream-1 run: 0.0 (both arms reached over the jig, the holder halves and the cell tray again and again, but it never picked up a holder half or a cell); demo: 1.0 (all four steps by step 1892, success at step 1971)

metadata.title: Lock a bayonet cap into its socket
metadata.instruction: Pick up the blue cap by its square head, line its orange lugs up with the slots in the round socket on the grey box, push it down, and turn it a quarter turn counterclockwise until it stops.
metadata.context: Bayonet mounts close battery compartments, lamp sockets, filter housings and quarter-turn connectors (O*NET 49-2094.00, 51-2028.00). Unlike screwing on a thread, the cap must be turned to match a keyed opening, pushed against a spring and turned to a stop.
metadata.setup: Positions in cm from the midpoint between the two arm bases, on the table (x forward, y left). Box: grey PLA 12 x 7 x 2.5 cm, 150 g, standing on a fixed grey 4 x 5 x 2 cm block centred at x 21, y -5, both turned 45 degrees clockwise seen from above. A round socket sits 3.4 cm in front of the box centre along its long axis: a 2.6 cm opening in a 4 mm roof, with two 6 mm wide slots along the box's long axis reaching 1.9 cm from the socket centre, over a chamber with two stops that let the cap turn only counterclockwise, up to just past 90 degrees. Under the opening, an orange PLA plate (2.2 x 2.2 cm) rides on a spring (1.5 N per mm, 6 mm travel) 3 mm below the roof's underside. Cap: blue PLA, 30 g: a 2.4 cm diameter, 2 cm tall barrel, a 2 x 2 x 2 cm square grip head on top, and two orange lugs (5 x 6 x 5 mm) sticking out 1.7 cm from its axis near the barrel's bottom; it stands upright on the table at x 12, y 15, lugs turned 30 degrees clockwise from the arms' forward direction.
metadata.scoring: Measured at the end from a top photo and a ruler. 0 if the box was at any point moved more than 3 cm, tilted more than 20 degrees or turned more than 20 degrees. Otherwise: 1.0 if the cap is locked: its axis within 3 mm of the socket centre, upright within 10 degrees, lugs turned more than 80 degrees from the slots and held up against the roof's underside (cap within 1.5 mm of that height), let go (both grippers at least 3 cm from the cap) and still (moving less than 1 mm and 2 degrees) over the last 1 s, for 1 s; 0.75 if, with the lugs pushed below the roof, the cap was turned more than 45 degrees; 0.5 if, after being lifted, the cap was pushed in with its lugs below the roof's underside; 0.25 if the cap was lifted 3 cm; else 0.
metadata.reset_notes: Turn the cap back clockwise to the slots, lift it out, and stand it on its mark with its lugs at the marked angle; set the box on its foot in its marked outline.
metadata.fidelity: Rigid bodies built from boxes and a cylinder; the foot is fixed. Lugs, slots, roof and stops are real colliders, so locking comes from contact alone; the spring is a prismatic joint with a spring drive and no preload. Contact offsets are 0.5 mm and light angular damping is added to the parts so the 1 mm fits do not chatter. No contact force cap is enforced in simulation.

metadata.title: Clamp a printed part in a vise at a marked height
metadata.instruction: Clamp the orange printed part upright and tight in the vise, with the black line round it level with the tops of the jaws.
metadata.context: Printed parts are clamped in a small vise to be drilled, tapped or deburred at a marked depth; clamped too deep or tilted, the hole lands in the wrong place. A loose part has to be held at height with one hand while the other closes the vise.
metadata.setup: Station table (top 0.7475 m). Robot base frame: x forward, y to the robots' left. Drill-press vise, fixed, painted cast iron: a 9 x 11 cm base plate 1 cm thick under a body 6 cm wide (x) running along y from y = -0.025 to 0.085 at x = 0.32, its top (the bed) 7.5 cm above the table. Fixed jaw at the left end: 6 cm wide, 2.5 cm thick, 3.2 cm above the bed (jaw tops 10.7 cm above the table), steel face at y = 0.060. Moving jaw on the bed, 6 x 2 x 3.2 cm, steel face at y = 0.030 (jaws 30 mm apart); it slides along y. Knob: black, ribbed, 4 cm across and 2 cm long, on an 8 mm shaft out of the body's right end, axis along y 6.5 cm above the table, centre at (0.32, -0.043), with a white index line on its end; clockwise seen from its end closes the jaw, 16 mm per turn (opening 1 to 42 mm). Part, loose, 15 g: orange PLA block 20 x 20 x 50 mm with a 1 mm black line round it 20 mm above its bottom, standing upright at (0.22, 0.20), faces square to x and y. No other objects.
metadata.scoring: Measured once everything has come to rest. 0 unless the part is between the jaws (the centre of its bottom face below the jaw tops, within the jaws' 6 cm width and between their faces). 0.25 if between the jaws but not clamped. Clamped: jaw gap within 0.5 mm of the part's 20 mm width and the vise tightened on it (at least 5 N; 1/32 turn past first contact). 0.5 if clamped but the line is more than 5 mm above or below the jaw tops, or the part is tilted more than 5 degrees. 0.75 if clamped and upright with the line within 5 mm of the jaw tops; 1.0 within 2 mm.
metadata.reset_notes: Nothing is consumed. Turn the knob back until the jaws are 30 mm apart, take the part out and stand it upright at its start position, faces square to the table's edges.
metadata.fidelity: Rigid bodies in PhysX at 240 Hz. The knob turns on a damped hinge; the moving jaw follows it through a stiff spring drive, geared faster than a real vise (16 mm per turn, real ones 2 to 3 mm), with the clamping force capped at 30 N in place of the screw's torque limit. The screw is not drawn. The part is a plain block standing in for a printed fixture; nothing is drilled.

metadata.title: Send a corded blender up a service lift without trapping its cord
metadata.instruction: Put the blender in the lift and press the green button to send it up.
metadata.context: Service lifts (dumbwaiters) shut their door and move off with whatever hangs over the sill; a cord left trailing out of the car is caught by the door and dragged by the rising car, crushing the cord and jamming the lift.
metadata.setup: Station table (wood); cm from the midpoint between the arm bases, x forward, y left. Two YAM arms, bases at y +30.5 and -30.5, start in the ready pose with the grippers open. A stainless steel service lift stands on the table with its front wall at x 31 to 33, centred on y 0: an opening 50 wide and 40 high, its sill 1.3 above the table; behind it a car 50 wide, 30 deep and 42 high inside, open at the front, its floor's front edge at x 34.2. A glass door in a steel frame (51.6 wide, 1.2 thick) slides vertically just in front of the opening; it starts open, its bottom 1 above the opening's top. To the right of the opening, a stainless console (13 x 9 x 6 high) centred at x 31, y -34 carries on its top a green push button (28 mm across, its face 1.9 above the console, 8 mm travel) at x 28.5, and a status lamp at x 34: green open, amber going up, red broken, dark arrived. A corded stick blender lies on the table along y, its axis at x 20 and its grip towards the left arm: total length 36, from y -18 at the foot to y +18 at the end of the grip; dark plastic grip 16.5 long and 6.6 across with a red switch; stainless shaft 2.2 across; stainless blending foot 7 across; 600 g. Its rubber cord (40 long, 7 mm thick) leaves the end of the grip and lies on the table curling back towards the robot and then to the right, ending in a plug (body 3.5 x 3 x 1.6, two round pins 1.7 long) at about x 13.7, y -10.4.
metadata.scoring: Each subtask is scored and reported. The line is 1 cm behind the car floor's front edge. S1 (blender in the lift): every part of the blender behind the line, resting on the car floor and not held. S2 (cord in the lift): every part of the cord and the plug, pins included, behind the line. S3 (button pressed): the button pushed in 4 mm or more. D (danger at the press): when the button is pressed, any part of the blender, cord or plug crosses the line (part behind it and part in front), or an arm is in the door's path. Total: if the button is pressed, 0.0 with D or if the lift breaks (door not closed 4 s after the press, or car 8 cm behind its target); 1.0 with S1 and S2 at the press; otherwise 0.0 (an empty or unready lift sent). If the button is never pressed: 0.5 for S1 and S2 at the end of the run, 0.25 for S1 alone, otherwise 0.0. S1, S2 and D are judged at the moment of the press (a tape line 1 cm behind the car floor's edge and a top-view photo).
metadata.reset_notes: Lay the blender and the cord in their starting layout (outline marked on the table), lower the car and open the door before each trial.
metadata.fidelity: Approximate: car and door are counterweighted force-limited drives (door 8 N, closed within 2 cm; car 0.2 m/s, 150 N). The cord is 20 rigid 2 cm capsules on damped hinges, no twist, about twice a real flex's mass; blender and plug are rigid. Physics runs at 240 Hz on GPU PhysX. After a press, a cord or plug caught by the door and car can sink up to 2.4 mm for a moment; the score is taken at the press. The door's glass collides as one solid box; the fingers are independent joints.

metadata.title: Read the status lamp's blink code, then swap the module it names
metadata.context: Servers and robots report which module failed as a blink pattern on a status LED; a service robot must read the pattern over time, replace the named field-replaceable unit and verify, without touching the healthy ones.
metadata.instruction: While you hold the white DIAG button the status lamp blinks the number of the failed socket (count the dots beside each socket); replace that module with the teal spare, then hold DIAG again until the lamp stays green.
metadata.setup: A rigid free-standing fixture (one 8.0 kg body, friction 1.0, not bolted down) on the station table (z = 74.8 cm) holds a 4-socket bus strip and a DIAG controller box. Four keyed sockets (pitch 7.0 cm, mouths at x = 24.0 cm, z = 2.5 cm above table) sit at y = -5.0 cm (socket 1, 1 dot), y = -12.0 cm (socket 2, 2 dots), y = -19.0 cm (socket 3, 3 dots), and y = -26.0 cm (socket 4, 4 dots), each with aluminium flange 56 x 42 x 6 mm, dark shell 38 x 30 x 24 mm, 30 x 18 mm cavity (1.0 mm clearance per side to 28 x 16 mm nose), 8 x 3 mm key slot, and 12 N/mm spring plunger (round 4 mm tip, 1.5 mm proud on +y wall). Controller box (140 x 120 x 40 mm, centre at x = 25.0 cm, y = 20.0 cm) holds a white DIAG button cap (36 x 36 x 12 mm, 4 g, centre at x = 22.0 cm, y = 20.0 cm, cap top 6.0 cm above the table at rest, 8 mm travel to a hard stop, soft 100 N/m spring) and a 60 mm diameter, 15 mm tall status lamp dome (centre at x = 28.5 cm, y = 20.0 cm; off = dark grey, blink = amber/yellow, verified = green, healthy missing = red). Four servo modules (80 g each, friction 0.8; 45 x 18 x 28 mm housing with grey band, steel nose 28 x 16 x 18 mm with key rib and detent groove) start seated in sockets 1 to 4 with nose pointing +x. One spare servo module with a teal band starts staged on the table at x = 38.0 cm, y = -15.0 cm.
metadata.scoring: Partial credit ladder: 0.25 if DIAG button is held >= 3 s once (held >= 60 control steps) or any module is touched / displaced > 5 mm or DIAG button depressed >= 2.0 mm; 0.50 if failed module (module 3) is out of socket 3 (depth < 16 mm, lateral offset > 1.5 mm, or angle error > 10.0 deg) with every healthy module (1, 2, 4) still seated; 0.75 if teal spare is seated in socket 3 (depth >= 16 mm, lateral error <= 1.5 mm, angle error <= 10.0 deg), failed module is not in any socket, and all healthy modules are seated; 1.00 if additionally DIAG is held >= 3 s showing steady green lamp, all four sockets seated, both grippers open, and all objects still (linear speed <= 5 mm/s, angular <= 0.2 rad/s) held continuously for 1.0 s (20 control steps). Zero-gate: any healthy module removed from socket for > 1 s (20 control steps) and not re-seated by end, fixture displacement > 5.0 mm, fixture tilt > 5.0 deg, or any module dropped off table (> 20 cm below table plane) permanently scores 0.0.
metadata.reset_notes: Return the original grey module to socket 3 and return the teal spare to its staging spot (x = 38.0 cm, y = -15.0 cm). If any healthy modules were disturbed, return them to their marked sockets (1 to 4). Release the white DIAG button. No parts or materials are consumed.
metadata.fidelity: Servos, keyed sockets (1 mm clearance per side, spring plunger) and the DIAG pushbutton (8 mm travel, hard stop, soft 100 N/m spring chosen for soft arm compliance) are simulated physically. Bus strip, sockets and controller box form one rigid fixture. Status lamp blinks and verification color states are computed in code and teleported as visual markers.

metadata.title: Stand a flat box, too wide for one gripper, on edge in a narrow slot beside a riser
metadata.instruction: Put the flat white box into the slot between the wooden riser and the wall, standing on edge with its longest side upright.
metadata.context: Flat cartons, trays and panels are stored on edge in slot racks, but they arrive lying flat. Lying flat, a wide carton cannot be picked up by one hand from above, and turning it on edge needs a lever or an edge to tip it over: lifted onto a ledge with both hands, it can be tipped over the ledge's edge into the rack, the way people stand up heavy panels.
metadata.setup: A table in front of two arms (bases 61 cm apart), seen by one overhead camera and a camera on each wrist. Distances are measured forward from the line between the arm bases and sideways from the midpoint between them. (1) A closed white corrugated cardboard box with no handles, 12 cm deep x 20 cm wide x 9 cm thick, 350 g, lying flat with its centre 15 cm forward on the centre line. Lying flat it is wider and deeper than a gripper opens (about 9 cm). (2) A fixed dark wooden riser, 12 cm deep x 12 cm wide x 10 cm tall (half the box's width), centred 30 cm forward and 4 cm right; its left face is 2 cm left of the centre line. (3) The slot: a 14.5 cm gap between the riser's left face and a fixed dark wooden wall (14 cm long x 1.5 cm thick x 9 cm tall) whose inner face is 16.5 cm left of the centre line, from 23 to 37 cm forward. Standing on edge in the slot, the box is 20 cm tall. The layout is the same in every trial, as in the screenshot.
metadata.scoring: Measured from the overhead and wrist videos, with a tape measure and a protractor. 1.0: the box stands on edge in the slot, on one of its 12 x 9 cm faces, with its 20 cm side within 20 degrees of vertical, its underside within 1.5 cm of the table and its centre between the riser and the wall and within the slot's length, still for 2 s. 0.5: the box lies flat on top of the riser (tilted under 10 degrees, its underside within 1 cm of the riser's top), lifted there but not stood up in the slot. 0.0: anything else, including the box on the table outside the slot, on its side or fallen off the riser.
metadata.reset_notes: Nothing is consumed: lay the box flat on its start mark. Replace it if squeezing has dented a side by more than 5 mm.
metadata.fidelity: Rigid-body PhysX (Isaac Sim 6.1, 20 Hz control) of a calibrated two-arm table. Simplified: the box is a rigid, uniformly dense block (no flex or shifting contents), the riser and wall are fixed, and the squeeze comes only from the arms' joint stiffness. Loose objects get rubber-like friction (1.2 static, 1.0 dynamic), so the box slides less readily than real cardboard. Dream-1 sees the 320 x 176 frames it expects; the demo video is rendered at 1280 x 720.

metadata.title: Pack a parcel following a printed packing plan
metadata.instruction: Pack the carton to match the two printed packing plans. The left sheet shows the bottom layer; the right sheet shows the top layer. Each plan has the same orientation as the carton. Leave boxes not shown on the plans outside the carton.
metadata.context: As in e-commerce order picking, the robot tightly packs selected box-like products into a parcel to match a printed two-layer plan, using placement and pushing with 5 mm positional tolerances.
metadata.setup: Coordinates: x forward from the line between the two arm bases, y to the left, from the midpoint between the bases. On the table: an open cardboard carton fixed to the table, centred at x 26 cm, y 0; inside 24 cm deep (x) by 18 cm wide (y) by 6.5 cm tall, 8 mm walls, 6 mm floor (outside 25.6 x 19.6 x 7.1 cm). Six loose rigid cardboard boxes stand on the table, sizes x by y by z: blue 16 x 6 x 3.5 cm, 0.20 kg, centred at (26, 27) cm; red 7 x 6 x 3.5 cm, 0.08 kg, at (42, 29) cm; yellow 9 x 6 x 2.5 cm, 0.06 kg, at (36, 19) cm; purple 7 x 6 x 5 cm, 0.12 kg, at (10, 17) cm; green 12 x 5.5 x 3.5 cm, 0.15 kg, at (26, -27) cm; orange 7 x 6 x 5 cm, 0.12 kg, at (42, -25) cm; all axis-aligned. The packing plan is printed on two paper sheets (15 x 12 cm) lying flat behind the carton, centred at x 47.8 cm and y +8 cm (left sheet: bottom layer) and y -8 cm (right sheet: top layer). Each sheet shows the carton's opening at half scale and in the carton's orientation (the sheet's far edge is the carton's far wall) as a black 3 mm outline, and each box of that layer as a filled rectangle in its colour. Bottom layer: blue in the far-left corner, green along the far wall to the right of blue, red along the left wall in front of blue. Top layer: yellow on blue, in the far-left corner. Blue has 3 mm clearance from the far and left walls; green has 3 mm clearance from the far wall and blue; red has 3 mm clearance from the left wall and blue. Yellow aligns with the far-left corner of blue and rests directly on it; remaining space stays empty. Purple and orange are not on the plan.
metadata.scoring: 0.25 for each of blue, red, green and yellow whose axis-aligned bounding box has every face (near, far, left, right, bottom, top) within 5 mm of where the plan puts it (the specified 3 mm clearances; yellow resting on blue). The score is 0 if the world-aligned bounding box of purple or orange intersects the carton's opening below its rim. Full score (1.0) needs all four packed boxes placed, with purple and orange outside the carton; the trial ends early once that holds with every packed box at rest (under 1 cm/s and 0.5 rad/s).
metadata.reset_notes: Nothing is consumed; put the six boxes back at their starting positions.
metadata.fidelity: Approximate: all boxes and the carton are rigid cuboids (no cardboard deformation, flaps or tape); contact uses PhysX default friction; the printed plan is modelled as thin 1-2 mm boxes on the table.

metadata.title: Bleed the air out of a brake caliper, shutting the bleeder each cycle before the pedal comes back up
metadata.instruction: Bleed the air out of this brake caliper.
metadata.context: Automotive service technicians and mechanics (O*NET 49-3023.00; about 826,000 US jobs, BLS) bleed brakes as a regular part of brake work, after a caliper or line is replaced: air in the line compresses, so the pedal is spongy and the car takes longer to stop. In the two-person pedal method one hand presses the pedal and keeps it down, the other opens the caliper's bleeder about a quarter turn so fluid and air push out into a catch jar and the pedal sinks, shuts it while the pedal is still down, and only then does the pedal come up; this repeats until no bubbles come out. Shop bleeding guides give this order because the master cylinder's piston springs back on the pedal's return and pulls on the line, so a bleeder that is still open draws air back in. Unlike tasks that hold a pedal while the other hand works, the score is the air left after repeated cycles, and each wrong release puts air back.
metadata.setup: Positions are in cm from the midpoint between the two arm bases, with x forward, y to the robot's left and the table top at z 0. A bench brake trainer, fixed to the table except for the pedal and the wrench. Pedal stand: a steel post 3 x 4 cm on a 12 x 10 cm foot plate, with the pedal's hinge at x 38, y 16, 8 cm up; a steel pedal lever 11 cm long runs from the hinge toward the robot to a black rubber pad 4.5 x 5 x 1.2 cm centered at x 27, y 16, its top 9 cm up at rest. The pedal goes down 3.3 cm at the pad (17 degrees) to a floor stop and a return spring brings it back up (about 2 N at rest, 4.5 N fully down). Behind the hinge, an aluminum master cylinder (3.2 cm across, 7 cm long, along x) with a translucent reservoir (6 x 4 x 4.5 cm, MIN and MAX lines, amber fluid) on top. The pedal's pushrod works its piston (19 mm bore) through a short arm, which covers the compensating port in the first 8% of the stroke and then pushes 4.2 mL into the line by the floor stop. With the bleeder shut, a push of about 6 N on the pad (6 psi in the line, a light push for one arm) stops the pedal partway down on the fluid, about 16% of its stroke with the starting air and about 9% once bled; with the bleeder open, the pedal sinks to the floor as fluid leaves. A car's pedal makes hundreds of psi; 6 psi is scaled to what the YAM can push, since the scored skill is the hydraulic order of events (press, open, shut, release), not the pressure. A 4.8 mm steel brake line runs from it along the table to a black cast-iron disc-brake caliper (9 x 6 x 6 cm) on a steel bracket, centered at x 30, y -12, from 3 to 9 cm up. The bleeder screw stands on the caliper's top at x 29, y -11 (an 11 mm hex, 12.7 mm across its corners, with a yellow paint ring and a nipple up to 11.8 cm). An 11 mm chrome box-end wrench is on the bleeder's hex: its handle is 12.5 cm long from the bleeder's axis, 1.6 cm wide and 0.8 cm thick, 10 cm up, and points along -y (bleeder shut) at the start; turned a quarter turn counterclockwise seen from above it points along +x (bleeder open), with click detents at shut and open and stops 3 degrees past each. A clear vinyl hose (4.8 mm inside, 8 mm outside) runs from the nipple up and over to a glass catch jar (7 cm across, 9 cm tall, in a wire holder) at x 21.5, y -4.5 holding 4.5 cm of dark old fluid, its end held 2 cm under the fluid inside an inverted graduated tube (1 cm across) that collects the air. The caliper and its line hold 8 mL, with 1.2 mL of air in them at the start; the bleeder is shut and the pedal is up. The real rig uses a clear-body caliper of the same size, so the air in it can be seen.
metadata.scoring: The score reads the air left in the caliper, because that air is what makes the pedal spongy and the car slow to stop. Air drawn back in, latched: 0 if more than 0.01 mL of air (one bubble, about 3 mm across) enters the caliper at any time. Air enters when the pedal comes up with the bleeder still open past 20 degrees, where it starts passing fluid: the master cylinder's piston, coming back on its spring, pulls about 5 psi of suction on the line, and air comes in around the bleeder's threads, which do not seal once its seat lifts. With the bleeder shut first, the piston only takes back what it pushed and no air enters. It stays latched because the order is the procedure's one rule, and the air let in would take more cycles to push out again. In a real trial, check on the video that the wrench was back inside a witness mark 20 degrees from shut before the pedal started up, and watch the real rig's clear-body caliper and the clear bleeder hose, where air drawn in shows as bubbles rising. At the end, also 0 if a gripper still touches the pedal pad or the wrench (its palm or fingers within 2 mm, the solver's resting gap: a hand still on either can hold the pedal down or turn the bleeder, so the job is not finished; video); if the pedal or the wrench still moves faster than 0.2 rad/s (still settling; video); if the wrench is more than 10 degrees from shut, outside its shut detent (the bleeder left open can leak fluid onto the caliper; witness mark); or if the pedal is more than 8% of its stroke (2.6 mm at the pad) down or its piston not back, since that keeps the compensating port shut and seals the line off from the reservoir, so the brake can drag (ruler at the pad). Otherwise by the air left in a final state held 1 s, read in a real trial as 1.2 mL minus the jar's graduated tube: 1.0 at 0.2 mL or less, the firm pedal a technician checks for (four correct cycles leave 0.15 mL, three leave 0.25 mL); 0.5 at 0.36 mL or less, 70% out but the pedal still a little soft, so the car is not ready (three cycles; two leave 0.42 mL); 0.25 at 0.84 mL or less, at least 30% out, real progress but still spongy (one cycle leaves 0.72 mL); 0 above that. Doing nothing, pumping the pedal with the bleeder shut, or opening the bleeder without pressing leave all 1.2 mL in and score 0. Where the arms end up does not count. Possible scores: 0, 0.25, 0.5 and 1.0. The volumes are scaled (1.2 mL of air in an 8 mL line) so that a few cycles clear it.
metadata.reset_notes: Put the wrench back at shut (pointing -y) and the pedal up. In the real rig, inject 1.2 mL of air into the caliper by syringe through its fill port, refill and re-invert the graduated tube in the jar, and top the reservoir up to MAX.
metadata.fidelity: No fluid is simulated: a pressure model of the line, caliper, jar and reservoir tracks the air in the caliper, shown as a white disc on its top whose area follows it, with bubbles at the jar as air leaves. The pedal moves with that model: pressed, it stops where the line reaches 6 psi and sinks only as fluid leaves the open bleeder; let up, its piston draws on the line. A real trial reads the air from the jar's graduated tube and the pedal's travel from a ruler.

metadata.title: Set up a machine from its setup sheet and start it with a two-hand control
metadata.instruction: Set the machine up for program P2 as the setup sheet says, then start it.
metadata.context: Operating machinery is a core job on shop floors, in labs and in kitchens: before a run the operator sets the machine up from a printed setup sheet (program, set points, options) on its control panel, then starts it. Presses, cutters and other dangerous machines are started with a two-hand control, which by safety standards (ISO 13851) needs both hands on two buttons, pressed together and held, so one hand cannot be in the machine. The task checks that a robot can read the sheet, find the right line, work several kinds of controls (rocker switches, a detented dial, friction sliders) to the stated settings, and make the two-hand start only once the machine is set up.
metadata.setup: Coordinates: x forward from the line between the two arm bases, y to the left, from the midpoint between the bases. A control panel (busybox) stands loose on the table, centred at (30, 0) cm: a dark grey case 25 x 37 x 5 cm (x by y by z), 2.5 kg, with six 11 x 11 cm grey modules on top in two rows. Far row, left to right as seen from the arms: (1) four rocker switches, 33 x 15.6 mm white rockers in 5 mm black frames, rocking 20 degrees either way, far end down is ON, a red lamp above each lit while it is on, numbered 1 to 4 from left to right; (2) a dial, a black bar knob 42 x 12 x 18 mm on a 40 mm disk with a white pointer, 8 detents 45 degrees apart, numbers 1 to 8 clockwise with 1 pointing away from the arms; (3) two sliders, black knobs 12 x 20 x 16 mm moving 72 mm along x against 1 N of friction, marks 1 (near) to 5 (far) printed between them. Near row: (4) a big button, 56 mm white cap labelled START, 5 mm travel; (5) a keypad, a small display reading WATER above six 23 mm keys with Greek letters (not used); (6) four 26 mm buttons, red and green (far), yellow and blue (near), 4 mm travel. A serial sticker KD4XR7 is on the case's left side face. Start: dial at 3, left slider at 2, right slider at 4, switches 1 and 3 on, 2 and 4 off. A printed setup sheet, a 20 x 32 cm white card, lies flat on the table between the arm bases and the box, 1 cm short of the box, centred at (6.5, 0) cm, its text upright as read from the arms' side. It reads: SETUP SHEET; columns PROG, DIAL, LEFT SLIDER, RIGHT SLIDER, SWITCHES ON; P1: 2, 1, 5, 2 3; P2: 5, 4, 2, 1 4; P3: 7, 3, 3, 1 2 3; 'Other switches off.'; 'To start: press START and GREEN together, hold 2 s'.
metadata.scoring: 0.15 each for the dial, the left slider (nearest mark), the right slider (nearest mark) and the four switches set as program P2 says (dial 5, left slider 4, right slider 2, switches 1 and 4 on, 2 and 3 off), judged at the end; plus 0.4 for a two-hand start made while all four were right: START and the green button pressed down (beyond 60 % of their travel) within 0.5 s of each other and both held down together for 2 s. A start with wrong settings earns nothing; correcting them and starting again counts. Full score (1.0) ends the trial: started while set up, and still set up 1 s later. 0 if the red, yellow or blue button or a keypad key was pressed at any time.
metadata.reset_notes: Set the dial back to 3, the left slider to 2 and the right slider to 4, switches 1 and 3 on and 2 and 4 off, and put the box back on its mark. Nothing is consumed.
metadata.fidelity: Approximate: rigid case and parts that don't collide with the case or each other; joint limits bound their travel. Switches are bistable and the dial has detents (weak springs); sliders are held by 1 N of friction; buttons are springs (2-3 N at full travel), pressed beyond 60% of travel. Lamps follow the switches. The sheet is a thin fixed box with a printed texture. Presses are sampled at 20 Hz. The machine behind the panel is not modelled: the start is judged from the buttons and settings.

metadata.title: Keep a cable clear of a hot plate
metadata.instruction: The red disc is a hot plate. Put the lamp cable's plug into the white holder in front of the grey socket box. Never let any part of the cable touch or pass over the red disc, and leave the cable lying on the table at least 5 cm from the disc's edge.
metadata.context: Cords resting on hobs, heaters and soldering stations melt and cause home and workshop fires; a household or workshop robot tidying cables must respect a keep-out zone for the whole cable body during the motion, not just put the plug where it was asked.
metadata.setup: Station table, positions in cm from the midpoint between the two arm bases projected onto the table (x forward away from the robot, y to the robot's left). Hot plate: red 120 mm diameter, 1 mm thick disc (3D-printed PLA or red vinyl, a cold stand-in for a hot plate) centred at x 30, y 0, lying flat on the table. Lamp base: white 3D-printed PLA cylinder, 90 mm diameter, 60 mm tall, centred at x 21, y 30, clamped to the table. Lamp cable: black 8 mm round PVC cord, 60 cm from the lamp base to the plug, leaving the right-hand (-y) side of the lamp base at x 21, y 25.5, glued/strain-relieved into the base; it lies straight towards the right (-y) along x 21, so its surface is about 2.6 cm from the near edge of the red disc; its free end ends at x 21, y -34.5. Plug: black 3D-printed PLA box 35 x 16 x 12 mm (long side along the cable), epoxied on the cable end, 10 g. Plug holder: white 3D-printed PLA U-slot, inner floor 45 mm long (x) x 24 mm wide (y), side walls 4 mm thick and 8 mm tall, open towards the robot (-x end) and closed at the far end by the socket box; slot centre at x 30, y -24. Socket box: grey 60 x 90 x 50 mm box (e.g. a surface-mount electrical box), its robot-facing side at x 32.25, centred at y -24. Lamp base, disc, holder and socket box are fixed to the table.
metadata.scoring: Score 0 if at any moment of the trial any part of the cable or plug is over the red disc in top view (touching it, lying on it, or held in the air above it), judged from the top-camera video. This counts for the whole trial: putting the cable back where it started afterwards does not undo it. Also 0 unless at the end both grippers have let go (released = both gripper centres, between the finger pads, at least 3 cm from the plug centre and from every part of the cable). Otherwise, with the plug seated in the holder (plug inside the slot, lying on its floor, at most 4 mm above lying flat, sticking out of the open end by at most 1 cm) and released: 1.0 if the whole cable lies on the table (nowhere more than 2 cm above it) and every part of it is at least 5 cm from the disc's edge (tape measure, horizontal distance from the disc edge to the cable surface); 0.7 if every part is at least 3.5 cm from the disc's edge but the 1.0 condition does not hold; 0.4 if some part is closer than 3.5 cm. Plug not seated (also a plug held or resting near the slot) = 0. Success (1.0) when the full condition holds for 1 s with the cable at rest.
metadata.reset_notes: Lay the cable straight from the lamp base towards the right along x 21 cm (tape marks at y 25.5 and y -34.5 cm), plug at the right end with its long side along the cable and lying flat; remove anything from the slot. Check the red disc and holder are at their tape marks.
metadata.fidelity: Cable is 30 rigid 2 cm capsule segments with bending springs, no twist, no plasticity; plug is a rigid box welded to the last segment; the lamp-base end is welded to the world. The hot plate is a 1 mm thin fixed red cylinder with no heat; contact with it is judged geometrically (top-view overlap). Lamp base, holder and socket box are fixed rigid boxes/cylinders. The holder has no retention latch: the plug only has to lie in the slot.

metadata.title: Pass a cable through a panel grommet
metadata.instruction: Push the cable's plug through the black grommet in the grey upright panel, take it on the other side with the other arm, and pull the cable through until the red band on the cable sits at the grommet.
metadata.context: Feeding cables through bulkhead grommets and panel cut-outs is a core step when electricians and panel builders wire enclosures, cabinets and machines (O*NET 47-2111.00 Electricians; 51-2022.00 Electrical and Electronic Equipment Assemblers). The panel keeps each arm on its own side, so the plug has to be handed over through the hole and drawn out over the duct wall on the far side.
metadata.setup: Station table, positions in cm from the midpoint between the two arm bases projected onto the table (x forward away from the robot, y to the robot's left). Panel: grey 3D-printed PLA (or 6 mm plywood) wall 280 mm long, 100 mm tall, 6 mm thick, standing upright on the midline (its faces at y -0.3 and y +0.3, facing the two arms), running from x 16 to x 44, screwed to the table with two L-brackets on the far-side face near its ends. Grommet: black 3D-printed TPU square grommet, 38 x 38 mm outside, 26 x 26 mm square bore, 10 mm deep (sticks out 2 mm from each panel face), fitted in a 38 mm square window in the panel; bore centred at x 30, bore bottom 10 mm and bore top 36 mm above the table. Junction box: grey 40 x 40 x 30 mm 3D-printed PLA block, screwed to the table, centre at x 14.6, y 12.6, turned 45 deg so one face looks diagonally away from the robot to the left; the cable leaves the centre of that face at x 16, y 14, 6.5 mm above the table. Cable: black 6 mm round PVC-jacketed cable (e.g. LiYY 4 x 0.5 mm2), 40 cm from the junction box to the plug, glued/strain-relieved into the box, lying straight on the table at 45 deg (away from the robot and to the left), its end at x 44.3, y 42.3. Plug: black 3D-printed PLA box 60 x 16 x 12 mm (long side along the cable), epoxied on the cable end, 12 g. Red band: 20 mm wide red heat-shrink or tape on the cable, spanning 24-26 cm from the junction box (centre 25 cm). Duct wall: white 3D-printed PLA (or a strip of 10 mm plywood) bar 240 x 10 x 30 mm (x by y by height) on the far (right-arm) side, parallel to the panel, centred at x 30, spanning y -13 to -14, screwed to the table; it stands for the side wall of the wiring duct the cable continues into. Panel, grommet, junction box and duct wall are fixed; the cable starts on the left-arm (+y) side of the panel.
metadata.scoring: Measured at the end with a tape measure. 0 unless all of: (a) the cable passes through the grommet bore and crosses the panel line nowhere else (not round either end of the panel, not over its top); (b) the whole plug is beyond the grommet's far (right-arm) face; (c) the plug has been carried over the duct wall: its centre at least 14.5 cm behind the panel's mid-plane (5 mm beyond the wall's far face). If those hold: red band centre within 2 cm of the panel's mid-plane, measured along the cable = 1.0 (success, must hold 1 s); otherwise 0.3 + 0.5 x max(0, (15 cm - band distance) / 13 cm), where band distance is measured along the cable from the band centre to the panel (either side; 15 cm is where the band is when the cable end has just come through). Score 0 if the panel, grommet, duct wall or junction box is moved or damaged, the grommet is pushed out of the panel, or the cable is pulled out of the junction box. Holding the plug at the end is allowed.
metadata.reset_notes: Pull the cable back out of the grommet to the left-arm side and lay it straight from the junction box at 45 deg (tape marks at the box face and at the plug end, x 44.3, y 42.3), plug lying flat with its long side along the cable. Check the band is at 24-26 cm and the grommet is seated flush in the panel.
metadata.fidelity: Cable is 20 rigid 2 cm capsule segments with bending springs, no twist, no plasticity; plug is a rigid box welded to the last segment; the junction-box end is welded to the world. Panel, grommet and duct wall are fixed rigid boxes (the grommet is rigid in sim, rubber/TPU in the real kit; the bore is square, 5 mm clearance around the plug's width and 7 mm over its height). The red band is a colour on one 2 cm segment and is scored by arclength from the box.

metadata.title: Release a camera from a cam-clamped quick-release mount
metadata.instruction: Remove the camera and its attached plate from the bench mount and set the assembly upright on the green pad. Keep the camera attached to the plate, do not drop it, and leave the assembly released.
metadata.context: Camera and robotics technicians remove mounted sensors for servicing and reconfiguration. A passive cam and rear retaining edge must be cleared before the camera assembly can be transferred to a supported resting place.
metadata.setup: Fixed calibrated bimanual YAM station with a nominal wooden 1100x1300x60 mm tabletop centred (0.36,0,0.7175) m, tabletop z=0.7475 m, x forward and y left from the midpoint between arm bases. Secured nominal aluminium fixture root (0.28,0,0.7675) m with 110x110x8 mm foot, 26x26x8 mm post, 70x52x9 mm adapter, 54x6x6 mm aluminium rear rail, 54x10x3 mm aluminium rear lip, two 4x38x4 mm aluminium guides and two 6 mm diameter screws with 2 mm visible height. Passive 18 g cam: 24x14x7 mm orange-finished aluminium lever, 22x8x5 mm aluminium bridge, 28x8x4 mm steel toe and 8 mm diameter by 8 mm steel pivot; pivot offset (25,-30,17) mm from fixture root, initially zero rotation, positive travel 0.95 rad. Camera and aluminium 50x38x5 mm plate plus 12 mm diameter by 7 mm aluminium spacer form one 83 g payload, spawned with plate underside (0.28,0,0.7775) m and settled to z=0.7765 m before the initial image. Camera uses a licensed D405 appearance, nominal aluminium housing and a 23x42x42 mm collision box in its mounted orientation. Fixed green nominal polyurethane pad 130x110x4 mm centred (0.20,0.14,0.7495) m, top z=0.7515 m. No cable. All task-object initial orientations aligned with the world; both arms start at [0,1,1,-0.6,0,0] rad with grippers open. The fixed overhead observation rig includes a 110x110x16 mm steel support foot, 24 mm diameter mast (928.321 mm capsule spine), 18 mm diameter support arm (53.852 mm capsule spine) and 50x42x22 mm ABS camera housing. setup-layout.json gives every local/world pose and background part; build_scene.py gives custom colliders. Materials and aggregate masses are nominal reconstruction parameters, not calibrated manufacturer properties.
metadata.scoring: Highest applicable endpoint tier, overridden by any permanent invalidation; otherwise 0.0. Scored mount surfaces are the enclosing boxes of the foot, post, adapter, rear rail/lip, side guides and cam lever/bridge/toe/pivot; fixed screw heads do not define clearance. 0.25: cam >=0.8 rad, payload-to-scored-mount clearance <10 mm, native contact present. 0.5: clearance >=10 mm and native contact present, if the pad tier does not apply. 0.75: plate centre <=20 mm horizontally from pad centre, full payload collision envelope over the pad, plate underside within 5 mm of pad top, tilt <=10 degrees, native contact present. 1.0: the 0.75 conditions hold, every robot collision envelope is >=30 mm clear, and every pose over a full 1 s window stays within 2 mm and 2 degrees of the window's first pose. Permanently score zero for fixture translation >5 mm or rotation >5 degrees, cam anchor error >2 mm, cam angle outside [-0.01,0.96] rad, non-finite/non-unit state, any payload collision corner outside x=[-0.19,0.91], y=[-0.65,0.65], z=[0.7425,1.2475] m, or downward travel >10 mm during an uninterrupted absence of contact. Native contact presence uses >0.02 N at 240 Hz; no real force sensor is required: use visible support/release, a ruler, protractor and video. Cam/fixture angles use their declared zero poses; payload tilt uses world vertical; stability uses the window's first pose. Endpoint pose conditions and the 1 s stability window are sampled at 20 Hz. All parts must remain intact and attached as declared. README.md defines conservative bounding-envelope approximations and real-world interpretation.
metadata.reset_notes: Restore the single declared layout, initialize the passive cam at zero, reset both arms and settle for 0.5 simulated seconds. Jitter is disabled. No consumables.
metadata.fidelity: Nominal rigid cam-and-lip mechanism with simplified collision boxes and a licensed D405 visual. Camera, plate and spacer form one rigid body. No deformation, breakage, wear, cable or camera operation is modeled. Friction and cam damping are authored, not calibrated; no hardware trial is claimed. Contact/motion audits approximate no-drop scoring; bounding envelopes measure clearance. Dream-1 gateway retries and target clipping are documented in README.md.

metadata.title: Carry a stack of three boxes onto a shelf in one trip, squeezed between both arms
metadata.instruction: Move the stack of three boxes onto the shelf in one go, keeping them stacked the whole time: do not lift any box off the one below it.
metadata.context: Moving house or unpacking a delivery, people carry a short stack of boxes in one trip by squeezing the bottom box from both sides while the boxes above ride on it. The bottom box is wider than one gripper opens, so both arms must hold it. Unlike TK-4E4YZF (one wide box squeezed and lifted) and pilots TK-CTCQVY and TK-TH7NBJ (carries of one object), the hard part here is keeping two loose boxes on top in place through the squeeze, lift, carry and set-down.
metadata.setup: World frame for this text: 'in front' is away from the arm bases, 'left' and 'right' are from the robot's view, heights are above the table top, and the midline is halfway between the two arm bases. Boxes (loose, light-to-mid brown cardboard, modelled as solid rigid blocks): bottom box 200 mm wide (left to right), 120 mm deep (front to back) and 50 mm tall, 120 g; middle box 120 x 120 mm and 35 mm tall, 60 g; top box 80 x 80 mm and 30 mm tall, 40 g. They stand in one stack, edges square to the table, each box centred on the one below, the stack's centre 20.0 cm in front of the arm bases on the midline: the bottom box spans 14.0 to 26.0 cm in front of the bases and 10 cm either side of the midline. The stack's top is 115 mm high. Shelf (fixed, grey painted wood, a solid block): 160 mm deep, 240 mm wide and 60 mm tall, spanning 29.0 to 45.0 cm in front of the bases and 12 cm either side of the midline, so its front face is 30 mm beyond the bottom box's far face. The gripper opens to at most 94 mm between its pads, less than either footprint side of the bottom box. Nothing else is on the table.
metadata.scoring:
Judged from the video and a ruler. Limits are inclusive.
Broken stack (score 0 for the whole trial): at any moment an upper box lifts more than 5 mm off the box below, slides more than 25 mm off its centre, or tilts more than 15 degrees. So carrying the boxes one at a time, or taking the upper boxes off and putting them back, scores 0.
Standing stack: all three boxes level (within 5 degrees) and still, each upper box resting on the one below.
1.0: never broken; standing on the shelf with the bottom box fully on the shelf top; each upper box within 10 mm of centre on the box below.
0.5: never broken; standing on the shelf with the bottom box's centre over the shelf top, but it overhangs an edge or an upper box is 10 to 25 mm off centre.
0.25: never broken; the stack was lifted as one (bottom box at least 20 mm off the table) and now stands on the table at least 30 mm from where it started, upper boxes within 25 mm of centre.
0 otherwise (stack not lifted, held more than 1 mm above the shelf, any box knocked off, or broken). Setting the stack down and regripping is allowed. The trial ends at 1.0 once that holds for 1 s. Exact definitions are in README.md.
metadata.reset_notes: Restack the three boxes at the start position, edges square to the table, each centred on the one below. Nothing is consumed.
metadata.fidelity: Approximate. The boxes are solid rigid blocks of the stated mass, smaller than moving boxes, with no flaps, contents or give, and rubber-like friction (1.2 static, 1.0 sliding), well above cardboard's, so upper boxes slide less than real ones. The upper boxes are narrower than the bottom one, so a squeeze on its sides leaves them free; the closed fingers widen upward, so the scripted squeeze presses on its top edges. The shelf is a solid block.

metadata.title: Snap a chalk line between two marks: pull it taut, pluck it straight up
metadata.instruction: Snap a chalk line between the two marks. The hook is on the far nail. Pull the reel to the near mark and hold the line taut across both marks, then lift the line straight up at its middle and let it go. Put the reel on its rest.
metadata.context: Carpenters (O*NET 47-2031) mark long straight lines by snapping a chalk line. One hand must keep it taut on the mark while the other lifts it straight up and lets go, and a slack line or a sideways pluck leaves a bowed or doubled print.
metadata.setup: Two YAM arms at the near edge of a table; positions are (x forward from the arm bases, y left) in cm, heights above the table. A board of MDF painted matt dark slate, 16 x 76 cm, 1.2 thick, centred at (33, 0), fixed to the table. Yellow cross marks at (33, 30) and (33, -30). A steel nail at the far mark, (33, 30), holds the hook of a bright orange braided polyester chalk line, 1.5 mm thick (drawn 7 mm thick so that it shows on camera), 1 cm above the board. A blue plastic chalk reel, 7.2 cm across, 4 tall, 0.2 kg with its chalk, stands on a grey rest, 9 x 9 cm and 3 high, fixed at (20, -30). Its case is a third full of white marking chalk, which coats the line as it pays out. The line leaves the reel at a nose on its +y side, 8 mm above the reel's base. Its crank is locked with 59.5 cm of line out from the nail, just short of the near mark's centre, so a reel pulled there holds the line taut. The line stretches less than 5 mm at 10 N. Held taut at 5 to 10 N, lifted at least 4 cm at its middle and let go, it strikes the board along its length.
metadata.scoring: Measured with a tape and a phone video. 1.0 when one snap leaves a white chalk line which, run on straight, passes within 5 mm of the near mark, bowed by at most 1 cm from straight, the reel stands on its rest, and fingers are at least 3 cm from the reel, for 1 s. 0.75 when one snap leaves a white chalk line passing within 5 mm of the near mark, bowed by at most 1 cm, but the reel is not on its rest or a finger is closer than 3 cm. 0.5 when it passes 5 to 15 mm from the near mark, bowed by at most 1 cm. 0 if there is no print, two prints, or the line is bowed more than 1 cm or passes more than 15 mm from the near mark. Letting go of a slack line leaves a bowed print.
metadata.reset_notes: Wipe the board, or turn it over. Rewind the reel to its lock, and stand it on its rest with the hook on the nail. Chalk is consumed.
metadata.fidelity: Rigid-body physics at 240 Hz on GPU. The line is drawn as straight segments, not a soft cable, with no collider, tension or stretch. It is pinched when closed fingers come within 2 cm of it. The print appears at a release at least 4 cm above the line's path. Taut needs a gripper closed on the reel and the nose 59.5 cm from the nail. A pluck over 1 cm sideways counts as bowed. Not tested on a real board, where a line 1 cm up may print less at its ends.

metadata.title: Take the cap off a child-resistant medicine bottle
metadata.instruction: Take the cap off the medicine bottle.
metadata.context: Most prescription medicines come in child-resistant vials, and many older people with stiff hands can't open them, so a robot helping at home has to. The common push-and-turn cap only unscrews while pressed down; turned without pressing, it just spins. Its top says PUSH DOWN & TURN. The vial stands free, so the robot should also keep it still, for example with its other arm. Doing nothing, or turning without pressing, scores 0.
metadata.setup: Positions in cm from the midpoint between the arm bases: x forward, y to the robot's left; heights above the table top. An amber pharmacy vial, 4.6 cm across with an 8.8 cm body (10.6 cm tall with its cap), holding pills (about 80 g, 90 g with its cap), stands free (not taped) with its centre at (34, 0). A white pharmacy label runs round its front: PHARMACY and Rx 0427 in a blue band, TAKE 1 TABLET BY MOUTH DAILY, and KEEP OUT OF REACH OF CHILDREN in an orange band. Its own push-and-turn child-resistant cap is on: white, 5.1 cm across and 2.2 cm tall, with a ribbed side and PUSH DOWN & TURN printed round an anticlockwise arrow on top. The cap presses down about 3 mm (2.4 N at the bottom in simulation; real caps are likely stiffer, so choose one the robot can press, and measure it) and comes free after about half a turn anticlockwise while pressed; turned without pressing, its outer shell spins and nothing unscrews; turned clockwise, it tightens. Both arms start at the ready pose with open grippers.
metadata.scoring: Judged from the video and, at the end, a photo and one hand test. 1.0 (success, held 2 s): the cap is off the vial (held or put down), no pills spilled, and the vial was never knocked over. 0.5: the cap is still on the neck but loose (lifted straight up by hand at the end, without pressing or turning, it comes off), vial never knocked over. 0: anything else, including doing nothing, turning without pressing however far, a cap screwed back on, and knocking the vial over at any time (tilted more than 45 degrees, even if stood up again). A vial lifted or held upright is not knocked over.
metadata.reset_notes: Put the cap back on and turn it clockwise until tight (it tightens without pressing); check that it doesn't open without pressing, and stand the vial on its mark.
metadata.fidelity: Rigid bodies, 240 Hz physics, 20 Hz control. The vial is a floating articulation standing free; pills are only mass. The cap has three joints: a 3 mm spring press, a free spin and a lift. The lock is task code: seated, the cap's turn relative to the vial counts anticlockwise only while pressed past 2 mm, clockwise always; after half a turn the lift unlocks. The freed cap lifts straight up its axis and counts as off once 1.5 cm up.
metadata.scores: Dream-1 run: 0.0 (both arms went to the vial; once it pushed the cap past the unlocking depth but turned it only about 3 degrees while pressing, so nothing came loose); demo: 1.0

metadata.title: Clear a photo-eye's beam
metadata.instruction: Clear the beam between the black photo-eye and the red reflector. Move only the cartons that block it, each no more than 10 cm, and leave every carton standing.
metadata.context: Packaging and conveyor lines stop when something breaks a photo-eye's beam to its reflector. The fix is to clear the line between the two without disturbing anything else on the line: nothing marks the beam, so the operator has to judge which items are actually in it and which only look close. Done by: packaging and filling machine operators.
metadata.setup: Positions are in cm on the table, from the midpoint between the two arm bases: x forward (away from the arms), y to the robot's left. A black plastic photo-eye on a black post (3 x 3 cm, 7 cm tall, housing and post as one block) is fixed at x 16, y 10, and a red plastic reflector on an identical red post is fixed at x 42, y 30; the two are turned to face each other, so the beam runs straight between them, 4 cm above the table, with nothing marking it. Four blue cardboard cartons (6 x 6 cm across, 8 cm tall, 150 g each) stand upright, square to the table edge, centred at (23.9, 12.1), (21.0, 23.9), (34.1, 16.1) and (35.1, 26.6). Nothing else is on the table.
metadata.scoring: The beam is the straight line from the photo-eye's post to the reflector's, 4 cm above the table; a carton blocks it if any part of it comes within 1 cm of that line. At the start, the cartons at (23.9, 12.1) and (35.1, 26.6) block it (the first only clips it, by 1 cm); the other two stand 2.0 cm and 3.8 cm clear of it. A carton is standing when its 8 cm axis is within 10 degrees of vertical (either way up) and its lowest point is within 3 mm of the table; it is still when it moves under 1 cm/s and turns under 0.5 rad/s; it is off the table when its lowest point is more than 1 cm below the table top. A carton is untouched when its centre is within 5 mm of where it stood and it has turned at most 5 degrees; a moved carton is measured centre to centre. 1.0 if, at the end, no carton blocks the beam, the two blocking cartons were each moved at most 10 cm, the other two are untouched, and every carton is standing and still. 0.5 if the beam is clear, the other two are untouched and every carton is standing and still, but a blocking carton was moved more than 10 cm. 0.25 if one of the two blocking cartons was moved clear (at most 10 cm) and is still, with the other two untouched. 0 otherwise: if either carton that didn't block the beam was moved, or any carton ends knocked over or off the table.
metadata.reset_notes: Stand the four cartons back at their marks, square to the table edge.
metadata.fidelity: No light is simulated: the beam is the straight line between the two posts, and the score checks it geometrically, with 1 cm to spare for the beam's width. The posts are fixed blocks with no lens or reflector face. The cartons are rigid boxes; every object has the same rubber-like friction (1.2 static, 1.0 dynamic), more than cardboard on a conveyor.

metadata.title: Clip a spring-hinged fingertip pulse oximeter onto a patient's index finger while steadying the hand
metadata.instruction: Put the pulse oximeter all the way onto the manikin hand's index finger without dragging the hand.
metadata.context: Taking vital signs, SpO2 by fingertip pulse oximeter included, is a core duty of nursing assistants (O*NET 31-1131.00: 'Record vital signs, such as temperature, blood pressure, pulse...'; about 1.4 million US jobs, BLS May 2024) and medical assistants (31-9092.00: 'measure their vital signs'; 811,000, BLS 2024), repeated every round of every shift. Errors: the fingertip stops short of the probe's stop, so the light misses the nail bed and the reading fails; the clip goes on the wrong finger or upside down; the patient's limp hand is tugged. The clip has to be squeezed open and kept open while it slides over a fingertip with only 2-3 mm to spare, then let go so its spring clamps. The patient's hand is light and loose on an elevation wedge and slides when pushed, so the other hand steadies it. Unlike #732 (a rigid sleeve; the hard part was deciding how to answer an alarm), this tests the squeeze-slide-release on a working spring clip.
metadata.setup: Metres; world x forward, y left, z up; origin midway between the arm bases (0,+/-0.305,0.750); table top z=0.7475. (1) Arm-elevation wedge, fixed (taped down): firm polyurethane foam, vinyl covered, 250 mm wide (x 0.085..0.335), sloping 20 deg up toward -y: 5 mm thick at its low end (y=0.141), 66.6 mm at its high edge (y=-0.028), 180 mm along the slope, a vertical face below the high edge.
