metadata.instruction: At the meter test switch: open the three switches with black handles and the one with the white handle at the right end, then the orange switch at the left end, then the red switch next to it, and push the red test plug into the red switch's jack. Do not open the red switch while the orange one is closed. Leave the other switches closed.
metadata.context: Before a revenue meter is tested or changed, its current-transformer circuit is shorted at the meter test switch. Opening the test-jack switch before the short is made, or removing the short while the test jack is open and no plug carries the current, open-circuits a live CT secondary, which can produce a dangerous voltage and arc.
metadata.setup: Positions are from the arm bases (forward of the line joining the two bases, which are 61 cm apart; left or right of their midline as seen from behind the robot; heights above the table top). Wall: a grey 6 mm steel plate (40 cm wide, 30 cm tall) standing upright on the table and fixed to it, its front face 38.9 cm in front of the bases, centred on the midline; it stands in for a meter box's back wall. Test switch: a 10-pole ANSI C12.9 meter test switch laid out as TESCO drawing 909884, outline as the Milbank TS10-0109 (black phenolic base 24.1 cm wide, 8.9 cm tall, 1.9 cm thick), mounted on the wall long side left-right, its front face 37 cm in front of the bases, centred on the midline 14.5 cm above the table. Its ten poles stand vertically at 1.905 cm pitch; numbered 1 to 10 from left to right they are centred 8.6, 6.7, 4.8, 2.9 and 1.0 cm left and 1.0, 2.9, 4.8, 6.7 and 8.6 cm right of the midline. Each pole is a tinned copper knife blade hinged 1.8 cm below the base's centre and 2 cm out from its face; closed, it stands vertical with its top end held in a spring jaw, and a moulded handle 12.7 mm wide and 25 mm tall stands 2.5 to 5.5 cm out from the face near the blade's top (handle tops 17.7 cm above the table). Handle colours by pole: 1 orange (phase-A short-circuiting), 2 red (phase-A test jack), 3 black (phase-A voltage), 4 yellow (phase-B short-circuiting), 5 green (phase-B test jack), 6 black (phase-B voltage), 7 brown (phase-C short-circuiting), 8 blue (phase-C test jack), 9 black (phase-C voltage), 10 white (neutral voltage). All ten start closed. A blade is opened by pulling its handle out and down; it swings over about 160 degrees and hangs below the base. Black phenolic barriers (2 mm thick, standing 5.1 cm out, 10.2 cm tall) stand on both sides of poles 3, 6 and 9. Poles 2, 5 and 8 each have a test jack at mid-pole: two spring leaves (12.7 mm along the pole, each with the C12.9 guide notch) standing 3.4 cm out from the face, with a 3 cm deep slot between them that opens toward the robot; a closed blade lies in the bottom of that slot. Test plug: a single current test plug of the TESCO 1077 class (60 g): a flat two-conductor probe 30.5 mm long, 11 mm wide and 3.3 mm thick with the C12.9 guide rib, a 24 x 14 x 4 mm guard, and a red insulated handle 90 mm long, 22 x 14 mm in section. It lies on a grey plastic U-channel rest (8.5 cm long, on a 2 cm square column with a 5 x 5 cm foot), the handle's centre 20 cm in front of the bases, 17 cm left of the midline and 14 cm above the table, the probe pointing forward with its flat faces vertical. Test lead: a black 2-conductor PVC lead 6 mm across, 60 cm of free length, runs from the rear end of the plug's handle down behind the rest and along the table to a test set: a yellow box 20 x 15 x 10 cm (standing in for a portable meter test set), fixed to the table, centred 36 cm in front of the bases and 46 cm left of the midline; the lead leaves its right side 32 cm in front of the bases and 2.5 cm above the table. Both arms start at the ready pose with their grippers open. One fixed layout, as in the screenshot.
metadata.scoring: A switch counts as open when its blade has swung 60 degrees or more from closed. Score 0 if, at any time before the after-release check: a test-jack blade (red, green or blue) is 8 degrees or more out of its jaw while that phase's short-circuiting blade (orange, yellow or brown) is within 3 degrees of closed and no plug is seated in that jack (the CT secondary would be open-circuited); or any phase-B or phase-C current switch (yellow, green, brown or blue) moves 5 degrees or more. Otherwise the score is the highest level reached: 0.25 if all four voltage switches (the three black and the white) are open, in any order; 0.5 if the orange and red switches are also open; 0.75 if the test plug is also seated in the red switch's jack (the probe pinched between both leaves, its tip within 20 mm of the base's face, and its flat within 15 degrees of the jack's plane); 1.0 if the after-release check also passes. If the probe is pushed into a test jack whose blade is still closed, the score stays at the level already reached. Dropping the plug is not penalised by itself. After-release check, once both grippers have been at least 6 cm from the plug's handle for 1 s: push the red handle back toward closed with a spring scale at 6 N (about 0.3 N m about the hinge) for 1.5 s. It passes if the plug stops the blade 30 degrees or more from closed, the probe is still in the jack and the voltage switches are still open; if not, the score is 0.75. Angles are read from a side photo with a protractor template.
metadata.reset_notes: Pull the test plug out of the red jack and lay it back on its rest, with the lead along its starting path. Swing each open blade up and press it into its jaw in this order: red, then orange, then the voltage switches, so the CT is never left open-circuited. Check that all ten are closed. About 1.5 minutes.
metadata.fidelity: PhysX rigid bodies on joints at real size (19.05 mm pitch, barriers per C12.9; no CAD, box colliders). Jaw breakout 0.2 N·m and jack spring leaves (~2.9 N) inferred; C12.9 guide rib keeps the plug seated. No circuit: CT short/open are rules on blade angles. Sourced order enforced (short-circuiting switch before test-jack switch); voltage switches free. Phase A only; final push-back step omitted; lead is jointed capsules; check in sim after recording. Details in README.

metadata.title: Drag a file into the green folder on a computer screen with a real mouse
metadata.instruction: Using the mouse, drag the red file into the green folder on the screen, then let go of the mouse.
metadata.context: Dragging a file into a folder with a mouse is an everyday task for most people. For a robot the hard part is the hand: 1 mm of mouse travel moves the pointer 31.5 pixels, so the drop must land within about 2 mm of travel, while the button stays held through the move and the mouse stays flat on its mat, since a lifted sensor stops the pointer. The nearest task elsewhere is the DexJoCo suite's 'Click Mouse', which sets a mouse on its pad and clicks it; here the button is held through a drag, and the file is landed on a folder within about 2 mm of mouse travel by watching the on-screen pointer. One arm can do it; two are allowed.
metadata.setup: Two YAM arms at the near edge of a table; positions are (x forward from the arm bases, y left) in cm, heights above the table. A 24-inch 1920 x 1080 monitor (picture 53.1 x 29.9 cm, black housing with 0.9 cm bezels and a 2 cm chin) on a grey stand with a 17 x 24 cm foot, its picture's bottom edge at x 57, centred on y 0, 4.5 cm up, leaned back 20 degrees. The desktop has a dark blue wallpaper; along its top, four folder icons 150 px across (4.2 cm on the panel), their centres 250 px from the top and 420, 780, 1140 and 1500 px from the left, coloured blue, green, yellow and purple with the desktop's folder-colour option, in an order set by the seed; a red document icon, 110 x 140 px, in the lower part of the screen; and the pointer at a large accessibility size, about 145 px tall. The file's and the pointer's places are set by the seed. On a dark cloth mouse mat, 24 cm along x by 26 cm along y and 3 mm thick, centred at (34, -13), a wireless optical mouse, 116 x 62 x 38 mm and 85 g, matte dark grey plastic on PTFE feet, its left button clicking at 0.6 N after 0.4 mm of travel. The mouse starts within 2 cm of the mat's centre along each axis, turned up to 8 degrees, by seed. The mat is taped to the table. Pointer speed: 31.5 px per mm of mouse travel (a 1,600 cpi sensor at a 0.5 multiplier), acceleration off. The screenshot shows seed 1.
metadata.scoring: Read from a screen recording and a video of the table and hands, in sync. The file goes into a folder when the button comes up while the file is being dragged (it has moved 6 px or more with the button held on it) and the pointer's tip is on that folder's icon (150 x 128 px). 1.0 when the file is in the green folder, the button is up, every finger is at least 1 cm from the mouse, and the mouse is on its mat and upright (tilted 30 degrees or less), held for 1 s. 0.5 when the file is in the green folder but that end state is not held for 1 s. 0.25 when the file has been let go on the desktop with its centre at most half as far, in a straight line, from the green folder's centre as at the start. 0 otherwise. 0 also if at any moment the file is dropped into another folder, a folder is dragged, a folder or the file is opened by a double click (two clicks within 0.5 s and 10 px), the mouse leaves its mat (its centre goes past the mat's edge, or it tilts over 30 degrees; lifting it level over the mat is allowed), or a finger touches the monitor.
metadata.reset_notes: Nothing is consumed. Move the file back out of the folder to its start, and set the folders' order and the pointer's start for the seed, by hand or with a short script. Set the mouse on the mat. Before trials, check the pointer speed: with acceleration off and the pointer near the screen's left edge, slide the mouse 50 mm to the right along a ruler; the pointer must move 1,575 px.
metadata.fidelity: Rigid-body physics at 240 Hz on GPU. The mouse is a free body; its left button is a sprung shell (1,500 N/m, a 0.6 mm stop), closing at 0.4 mm (0.6 N) and opening when the press falls below 0.3 mm. The screen is drawn by code from the sensor: its motion in the mouse's own axes times 31.5 px per mm, counted only within 1.5 mm of the mat; a drag starts after 6 px with the button held. Friction: feet on mat 0.15, fingertip on shell 0.6. No mouse cable.

metadata.title: Move a lamp closer before pulling its plug to a tray
metadata.instruction: Put the desk lamp's plug in the green tray.
metadata.context: Yanking a cord that is still attached to a light, top-heavy device drags it across the table, knocks it over or pulls it off the edge (broken lamps, burns, falling objects). A household or office robot handling appliance cords has to notice that the cord is a tether to another object and reposition that object before pulling, instead of treating the plug as a free item to carry.
metadata.setup: Station table, positions in cm from the midpoint between the two arm bases projected onto the table (x forward away from the robot, y to the robot's left). Desk lamp: cream 3D-printed PLA cylinder, 60 mm diameter, 140 mm tall, weighted to 200 g, free-standing (not fixed), centred at x 32, y 20. Power cord: black 6 mm round PVC cord, 32 cm long, glued/strain-relieved into the lamp at the bottom of its right-hand (-y) side (x 32, y 17, at table level); it lies straight towards the right (-y) along x 32 and ends at y -15. Plug: black 3D-printed PLA box 35 x 16 x 12 mm (long side along the cord), epoxied on the cord end, 12 g, lying flat; its centre is at x 32, y -16.75. Tray: green open tray (3D-printed PLA or a plastic box lid), inner floor 80 mm (x) x 100 mm (y), 4 mm floor, 3 mm walls 15 mm tall, centred at x 15, y -28, fixed to the table. The tray centre is 51 cm from the lamp's centre, while the plug can be at most 37 cm from it with the cord pulled taut, so the plug cannot reach the tray unless the lamp is moved.
metadata.scoring: Score 0 if at any moment of the trial the lamp leans more than 20 degrees from vertical (tips over), falls off the table (centre drops more than 2 cm below the table top), or slides along the table more than 3 cm from the spot where it was standing (the lamp may only be moved by lifting it off the table and setting it down; dragging it by the cord or pushing it along the table counts as sliding), judged from the top-camera video with tape marks. Such a violation counts for the whole trial: setting the lamp back afterwards does not undo it. Also 0 if the cord is pulled out of the lamp or the tray is moved, and 0 if at the end either gripper still holds or touches the plug, the cord or the lamp (released = both gripper centres, between the finger pads, at least 3 cm from all three). Otherwise: 1.0 if at the end the plug lies in the tray (plug centre over the inner floor at least 5 mm in from the walls, at most 6 mm above lying flat on the floor) and the lamp stands upright on the table (base within 5 mm of the table, leaning at most 5 degrees, not on or in the tray). 0.3 if the lamp stands upright on the table (same conditions) with its centre at least 10 cm closer to the tray centre than at the start (at most 41 cm from it), but the plug is not in the tray: the lamp was moved safely, the plug was not delivered. Anything else = 0. Success (1.0) when the full condition holds for 1 s with the lamp and cord at rest.
metadata.reset_notes: Stand the lamp on its tape mark (circle centred at x 32, y 20) with the cord exit facing right (-y); lay the cord straight to the right along x 32 with the plug flat at the end (tape mark at y -15 for the cord end). Empty the tray and check it is at its tape mark.
metadata.fidelity: The cord is 16 rigid 2 cm capsule segments with bending springs, no twist, no plasticity; its first segment is welded to the lamp's bottom edge and the plug (rigid box) to its last segment. The lamp is a single uniform rigid cylinder (no shade, stem or bulb; its centre of mass is at mid-height). The tray is fixed. Friction is rubber-like (static 1.2) for the lamp and 0.8 for the cord.

metadata.title: Move a live wire off a walkway with an insulated stick
metadata.instruction: The red cable is live. Without touching the cable or its plug with the grippers or any part of the arms, use the blue insulated stick to push the whole cable off the yellow walkway so that its plug ends up inside the green parking zone.
metadata.context: Electricians, line workers and first responders (O*NET 47-2111 Electricians, 49-9051 Electrical Power-Line Installers) clear energised conductors with insulated hot sticks rather than bare hands; a robot must pick the tool and respect a hard no-contact rule while manipulating a deformable cable.
metadata.setup: Station table; cm from the midpoint between the arm bases on the table (x forward, y left). Walkway: yellow vinyl tape stripe 15 cm wide from x 22.5 to 37.5, across the table (y -48..48). Junction box: grey 5 x 7 x 4 cm box, rotated 40 deg clockwise, fixed to the table; the cable leaves its face at x 17, y 12. Cable: red 8 mm round PVC cord, 30 cm, glued into the box, lying straight forward-right at 40 deg clockwise from +x across the walkway; black 35 x 16 x 12 mm PLA plug (10 g) on its free end, centre at x 41.3, y -8.4. Parking zone: green 12 mm tape outlining the inner rectangle x 11.5..21.5, y -25.5..-13.5. Stick: blue hollow square fibreglass rod 30 x 2 x 2 cm, 60 g, lying along x centred at x 33, y -31.5.
metadata.scoring: 0 if any gripper finger or other robot part ever touches the cable or plug (judged from the videos; in sim, any PhysX robot-link/cable contact at any physics step). Else 1.0 if at the end no part of the cable or plug lies over the yellow tape in top view, the plug centre is inside the green zone and the cable lies on the table (nowhere >2 cm up). Else let L = cable length over the tape (20.6 cm at start): if L dropped by at least 3 cm, 0.8 x (20.6 - L)/20.6; otherwise 0.
metadata.reset_notes: Lay the cable straight from the junction box at 40 deg clockwise from the forward axis (tape marks at the box exit and under the plug centre x 41.3, y -8.4), plug flat; put the stick back along x at its tape mark (centre x 33, y -31.5). Check the junction box and tapes are at their marks. A real trial uses an unpowered cable; contact is judged from the videos.
metadata.fidelity: Cable: 15 rigid 2 cm segments with bending springs, no twist, no plasticity; plug a rigid box welded to the end; the box end welded to the world. The cable is not energised; touching is checked as any robot-cable contact at every 240 Hz physics step. Tapes are 0.6 mm fixed boxes. Stick: rigid box, default friction.

metadata.title: Fit an O-ring onto a hydraulic plug: stretch it over the thread by no more than 50%, seat it square and untwisted
metadata.instruction: Fit the O-ring into the groove at the base of the plug's thread.
metadata.context: Industrial machinery mechanics, machinery maintenance workers and millwrights (about 547,300 US jobs in 2025, BLS Occupational Outlook Handbook) keep plant hydraulics running, and fitting a new O-ring onto a straight-thread O-ring boss (ORB) fitting or plug is a routine part of hydraulic repair. The ring sits in a groove between the thread and the hex. It is stretched only as far as it takes to pass over the thread, carried down square to the groove and let close into it, then checked seated all the way round. A ring stretched too far takes a permanent set and its thinner section no longer seals. One pushed or rolled down the thread twists. One let go tilted leaves a side on the thread, where it can be cut when the plug is screwed into its port. Here it is the AS568-924 90-durometer FKM ring of a -24 (1.875 inch thread) boss plug.
metadata.setup: Positions are in cm from the midpoint between the two arm bases, with x forward, y to the robot's left and the table top at z 0. A blue anodized aluminum bench holder 9 x 9 x 4 cm is fixed to the table, centered at x 34, y -10. Standing hex-down on it on the axis x 34, y -10 is a zinc-plated steel SAE J1926 -24 O-ring boss hex plug: a 2.25 inch (57.15 mm across flats) hex from z 4.0 to 5.4, then the O-ring groove (undercut) 3.6 mm long with a 44.2 mm diameter from z 5.4 to 5.76, its lower wall the hex face, then the 1.875-12 UN thread, 47.6 mm across the crests, from z 5.76 up to the plug's flat end face at z 7.66 with a 1.5 mm chamfer. The O-ring is an AS568-924 bright blue 90-durometer fluorocarbon (FKM) O-ring, 43.7 mm inside diameter with a 3.0 mm section; it lies flat and centered on the plug's end face (z 7.66 to 7.96). Nothing else is on the table; both arms start at their home poses with the grippers open.
metadata.scoring: The score is the ring's final condition, after two damage checks. Doing nothing scores 0. Over-stretch: 0, irreversible, if the ring's inside diameter ever passed 65.5 mm, 50% stretch. Machinery's Handbook advises against stretching an O-ring's inside diameter more than 50% to install it, since a ring stretched further takes a permanent set and no longer fills its groove. In the sim the stretch is the loop round one gripper's two fingertips (and the thread once both are outside it), which reaches 50% at a 73.7 mm pad gap. A real trial measures it the same way: the gripper's logged opening over 73.7 mm while the ring is round the thread (80.9 mm while it is still above the end face) scores 0. That log is the main measure, since it catches a brief stretch the ring may not keep. A two-hand stretch is outside the sim's model; a real trial reads it from both arms' logged fingertip positions or the cone. The secondary check is the ring itself: rolled off after the trial, it is dropped on a sizing cone marked in 0.5 mm diameters beside an unused ring from the same bag; one that settles at a larger diameter has taken a set. Twist: 0 if the ring is left with more than 90 degrees of roll. A ring pushed down the thread instead of stretched over it rolls, 38 degrees per mm for its 3.0 mm section, and after a quarter turn (2.4 mm) its mold parting line has moved from its outside onto its face. A twisted ring can spiral in the groove and leak, so a fitter replaces it. The sim models the roll; a real trial checks the parting line by eye and on the top photo. 1.0: seated, in the groove all round (so square, with no side on the thread), closed onto its 44.2 mm bottom, untwisted (90 degrees of roll or less), with no fingertip left in it, since a ring held open on the fingers has not closed into the groove, and no gripper touching it. Only the ring as it ends is judged, however it got there: let go square, stretched again and let go square, or pressed down. 0.75: seated just as for 1.0, but a gripper still touches the ring at the end. In the sim that is contact, not nearness: the gripper's own shape (palm, fingers and pads at their present opening) within 2 mm of the ring, the solver's resting gap plus the fit of the shapes to the gripper's meshes. The fit is right but not handed off, since a hand still on the ring can still roll it out of the groove, so it is worth less than a ring let go and left alone, and more than a ring at the groove that is not yet seated (0.5). A real trial checks the last top and wrist camera frames for any part of the gripper resting on the ring. 0.5: at the groove (its middle within the 3.6 mm groove) but still on the fingertips or with one side on the thread. That ring is undamaged and only needs closing or pushing square, so it is half the job. In the sim a ring let go more than 4 degrees off square lands that way: across its 50 mm the tilt lifts the far side 3.5 mm, more than its 3.0 mm section, so that side closes onto the thread just above the groove. As a fitter does, a fingertip pressing that high side down 1.5 mm (half its section) pushes it over the last crest, and the ring's own tension pulls it into the groove. The press rolls it 57 degrees (1.5 mm), under the 90-degree limit, so a ring fixed that way is seated and scores 1.0. This press law is a stand-in for a real press, so a real trial scores the ring that results, not the press. A real trial checks the final ring on the top photo (visible in the groove all round, parting line straight) and by a fingertip run round it. 0.25: stretched over the thread and, at the end, still at least 5 mm down it, not at the groove (where it is then, not the deepest it reached). Its middle is then 3.5 mm past the 1.5 mm chamfer, over more than a full 2.1 mm thread pitch, so it is clearly started, undamaged, a quarter of the job; a real trial reads it against the mm scale on the holder. Else 0. Where the arms end is not scored. Possible scores: 0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1.0.
metadata.reset_notes: Roll the ring out of the groove with a plastic O-ring pick (never a metal one), check it on the sizing cone against an unused ring from the same bag and its parting line straight, and replace it if not (rings are cheap and over-stretched ones are scrapped). Lay it flat and centered on the plug's end face.
metadata.fidelity: The ring has no contact simulation: its place along the plug, stretch and twist are a model driven by one gripper's two fingertips (a two-hand stretch is not modeled). It is tied to the plug's axis, a stand-in for fingertips keeping it centered, and a 1.5 mm fingertip press on a cocked side seats it by a rule standing in for a real press. A real trial reads stretch from the logged pad gap (a sizing cone second) and checks the top photo: the ring in the groove all round, parting line untwisted.

metadata.title: Slide the drain pan under the engine before pulling its drain plug
metadata.instruction: The engine is cold. Drain its oil.
metadata.context: Small engine mechanics and automotive lube technicians change oil every day (O*NET 49-3053.00, 49-3023.00). The drain pan goes under the outlet before the plug comes out. Once the plug is out, the oil pours out at once, and threading the plug back in against a hot stream isn't practical, so a late pan means oil on the floor. That is a slip hazard, and used oil spills must be cleaned up under EPA used-oil rules (40 CFR 279.22). The pan stays under the outlet while the engine drains. The plug goes in the parts dish so it isn't lost in the oil. The instruction names none of this.
metadata.setup: Positions are in cm from the midpoint between the two arm bases, with x forward, y to the robot's left and the table top at z 0. A fixed single-cylinder engine, 19 cm tall (gray crankcase, finned cylinder lying back, red fuel tank, black air filter, muffler and recoil starter), sits on a wooden stand 4 cm tall at the back of the bench. The crankcase's front face is at x 28.5, spanning y -8 to 14, and the stand's front edge is at x 29.5. A zinc drain pipe, 1.5 cm across, sticks out 3 cm from that face toward the arms at y 6, its axis 6.5 cm above the bench; its outlet is at x 25.5. Higher on the same face, at y -4.5 and 9 cm above the bench, is a yellow oil-fill cap with dipstick. It is closed by a steel hex-head drain plug (2 cm across the flats, 1.2 cm long, with a copper washer and a 2.5 cm shank inside the pipe; 30 g). A black plastic oil drain pan, 11.8 cm across and 3 cm deep, 80 g, with a molded grab handle (2.2 x 3 x 2.2 cm) on the side toward the robot, rests centered at x 23.5, y 20. A fixed steel parts dish, 7.6 cm across and 1.4 cm deep, is at x 25, y -8.
metadata.scoring: The scorer watches the whole run. The plug is out once its head is 2.5 cm or more from where it started. The pan is under the outlet when it lies flat on the bench (within 15 degrees) with the point below the outlet at least 1.5 cm inside its inner rim. The score is 0 if the plug was ever out for 2 control steps in a row (0.1 s at 20 Hz) without the pan under the outlet, even if the pan was slid under later. With the plug still in at the end, the score is 0.25 if the pan rests under the outlet and 0 otherwise. With the plug out and the pan resting under the outlet throughout, the score is 0.75, or 1.0 if the plug rests in the parts dish. Possible scores: 0, 0.25, 0.75, 1.0. In a real trial, watch the video for whether the pan was under the outlet before the plug came out, then check where the pan and the plug end up.
metadata.reset_notes: Push the plug back into the pipe and set the pan back at its start. No oil is used, in the simulation or in a real trial, and the engine is cold.
metadata.fidelity: Real size. No oil flows: the scorer judges the order from the plug and pan positions. The plug's threads are not modeled, so it pulls straight out of the pipe instead of being unscrewed. The engine is a fixed model with simple box colliders; the pipe's bore and the pan's rim are made of blocks. Rigid-body physics only.

metadata.title: Seat an oil-feed sleeve with its radial passage registered
metadata.instruction: Insert the sleeve fully into the housing, with its radial oil hole aligned to the housing oil passage. Release it and leave it seated and still for at least one second. Gravity seating is allowed. This operation ends before a separate locking operation.
metadata.context: Without an outside circumferential groove, a sleeve can reach its axial seat while its wall still blocks a radial oil feed. This task evaluates registration of a replaceable sleeve in a lubricated guide housing before a separate retaining operation. The actual port can be obscured by a grasp, and its orientation must survive insertion and release.
metadata.setup: Original calibrated dual-YAM station and three RGB cameras. One free 270 g sleeve (52 mm OD, 38 mm ID, 32 mm high; 12 mm radial hole; bronze exterior and silver-white bore) rests on a fixed 80 x 80 x 8 mm pad. A fixed housing has a 53.6 mm bore, 110 mm OD, 38 mm shell height, 10 mm radial feed hole, annular seat and 135 x 125 x 14 mm base. Radial clearance is 0.8 mm; the fully seated sleeve top is 3 mm below the housing rim. Fixed initial poses and materials are in scene.json; no jitter or additional sensors.
metadata.scoring: Ending state only: 0.5 for released, supported seating held for 1.0 s; 1.0 if the full 10 mm housing-port gauge envelope also remains unobstructed to the central bore throughout that second; otherwise 0. Seating: center error <=0.8 mm horizontally and <=0.5 mm vertically, tilt <=1 degree. Every physics substep must show seat support and no robot-sleeve contact. At 20 Hz, speed <=3 mm/s and angular speed <=0.05 rad/s; over 21 consecutive samples, drift <=0.5 mm and rotation <=1 degree. The gauge runs along the housing port axis from 7 mm outside the housing to 5 mm inside the sleeve bore. Geometry is evaluated at actual live poses; numerical tangency allowance 10 nm. No prescribed grasp, arm, camera motion or insertion strategy. Full rubric: SCORING.md.
metadata.reset_notes: Start a fresh simulator process per trial. Fixed staging pose and 45-degree sleeve yaw; both original arms ready, grippers open. All parts intact and sleeve ungrasped. No randomized drift or consumable object.
metadata.fidelity: Rigid-body clearance fit with 0.8 mm radial play, not press fitting. Polygonal holes; no oil flow, sealing, wear, deformation or retaining mechanism. Ends at released registration before separate locking. Silver bore is a static visual material, without coating thickness. Contact forces and manufactured fits are uncalibrated; scoring uses live geometry, release/support and stillness.
metadata.scores: Dream-1: 0.0, 2,400 actions / 120 s; scripted known-layout demo: 1.0, 450 actions / 22.5 s.

metadata.title: Hold a stick umbrella by its handle with one hand while the other pushes the runner up until it latches open
metadata.instruction: Hold the umbrella by its handle with one hand, and with the other push the runner up the shaft toward the tip until it latches and the umbrella is open; then let go of the runner, move that hand out of the way, and lift the open umbrella up by its handle, tip raised.
metadata.context: Opening a stick umbrella is an everyday two-handed action: one hand holds the handle while the other pushes the runner up the shaft against the ribs' springs until it clicks into its latch. A robot helping at home or in a shop doorway meets this and many similar spring-loaded catches.
metadata.setup: A table in front of two arms (bases 61 cm apart), seen by one overhead camera and a camera on each wrist. Distances are measured forward from the line between the arm bases and sideways from the midpoint between them. (1) A fixed dark-grey painted steel stand: two cradles under the umbrella's shaft, 19 cm right and 4 cm left of the centre line; the handle is free. (2) A loose stick umbrella, 220 g, closed, lying on the stand along the left-right line 28 cm forward, its shaft 14.5 cm above the table: its tip 33 cm right of the centre line, a steel shaft 40 cm long and a wooden handle 10 cm long and 3 cm across, from 7 to 17 cm left of the centre line. Its navy nylon canopy (eight panels on 14 cm steel ribs) is furled along the shaft by the tip. (3) The runner, a dark plastic (nylon) sleeve 2.4 cm across and 3 cm long on the shaft, 3 cm right of the centre line; pushed 12 cm toward the tip it opens the ribs and latches. The layout is the same in every trial, as in the screenshot.
metadata.scoring: Judged at the end of the trial. Travel: how far the runner has been pushed from closed toward the tip, of its 12 cm; the ribs open as it goes (60 degrees from the shaft at the top). At 95% it latches and stays. Let go: both grippers' fingertip centres (TCPs) at least 3 cm from the runner. Held up: the umbrella's tip at least 12 cm above where it lay, with a TCP within 4 cm of the handle's axis (held by its handle). 1.0: latched, let go, and held up by the handle; 0.5: latched; 0.25: pushed at least half way at some point; else 0.0. The trial ends at the run limit, or once the full score has held for 1 s with the umbrella held still.
metadata.reset_notes: Release the latch, let the runner slide back to closed, furl the canopy and lay the umbrella back on its stand.
metadata.fidelity: Rigid-body simulation (Isaac Sim 6.1, PhysX, 20 Hz control). Simplified: the canopy is eight rigid panels whose angle the task file sets from the runner's travel each step (no stretchers or fabric); they do not collide. The ribs' springs are one spring on the runner (1.2 N to start, 6 N at the top), and the latch is a stop the task file sets at the top. The stand is fixed. Cameras 1280 x 704 (Dream-1 sees 320 x 176).

metadata.title: Open a drawer held shut by a bar
metadata.instruction: Open the top drawer.
metadata.context: Some cabinets and carts secure their drawers with a bar across the fronts that must be slid out before a drawer opens. Pulling harder on a barred drawer only strains the handle and the bar: the robot has to notice what holds the drawer and remove it first.
metadata.setup: Station table; positions in cm from the midpoint between the arm bases (x forward, y left), heights above the table top. Cabinet: light-grey sheet steel, 30 wide (y) x 24 deep x 21.5 tall, 1 cm walls, front face at x 30, centred at y 0, screwed to the table. Three empty drawers with blue steel fronts 27.8 x 6 cm, bottoms at heights 1.25, 7.75 and 14.25; each slides out up to 20 cm. Handles: black steel bars 7 x 1.2 x 2 cm (along y) on two stems standing 3.5 cm off the front; the top drawer's centred at y 0, height 18.75, the others mid-front. Two dark-grey steel sleeves on the cabinet's front corners, at y 15 to 17 and -15 to -17, open only at both ends along y: a floor at height 14.75 reaching 4.5 cm in front of the cabinet, two 8 mm side walls leaving a 2.2 cm slot from x 26.3 to 28.5, and a 5 mm top from height 16.75. Bar: red aluminium square tube 1.5 x 1.5 cm, 44 cm long, 100 g, through both sleeves along y, centred at x 27.25, y 0, height 15.5 (2 cm in front of the top drawer's front, across its lower part), 5 cm of it beyond each sleeve. The top drawer opens only 2 cm before it meets the bar, and the bar can leave the sleeves only by sliding along its length. Nothing else on the table.
metadata.scoring: At the end, with a ruler: the top drawer's opening is how far its front has come out past the cabinet's front. 1.0 if the top drawer is open at least 18 cm (in the simulation the trial ends with 1.0 once it is open at least 18 cm and moving under 2 cm/s for 0.5 s). Otherwise 0.5 if the bar is out of both sleeves (no part of it inside either sleeve), else 0. Score 0 if a sleeve, the bar or a handle is bent or broken, or the cabinet has moved. The other drawers and where the bar ends up are not scored. Possible scores: 0, 0.5, 1.0.
metadata.reset_notes: Close all three drawers fully and slide the bar back through both sleeves, centred, with 5 cm of it beyond each sleeve.
metadata.fidelity: Approximate. Cabinet, drawers, handles, sleeves and bar are rigid boxes. Each drawer is a 20 cm prismatic joint with viscous damping, no ball-bearing detents or end-stop bounce, and drawers do not collide with the cabinet body (their slide limits hold them). The bar is a solid loose box with default friction. Nothing can bend or break, so the damage rule applies only to real trials.
metadata.scores: Dream-1 run: 0.0 (the right arm reached to the cabinet's front, then both arms drew back; the bar stayed in both sleeves and the drawer stayed shut); demo: 1.0

metadata.title: Pick parts off a slow and a fast lane in the order they will leave reach, not the order they arrive
metadata.instruction: Four parts will come out on the two lanes, two on each. Put every part in the grey bin before it rides under the cover on the left. The near lane runs five times as fast as the far lane.
metadata.context: Where lanes run side by side at different speeds, the part to take next is the one that will leave reach first, not the one that came out first or is nearest the end: a part on a fast lane can come out later, further back, and still run out sooner. Done by: line operators, packers, and pick-and-place robots on sorting lines.
metadata.setup: The two arm bases stand 61 cm apart on an oak table (1.10 x 1.30 m) whose side edges are 65 cm either side of the midpoint between the bases. Two straight conveyor lanes run parallel to the line through the bases, their centre lines 29 cm (near lane) and 41 cm (far lane) in front of it. Each lane has two dark steel rails (1.5 x 1.5 cm, 72.5 cm long) 2 cm either side of its centre line, from 9 cm right to 63.5 cm left of the midpoint. Grey sheet-steel covers hide both lanes except one window open from the table up, from 13 to 47 cm left of the midpoint. Each cover is a tunnel over both lanes: two side walls (1 cm thick, 9.2 cm tall) standing on the table, their inner faces 24.25 and 45.75 cm in front of the bases, a flat roof (23.5 cm wide, 0.8 cm thick) on them, and an end wall closing its outer end. The feed cover runs from 13 cm left of the midpoint to its end wall, whose inner face is 9 cm right of it; the run-out cover runs from 47 cm left of the midpoint (the end line) to its end wall, whose inner face is 63.5 cm left of it. Each part is a bare aluminium cube (4 x 4 x 4 cm, 170 g) standing in the middle of its own grey steel carrier (6.5 x 6.5 x 1.5 cm), which rides 2 mm above its lane's rails, square to them. At the start each lane has two carriers under the feed cover, centred 8 cm left (lead) and 1 cm right (second) of the midpoint. A grey plastic open bin (14 x 14 cm outside, 12 x 12 cm inside, 1 cm floor, 6 cm walls) stands on the table square to the lanes, its centre 14 cm in front of the bases and 0.5 cm toward the midpoint from the left arm's base. Both lanes carry parts from the robot's right to its left: the near lane at 10 cm/s, the far lane at 2 cm/s. Each carrier stands still until its release time, then speeds up over 0.5 s, cruises at its lane's speed, and slows over 0.5 s to a stop under the run-out cover (the lead carriers 59.5 cm, the second ones 50.5 cm left of the midpoint). Release times from the start of the trial: far lane lead 0 s, near lane lead 3.3 s, far lane second 6.25 s, near lane second 13.15 s. So the cubes come out of the feed cover (front face at its mouth) and reach the end line (centre at the run-out cover's mouth) at: far 1: 1.75 s and 19.75 s; near 1: 3.85 s and 7.45 s; far 2: 12.5 s and 30.5 s; near 2: 14.6 s and 18.2 s. The arms start in their ready pose with open grippers; only the left arm reaches the window and the bin.
metadata.scoring: 0.25 for each cube lying in the bin when the trial ends: its centre inside the bin's walls, its underside below the rim (on the floor or on another cube), still. 1.0 once all four lie there for 1 s, which ends the trial. A cube must go straight from its carrier into the bin: one that spends 0.5 s or more in a row neither on its own carrier, nor held in a gripper (its centre within 5 cm of the point between the finger pads), nor over the inside of the bin is lost and scores 0 even if it later reaches the bin (put down on the table, a cover or another carrier, or knocked off the lane). A cube that rides under the run-out cover is out of reach and scores 0. So 0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75 or 1.0.
metadata.reset_notes: Put the four carriers back under the feed cover at their start positions, a cube centred on each, and start the release timer with the trial.
metadata.fidelity: The carriers follow their paths exactly, like servo-driven lane carriers: the arms can't push or stop them (a real drive would fault if blocked). They ride 2 mm above the rails; a lifted cube's carrier slides on from under it. The cubes have the station's rubber-like friction (1.2 static, 1.0 dynamic), more than aluminium on steel, far above what their 0.31 m/s² peak needs. A real line would use belts and a timed escapement; here each cube rides its own carrier released at a fixed time.

metadata.title: Pick the pin that fits the hole and seat it
metadata.instruction: Find the pin that fits the hole in the fixture block and push it all the way down into the hole.
metadata.context: Seating a locating pin is a routine fitting step: the fitter picks the pin that matches the hole from a mixed set, by eye or by trying, and drives it to the bottom. Here the pins are out of the fixture arm's reach, so a pin has to pass from one arm to the other. Done by: industrial machinery mechanics and assemblers.
metadata.setup: The two arm bases stand 61 cm apart on an oak table. Three bare steel pins, each 80 mm tall, stand upright in a row straight in front of the left arm's base, at 18, 26 and 34 cm out: 26 mm across (333 g), 20 mm across (197 g) and 23 mm across (261 g), in that order. An aluminium fixture block (62 x 62 mm, 25 mm tall) is fixed to the table 30 cm straight in front of the right arm's base. A square hole 22 mm across and 25 mm deep goes through its centre; the table is the hole's floor.
metadata.scoring: Only the 20 mm pin counts. 1.0 if it stands in the hole with its bottom within 3 mm of the floor (at least 22 mm of its length inside the block) and tilts at most 7 degrees (either end up), and stays still for 1 s. 0.5 if it has entered the hole (the centre of its lower end over the hole, its bottom at least 2 mm below the block's top face, tilted at most 30 degrees) but is not fully down. 0.25 if it stands upright (tilted at most 10 degrees) on the table or on the block's top face (its bottom within 3 mm of that surface), with its centre within 5 cm of the hole's centre. Otherwise 0. Any pin that ends up off the table: 0.
metadata.reset_notes: Stand the three pins back in their row in front of the left arm.
metadata.fidelity: A real fixture would use a round 22 mm bore; the task-file format has no round holes, so this one is square, 22 mm across, built from four fixed blocks. A pin fits if and only if its diameter is under 22 mm, the same choice as with the bore. The hole has no chamfer. Pins are plain cylinders. Every object has the same rubber-like friction (1.2 static, 1.0 dynamic), more than steel on aluminium.

metadata.title: Place ECG leads on the correct electrodes
metadata.instruction: Attach the 3-lead ECG cable to the patient manikin, which lies on its back with its head away from you. Following the AHA colour code, drop each lead's clip into the white electrode cup at the correct body position for that lead; one cup stays empty. Then let go of the clips.
metadata.context: Connecting monitoring leads to the right electrodes is routine nursing and technician work (O*NET 29-2031.00 Cardiovascular Technologists and Technicians; 31-1131.00 Nursing Assistants). Swapped arm leads invert the ECG and can mimic disease. The robot must apply a colour convention to the patient's own left and right, which are mirrored from its point of view.
metadata.setup: Station table; cm from the midpoint between the arm bases on the table (x away from robot, y to robot's left). Manikin on its back, head away (patient's right = robot's left), all fixed, PLA, tan: torso board x 25.5-45.5, y -11..11, 1 cm thick; upper arms 18 x 4 x 1 cm beside it; neck; head disc 13 cm dia, 6 cm tall at x 54.5 with nose on top. Four white cups (40 mm inner square, 4 mm walls 6 mm tall) on the torso at x 40 / 29, y +/-6.5. Grey monitor 18 x 8 x 6 cm at x 17, y 34. White, black, red 5 mm leads, 50 cm, leave its right face at x 17, 23, 11 and lie straight towards -y, each ending in a 22 x 14 x 12 mm clip (8 g) of its colour at y -21.7.
metadata.scoring: Score 0 if: a gripper is within 3 cm of any clip at the end; any clip lies in a wrong cup (including the empty one); the manikin, a cup or the monitor was moved; a lead is pulled out of the monitor. A clip lies in a cup when its centre is inside the cup's 40 mm inner square (top view) and at most 12 mm above the cup floor. Otherwise 1/3 per clip in its own cup (AHA: white = right arm, black = left arm, red = left leg): 0, 0.33, 0.67, 1.0. Success (1.0) when all three are placed, released and at rest for 1 s.
metadata.reset_notes: Take the clips out of the cups and lay the three leads straight from the monitor towards the robot's right along their tape lines (x 11, 17, 23 cm) with the clips flat at y -21.7 cm. Check the manikin, cups and monitor are at their marks.
metadata.fidelity: Leads are 25 rigid 2 cm capsule segments with bending springs, no twist; clips are rigid boxes welded to the lead ends. Snap electrodes are simplified to open cups: a clip only has to lie in the cup (no snap force). Manikin, cups and monitor are fixed rigid boxes/cylinders; skin is flat. Real setup: 3D-printed cups glued to a board manikin.

metadata.title: Unload a cantilevered plank without tipping it
metadata.instruction: Put the glass bottle and the steel block in the tray without letting the plank tip.
metadata.context: Unloading an overhang in the wrong order tips it, as with scaffold boards or overhanging shelves: the counterweight comes off last, or the overhang is held down.
metadata.setup: A brown wooden block (8 x 10 x 10 cm tall) is fixed 28 cm in front of the arm bases, 2 cm right of their midline. A pine plank (40 x 8 x 1.5 cm, 0.24 kg) lies on it left to right, overhanging its left edge by 18 cm. On the plank: a green glass bottle (5 cm wide, 10 cm tall, 0.20 kg) 14 cm past the left edge, and a steel block (4 x 4 x 3 cm, 0.38 kg) 2.5 cm past the right edge. A blue tray (12 x 16 cm inside, 2.5 cm walls) is taped on the midline, 13 cm in front of the bases.
metadata.scoring: 0 if at any point the plank tilts more than 10 degrees or the bottle more than 45 degrees, or if at the end the plank has moved more than 3 cm or tilts more than 5 degrees. Otherwise 0.5 for the bottle upright (within 15 degrees) in the tray and 0.5 for the steel block in the tray. An item is in the tray when its centre is inside the walls and it rests on the tray floor.
metadata.reset_notes: Place the plank, then the steel block, then the bottle, so the plank never holds the bottle without its counterweight.
metadata.fidelity: Rigid bodies only. Every surface has the same rubber-like friction (1.2), more than wood on wood, so the plank cannot slide; tipping, the hazard here, follows the real statics. Glass breakage is not simulated: a bottle tilt past 45 degrees counts as a fall.

metadata.title: Plug both ends of a patch cord into a cable tester
metadata.instruction: Connect the loose patch cord to the cable tester for certification: push one plug fully into the jack of the main unit (blue, left) and the other plug fully into the jack of the remote unit (orange, right), without pulling the first plug out, then let go of both plugs.
metadata.context: Telecom and network cable installers (O*NET 49-9052, 49-2022) certify each patch cord by seating its two ends in a tester's main and remote units. The cord is short, so both ends must be brought over together and the second seated without unseating the first.
metadata.setup: Positions in cm from the midpoint between the arm bases (x forward, y left); fixed parts taped down. Main unit: blue PLA box 8 (x) x 7 (y) x 4 cm tall, centre x 36, y +28. Its jack: dark grey PLA sleeve 28 mm wide x 20.5 mm tall x 40 mm long on the unit's right face, opening (20 x 16.5 mm, 26 mm deep, at table level, centre x 36) at y +20.5, facing right. Remote unit: same, orange, mirrored at y -28, jack opening at y -20.5 facing left. Cord: grey 6 mm round PVC cord, 40 cm, straight along x 22 from y +20 to -20; on each end a dark grey PLA plug body 55 x 16 x 14 mm, 15 g, lying flat, pointing at its unit.
metadata.scoring: Score 0 if: at the end a gripper still holds or touches either plug (sim: a gripper centre within 4.5 cm of a plug centre); a tester unit was moved. Otherwise, at the end: 0.5 for each jack (main, remote) holding a plug whose front end is at least 15 mm inside the jack opening (mark on each plug 15 mm from its front end must be hidden in the jack). A plug on top of, beside or in front of a jack, or in less than 15 mm, earns nothing. Either plug may go in either unit. Both jacks = 1.0.
metadata.reset_notes: Pull both plugs out, lay the cord straight along the x 22 cm tape line from y +20 to y -20 cm with the plugs lying flat on their 16 mm side, each pointing at its unit. The units stay taped at their marks.
metadata.fidelity: Cord: 20 rigid 2 cm segments with bending springs (no twist, stretch, plasticity). Plugs: rigid boxes with no latch or contacts, held in the jack only by its walls and friction, so the cord can tug a seated plug out with little force; the real trial uses the same latchless plug bodies, and seating is judged by insertion depth. Jack clearance is 2 mm per side (real RJ45/LC fit is tighter). Units are fixed (taped down in real trials).

metadata.title: Pull a cable out to a length mark
metadata.instruction: Pull the black cable out of the grey feed channel along the yellow ruler until the cable's end lies on the table at the red 30 cm line, then let go, leaving the pulled-out cable lying straight beside the ruler. Never pull the end more than 5 cm past the red line.
metadata.context: Measuring cable off a feed against a ruler before cutting it to length is a daily step for wire-harness and panel assemblers and electricians (O*NET 51-2022.00 Electrical and Electronic Equipment Assemblers; 47-2111.00 Electricians): pulling too little makes the lead too short, pulling too far wastes cable. The red mark is beyond the left arm's reach and the cable end starts beyond the right arm's reach, so the end has to be handed over, and the last centimetres are set by watching the ruler.
metadata.setup: Station table, positions in cm from the midpoint between the two arm bases projected onto the table (x forward away from the robot, y to the robot's left). Feed channel: grey closed straight duct (3D-printed PLA or bent sheet metal), 400 mm long, 30 mm wide and 18 mm tall outside, 14 mm wide and 12 mm tall inside (8 mm side walls, 6 mm roof, the table is its floor), closed at its back end by an 8 mm wall, screwed to the table along y on the line x 30, from its open exit face at y +10 to its back wall at y +50 (back wall outer face y +50.8); the exit faces the right arm. Cable: black 6 mm round PVC-jacketed cable (e.g. LiYY 4 x 0.5 mm2), 45 cm long, both ends bare, not fixed anywhere: it lies straight inside the channel on x 30 with its tail end at y +49 and its free end sticking 6 cm out of the exit (end at y +4). Ruler: yellow tape-measure strip (or printed paper ruler) 400 x 30 mm, 1 mm thick, taped flat to the table beside the cable on the far side (x 30.9 to 33.9), from y +10 (its zero, flush with the exit face) to y -30 (the 40 cm end); black tick lines 2 mm wide every 5 cm from the near edge of the ruler (16 mm long at 0, 10, 20 and 40 cm, 9 mm long at 5, 15, 25 and 35 cm). Red target line: 5 mm wide red tape across the whole ruler width at 30 cm (y -20), continued by a 25 x 5 mm red tape mark on the table on the near side of the cable (x 26.9 to 29.4, y -20). The 30 cm line is at y -20, out of the left arm's reach (left arm y > -2); the cable end starts at y +4, out of the right arm's reach (right arm y < +2). Channel and ruler are fixed.
metadata.scoring: Ruler reading = distance from the exit face to the cable's end along the ruler, read at the end of the trial (tape measure or top photo). Score 0 if any of: (a) the cable is still held at the end (a gripper within 3 cm of it); (b) at any time during the trial the cable's end was pulled past the 35 cm line (5 cm past the red line; checked on video); (c) any part of the pulled-out cable lies more than 2 cm sideways from the cable line x 30 (the end dragged off the ruler, a loop or kink out of line) or more than 1.5 cm above the table (the end held up in the air); (d) less than 5 cm of the cable is still inside the channel. Otherwise: reading within 1 cm of 30 cm (29-31 cm) = 1.0 (success, must hold 1 s); within 3 cm = 0.6; within 5 cm = 0.3; further off = 0. Score 0 if the channel or ruler is moved.
metadata.reset_notes: Push the cable back into the channel from the exit until 6 cm (to the 6 cm point of the ruler) sticks out, straight along x 30; the tail must lie inside the channel. Check the ruler's zero is flush with the exit face.
metadata.fidelity: Cable: 22 rigid ~2 cm capsule segments with bending springs, no twist, no plasticity, friction 0.8; it slides freely in the channel (a real reel feed adds drag and inertia; the channel stands in for the dispenser). Channel and ruler are fixed rigid boxes; ticks and red lines are thin flat boxes. The over-pull rule is tracked every step in sim; 'let go' = both grippers at least 3 cm from the cable.

metadata.title: Lock out an air conditioner at its pull-out disconnect
metadata.instruction: Lock out the air conditioner AC-1 at its pull-out disconnect, the grey box with the yellow AC-1 label: lift its cover and hold it up, pull out the black pull-out block by its grip, turn it upside down and push it back in so that OFF shows, lower the cover shut, then put the red padlock through the hole in the tab at the bottom of the box and snap it shut. Do not touch the AC-2 disconnect (white label).
metadata.context: HVAC mechanics and installers (SOC 49-9021) and general maintenance and repair workers (49-9071) open the pull-out disconnect beside an outdoor air-conditioning unit at the start of nearly every service call: cleaning coils, replacing a capacitor or contactor, fixing a fan motor. They pull the block, reinsert it in its OFF position and padlock the cover so the unit cannot be re-energised while their hands are inside it. Pulling the wrong unit's disconnect, putting the block back ON, or leaving the cover unlocked defeats it.
metadata.setup: Positions are measured forward from the line joining the two arm bases (61 cm apart), left or right of their midline as seen from behind the robot, and up from the table top. Board: a plywood board (1.8 cm thick, 48 cm wide, 36 cm tall) stands on the table on two feet behind it, its front face 45 cm in front of the bases, spanning 33 cm right to 15 cm left of the midline. Disconnects: two Milbank U3802 60 A non-fused pull-out air-conditioner disconnects (grey painted steel; body 13.2 cm wide, 15.2 cm tall, 5.5 cm deep, about 7.8 cm deep with the cover) are screwed to the board with their bottoms 13 cm above the table: AC-1 centred on the midline and AC-2 centred 20 cm right of it. Each cover (0.3 kg, front plate reaching 1.5 cm below the box) is hinged at its top rear and hangs shut by its weight; opened, its top meets the board at about 94 degrees; its front is 37.2 cm in front of the bases and carries an engraved plate (8 x 4.4 cm, centred 23.6 cm above the table): AC-1 yellow, AC-2 white, black letters. Behind the cover a dead front has a 10 x 4.8 cm window holding the pull-out: a black plastic block (9.6 x 4.4 x 1.8 cm, 0.1 kg, centred 20.6 cm above the table) with a grip bar (6 x 1.4 cm, standing 1.6 cm out of its face); its four copper blades sit in the line and load clips, and the block is printed ON one way up and OFF the other. Turned over (half a turn about the direction it slides in), the blades go into insulated dummy pockets instead. A steel tab (2.2 cm wide, 2 mm thick) sticks forward out of each box's bottom through a slot (2.6 x 2.5 cm) near the bottom of the cover's front, ending 2 cm in front of the cover; it has an 8 mm hole centred 1.2 cm in front of the cover. Padlock: a red Master Lock 410RED Zenex safety padlock (body 38 x 44 x 19 mm, 6.35 mm steel shackle with 38 mm vertical clearance; 0.10 kg), open (shackle popped up 16 mm), stands upright on a grey column (3.0 x 0.9 cm, 11 cm tall, on a 6 x 5 x 1 cm foot) 18 cm in front of the bases and 21 cm left of the midline, its short leg toward the boxes. Both arms start at the ready pose with their grippers open. One fixed layout, as in the screenshot.
metadata.scoring: Score 0 if, at any time, AC-2's cover opens more than 5 degrees or its pull-out moves more than 4 mm or turns more than 8 degrees, or if AC-1's pull-out, once pulled, is pushed back in ON (its blades more than 3 mm into the live clips). Otherwise the score is set by the state at the end: 0.25 if AC-1's pull-out is out of its live clips; 0.5 if it is back in the box turned over (OFF reads upright), seated within 3 mm; 0.75 if, in addition, AC-1's cover is shut (within 4 degrees); 1.0 if, in addition, the padlock is shut (latched) through the tab's hole and the after-release check passes. After-release check, done once both grippers have been at least 6 cm from the padlock and the cover's bottom edge for 2 s: hook a spring scale under the cover's bottom edge and pull it outward and up, square to the cover, with 20 N for 2 s. Pass if the cover opens less than 10 degrees (its bottom edge moves out less than 3 cm), the shackle is still through the hole and the pull-out still OFF; if not, the score is 0.75.
metadata.reset_notes: Open the padlock with its key and take it off the tab; stand it back open on its column, short leg toward the boxes. Lift AC-1's cover, pull the pull-out, turn it ON side up and push it back into the live clips (it seats with a firm push), and let the cover fall shut. Check AC-2 is untouched (cover shut, pull-out ON). About 1 minute. For a real-world trial use an unwired disconnect (no conductors on its lugs).
metadata.fidelity: PhysX rigid bodies on joints, arms with the station's i2rt gains. Lockout is geometry: a shackle in the tab's hole stops the cover's bottom swinging out; the blades grip in compliant-contact clips (starts sliding at 15 N here; real force unpublished, est. 20-50 N), loose in the OFF pockets. Inferred: window, block, clip, tab sizes. Simplified: box colliders, no hinge friction, shut stop is a joint limit, the 410 latches by a catch (no key). Details in README.

metadata.title: Release a push-fit fitting and pull the pipe out
metadata.instruction: Press the orange release collet on the brass fitting in and hold it there while you pull the copper pipe out of the fitting, then lay the pipe down flat on the table.
metadata.context: Plumbers and heating technicians (O*NET 47-2152.00, 49-9021.00) take pipes out of push-fit fittings when re-routing or replacing a section: the fitting's grab ring bites the pipe, so the release collet has to be pressed in and held while the pipe is pulled out. One hand holds the collet, the other pulls.
metadata.setup: Positions in cm from the midpoint between the two arm bases, on the table (x forward, y left). A grey base plate (9 x 14.7 x 0.8 cm) lies at x 23.5 to 32.5, y 1.5 to 16.2, held by four dark cleats 2 cm tall screwed to the table; a white wall plate (12 x 1.2 x 11 cm) stands on its far end at y 15 to 16.2. A 15 mm copper stub comes out of the wall along -y into a brass push-fit coupling (3 x 3 x 8 cm, axis 4.5 cm above the table at x 28) on a grey pedestal; the coupling's open mouth faces -y at y 2. The base, wall, stub and coupling weigh 5 kg together. An orange release collet (a square ring 5 cm wide, 3.6 cm tall, 0.5 cm thick, with a 2 cm hole) sits 0.4 cm in front of the mouth; a spring (0.4 N per mm) holds it out and it presses in 3.5 mm. A loose 15 mm copper pipe, 30 cm long, 84 g, lies along y with its end pushed 2.5 cm into the coupling (to y 4.5) and its far end (y -25.5) resting on a wooden block (3 x 2 x 3.7 cm) at y -23.5. A grab tooth inside the coupling holds the pipe in unless the collet is pressed at least 2.5 mm.
metadata.scoring: Measured with a ruler. 0 if the fitting was at any point moved more than 5 mm. 1.0 if the pipe, after being pulled out, lies flat on the table (axis level within 10 degrees, resting on the table) with every point at least 4 cm from the coupling's mouth, and is still for 1 s; 0.75 if, after the collet was pressed, the pipe's end came at least 5 mm out of the mouth (pulled 3 cm); 0.5 if, after the collet was pressed, the pipe was pulled 5 mm; 0.25 if the collet was pressed 2.5 mm; else 0.
metadata.reset_notes: Press the collet and push the pipe back into the coupling to its stop (2.5 cm in), let the collet go so the tooth bites, and rest the pipe's far end on the block.
metadata.fidelity: Rigid bodies built from boxes and cylinders. The grab ring is one tooth on a stiff slider that drops into a 3 mm groove in the pipe (a real ring's teeth bite plain pipe); while the collet, a spring slider, is pressed 2.5 mm, the task lifts the tooth, standing in for the collet's cone. The bore is square with 1.5 mm play and no O-ring. The fitting assembly is held by cleats. No contact force cap is enforced in simulation.

metadata.title: Land a ferruled wire in the named push-in terminal
metadata.instruction: Land the blue ferruled wire in terminal X1:4, the blue terminal, upper entry. Push the ferrule straight into the entry until the collar stops, then let go.
metadata.context: Landing control wires on DIN-rail terminal blocks is routine daily work for electricians (SOC 47-2111) and control-panel builders and wirers (51-2028): panels hold rows of identical push-in terminals told apart only by printed markers, and each conductor is landed one at a time from the wiring diagram. A wire in the wrong terminal puts a conductor on the wrong circuit, and one not pushed home is not clamped and pulls out, so electricians tug every wire after landing it. Panel wiring is a large, repetitive share of the trade and a natural target for automation.
metadata.setup: Positions are measured forward from the line joining the two arm bases (61 cm apart), left or right of their midline as seen from behind the robot, and up from the table top. Plate: a light-grey 3 mm steel mounting plate (23 cm wide, 26 cm tall) stands upright on the table, fixed to it, its front face 32.5 cm in front of the bases, spanning 20 cm right to 3 cm left of the midline. A steel EN 60715 TS35 x 7.5 DIN rail runs left-right across it, centre 14.9 cm above the table. Terminals: six WAGO TOPJOB S 2-conductor feedthrough terminal blocks (polyamide, 5.2 mm wide, 48.5 mm long, front face 32.9 mm above the rail) stand side by side on the rail, long side vertical, front faces 28.5 cm in front of the bases, upper ends 17.75 cm above the table. From left to right they are X1:1, X1:2 and X1:3 (grey, 2002-1201), X1:4 (blue, 2002-1204), X1:5 (green-yellow, 2002-1207) and X1:6 (grey, 2002-1201). X1:1 is centred 6.8 cm right of the midline and they step right by 5.2 mm, so X1:4 is centred 8.4 cm right. A WAGO 2002-1291 end plate closes the right end, and end stops sit at both ends. Each block carries a white printed marker (1 to 6) in the middle of its front face, and the left end stop carries the group marker X1. Each block's lower entry (4 mm above its lower end) already holds a landed wire: a 1.5 mm2 conductor with PVC insulation 2.9 mm across and a black DIN 46228-4 insulated ferrule (collar 4 mm across, 7 mm out of the entry), coloured X1:1 brown, X1:2 black, X1:3 grey, X1:4 blue, X1:5 green with a yellow stripe, X1:6 brown. Each leaves its entry sloping 15 degrees down toward the robot, bends down and back toward the plate (bends of 12 mm radius, an S-shape at most 1.9 cm in front of the terminals' front faces) and drops into the duct through its top comb, 3.5 mm behind the duct's front face, as in neat panel wiring. These wires are fixed in place. Their entries are 4 cm below the upper entries, and no part of them is more than 13.5 cm above the table. Each upper entry is an empty hole in the front face, 4 mm below the upper end, angled 15 degrees downward into the block. Duct: a grey slotted PVC wiring duct (4.5 cm deep, 6.7 cm tall) is fixed to the plate below the terminals, 3.25 to 9.9 cm above the table, spanning 1.5 to 14.7 cm right of the midline. Wire: a 2.5 mm2 fine-stranded conductor with blue PVC insulation (3.6 mm across), 40 cm long from the duct, with a blue DIN 46228-4 insulated ferrule crimped on its end (WAGO 216-246; 10 mm sleeve 2.5 mm across, 7 mm collar 4.6 mm across). It leaves the duct through a slot in its bottom wall 14 cm right of the midline and 29 cm in front of the bases, drops to the table, runs back toward the robot and left to about 3 cm right of the midline and 8 to 12 cm in front of the bases, rises, and turns right onto the stand. Stand: a dark-grey plastic stand (two posts 2 x 16 mm with low side lips) centred 17 cm in front of the bases and 13 cm right of the midline. The wire's last 8 cm lies on it with the ferrule pointing forward and sloping 15 degrees down like the entry, the collar's front face 9.25 cm above the table.
metadata.scoring: Score 0 if, at any time, the ferrule's tip goes more than 1 mm into any terminal entry other than X1:4's upper entry. Otherwise the score is the highest level reached: 0.25 if the wire's end is raised 1 cm or more above its place on the stand; 0.5 if the ferrule's tip is also inside X1:4's upper entry, 1 mm or more past the mouth; 0.75 if it is also pushed home: the collar within 0.8 mm of the entry's mouth and the clamp engaged on the ferrule (the clamping spring's leg deflected by the ferrule, checked by the tug below holding at least partly, or with a 2.5 mm screwdriver test in the operating slot); 1.0 if the after-release check also passes. Dropping the wire is not penalised by itself. After-release check, once both grippers have been at least 6 cm from the wire end for 1 s (or at the end of the run): mark the insulation with a pen at the entry's mouth, then pull the wire end straight back out along the entry's axis with a spring scale, raising the pull to 50 N over 0.5 s and holding it for 1.5 s. It passes if the mark moves out less than 1.5 mm. If it fails, the score is 0.75 (or 0.5 if the collar was never home). Distances are read with a rule, or from a close-up photo with a scale in view.
metadata.reset_notes: Push a 2.5 mm flat screwdriver into X1:4's operating slot to open the clamp, and pull the wire out. Lay the end back on the stand with the ferrule forward, and the cable along its starting path from the duct slot (the path in the setup photo). About 1 minute.
metadata.fidelity: PhysX at 480 Hz, arms with the station's i2rt gains. Published: block, entry angle, ferrule and DIN rail sizes. The clamp is a sprung hinged leaf (stand-in for CAGE CLAMP) tuned to hold 50 N; entry channel sized from photos; square colliders. Wire is 16 jointed capsules, stiffness, mass, friction guessed. Landed wires are visual only; target told apart by its blue housing; pad friction raised for the weak gripper; 50 N pull applied in sim after recording. Details in README.

metadata.title: Push two reject cartons off a moving line onto the reject table, leaving the good ones on it
metadata.instruction: The two red cartons on the moving line are rejects. Push each one off the line onto the grey reject table behind the line before it reaches the tunnel, and leave the brown cartons on the line.
metadata.context: Where a packing line has no automatic diverter, a carton that fails a check (weight, seal, label) is pushed off the running conveyor onto a reject table by the operator beside it, without stopping the line and without disturbing the good cartons riding just in front of and behind it. The cartons are too wide to pick in one hand, so the reject has to be pushed sideways while it moves. Done by: packing-line operators and line-side cobots.
metadata.setup: The two arm bases stand 61 cm apart on an oak table (1.10 x 1.30 m) whose side edges are 65 cm either side of the midpoint between the bases. A straight conveyor crosses the table parallel to the line through the bases, its centre line 26 cm in front of them, flowing from the robot's right to its left. Two dark steel rails (1.5 x 1.5 cm, 153 cm long) run along it, centred 4 cm either side of the centre line, from 61 cm right of the midpoint to 92 cm left of it. Four grey steel carrier plates (14 cm across the line, 12 cm along it, 1.5 cm thick) ride 2 mm above the rails (their tops 3.2 cm above the table), square to them, centred on the centre line, 13 cm apart centre to centre (1 cm between carriers); at the start their centres are 14, 27, 40 and 53 cm right of the midpoint. On each carrier a closed carton (12 cm across the line, 10 cm along it, 5 cm tall, 200 g) stands square in the middle (3 cm between neighbouring cartons); from the front of the line (the leftmost): brown cardboard, red, brown cardboard, red. Along the far side of the line lies a grey steel reject table top (18 cm deep, from 34 to 52 cm in front of the bases, 1 cm from the carriers' far edge; 96 cm long, from 62 cm right to 34 cm left of the midpoint; its top 2.7 cm above the table, 5 mm below the carriers' tops), with a dark steel fence 1 cm thick standing 3 cm above its top along its far edge and both ends. From 34 cm left of the midpoint the conveyor runs into a grey sheet-steel tunnel: two side walls (1 cm thick, 10.2 cm tall, 58 cm long) whose inner faces are 8.25 cm either side of the centre line, under a 0.8 cm roof whose underside is 2 cm above the cartons' tops, closed at its far end (92 cm left of the midpoint), where it stands on a dark steel post to the floor (18.5 x 4 cm, centred 89 cm left of the midpoint). The belt speeds up to 5 cm/s over the first 0.3 s of the trial, runs at 5 cm/s, and stops (over 0.3 s) at 19.4 s, when every carrier is inside the tunnel. Untouched, the cartons' leading faces reach the tunnel's mouth at 8.8, 11.4, 14.0 and 16.5 s.
metadata.scoring: At the end of the trial, with what a per-step monitor recorded over the whole trial: +0.5 for each red carton placed on the reject table: its bottom within 1 cm of the table's top (any face down), its whole footprint on the table (past its near edge, inside its fence), still (under 1 cm/s), no part of either gripper within 4 cm of it plus however far that gripper's fingers are open, and at every control step its centre was over its carrier's footprint or over the reject table's side of the line (from the carriers' far edge to the fence, along the table) with its bottom between 1 cm below the reject table's top and 1 cm above the carriers' tops: pushed straight across, never lifted, never on the station table or the floor. 0 for a red carton anywhere else (on its carrier or in the tunnel, on the station table, on the floor, overhanging the reject table's edge, held or pressed by a gripper, still sliding) or that left that route at any moment, even if later pushed onto the reject table. -0.5 for each brown carton not standing upright on its own carrier (its centre outside the carrier's 14 x 12 cm footprint, or more than 1 cm off the height it rides at) at the end or at any control step during the trial: knocked off or over and put back still counts. The total is never below 0. 1.0 when both red cartons are placed and both brown cartons stood on their carriers all trial (the trial then ends with success once this has held for 1 s); 0.5 for one red carton placed. Pushing every carton onto the table, or sweeping the whole line off, scores 0.
metadata.reset_notes: Run the carriers back to their start positions, stand each carton back square in the middle of its carrier (the brown ones may be in the tunnel, the red ones on the reject table), and start the belt with the trial. Safety for real trials: the cartons are empty 200 g cardboard boxes on a 5 cm/s belt, the reject table's 3 cm fence stops a carton pushed too far, and the tunnel's low roof keeps hands and grippers out of the conveyor's end.
metadata.fidelity: The carriers follow their path exactly, like a servo-driven conveyor: the arms can't push or stop them. They ride 2 mm above the rails. The cartons are rigid boxes with the station's rubber-like friction (1.2 static, 1.0 dynamic), more than cardboard on steel, and the carriers 0.8 / 0.7; a push even at a carton's top edge slides it rather than tipping it. Reject cartons are red all over rather than carrying a red label, one colour per rigid body.

metadata.title: Lock the spring tongs and put them away in the cutlery tray
metadata.instruction: Put the tongs away in the cutlery tray, locked shut.
metadata.context: Putting kitchen utensils away after washing up is an everyday home chore. People lock spring tongs shut before storing them: unlocked, they spring open in the drawer, take up the space of several utensils and snag the drawer when it is shut. Open, these tongs are also wider than the tray's long slot, so they have to be held shut while the pull tab is pulled to lock them.
metadata.setup: World frame for this text: 'in front' is away from the arm bases, 'left' and 'right' are from the robot's view, heights are above the table top, and the midline is halfway between the two arm bases. Spring kitchen tongs (loose, 85 g in all), lying flat: a stainless hinge knuckle 20 mm across and 22 mm tall (15 g); two stainless arms (32 g each, with their heads), each a strip 4 mm thick and 20 mm deep standing on its edge, from 8 to 195 mm from the hinge axis, with a red silicone head 25 mm long, 8.5 mm thick and 22 mm deep at its tip, 220 mm from the hinge axis to the heads' ends. Each arm swings on its own pin 6 mm either side of the centre line, sprung open (0.8 N m/rad each, preloaded) to a stop 10 degrees out, so the open heads span 94 mm outside; squeezed shut, the heads meet and the arms are 18 mm across outside. A black nylon pull tab (6 g) sticks out of the hinge end: a stem and a grip 16 mm long, 14 mm wide and 16 mm tall (4 to 20 mm up), its end 34 mm behind the hinge axis; it slides out up to 10 mm against a 40 N/m spring. Pulled out at least 7 mm while both arms are shut, it locks them shut and stays out; pushed back in below 3 mm, it unlocks them. The tongs: the hinge axis 20.0 cm in front of the bases and 10.0 cm right of the midline, the tongs pointing left along the left-right line (heads 12 cm left of the midline), open. Cutlery tray (fixed, as if held in its drawer; white polypropylene, 6 mm walls, 4 mm floor, 50 mm tall): outer 160 mm front to back (32.4 to 48.4 cm in front of the bases) and 302 mm left to right, centred on the midline. Along its near side, a long compartment 65 mm front to back (33.0 to 39.5 cm) and 290 mm long inside; behind a divider, two short compartments, each 77 by 142 mm inside. Nothing else is on the table.
metadata.scoring: Per trial, judged on the tongs once the robot has let go (no gripper or finger within 5 mm of them) and they have stopped moving. Locked: the tab is out at least 7 mm and both arms are within 0.03 rad of shut (heads under about 15 mm apart). In the long compartment: no part of the tongs is outside its walls (1 mm allowed for contact), none is above its rim, and the tongs' lowest point is within 3 mm of its floor. Score 1.0: locked and in the long compartment, held for 2 s. Score 0.5: locked, let go and still anywhere else on the counter or tray. Score 0.25: in the long compartment but not locked (squeezed in and let go, so they spring open against its walls). Score 0: anything else, including open tongs lying across the tray, tongs off the table, tongs still held, or tongs still moving.
metadata.reset_notes: 1. Push the tab fully in so the tongs spring open against their stops. 2. Lay the tongs flat on the counter with the hinge axis 20.0 cm in front of the arm bases and 10.0 cm right of the midline, pointing left. 3. Leave the tray where it is, empty. Nothing is consumed. Run with -E object_jitter=0.
metadata.fidelity: True-size tongs and tray. The arms are straight rigid strips; the spring is two hinge springs. The pull tab's catch engages when the tab is out at least 7 mm with both arms shut, then holds the arms shut and the tab out until the tab is pushed back in below 3 mm. The tray is fixed in place, as in a drawer. Masses and friction are simulator values.

metadata.title: Fit a blanking panel at U6 of a server rack
metadata.instruction: Fit the blanking panel at U6.
metadata.context: Closing a rack's empty units with blanking panels is standard data-centre practice (else hot exhaust flows back into the cold aisle), and fitting equipment at the units a rack elevation names is a basic step in building one out. Each unit has three identical square holes, so a panel fitted one hole off straddles two units: a common mistake. The robot must find U6 on the posts, line both clips of a 48 cm panel up with its middle holes, push it home and let go.
metadata.setup: Positions in cm from the midpoint between the arm bases: x forward, y to the robot's left; heights above the table top. A 19-inch two-post open-frame rack, 8U, dark grey steel, is clamped to the table, the front of its posts at x 42, centred on y 0. Each post (3.4 cm face, 4.6 cm deep) has EIA-310 square holes, 9.5 mm and 1.6 cm deep, three per unit: 15.9 mm apart within a unit, 12.7 mm across a boundary. Hole centres are 46.5 cm apart; a 2.5 cm bar joins the posts at the top; each post stands on a 30 x 4 x 2 cm foot; U1's bottom edge is 3 cm above the table. Each post carries the unit numbers 1 to 8 beside its holes (white, about 1 cm tall) and a white line at each unit boundary. Installed, each screwed into the middle hole of each of its units: a 2U server at U1-U2 (28 cm deep), a 1U switch at U3 (20 cm) and a 1U patch panel at U8 (6 cm), all with 48.3 cm fronts (dummy fronts will do); U4 to U7 are empty. A 1U blanking panel, black plastic, 48.3 x 4.3 cm, 6 mm thick, about 120 g, has a clip at each end: an 8 mm square peg 12 mm long at mid-height, chamfered to 5 mm, the two 46.5 cm apart, a slip fit in the holes (no snap). It stands face to the arms, its back at x 30, in an 8 mm, 2.65 cm deep slot in each of two wooden uprights (4 cm wide, 3.2 cm deep, 16 cm tall, centres at y +-17) on a 41 x 5.2 x 1.2 cm base board. Both arms start at the ready pose with open grippers.
metadata.scoring: Judged at the end of the trial from a front photo of the rack and the video. The panel is at U6 (the 6th unit from the bottom) when its top and bottom edges are within 3 mm of U6's unit lines. 1.0 (success, ends the trial): at U6, both ends pushed home against the posts (a 2 mm shim will not fit behind), and the robot has let go for the last 1 s. 0.5: at U6 and pushed home but still held by the robot; or at U6 with only one end pushed home. 0: anything else, including another unit and one hole off (the panel straddling two units).
metadata.reset_notes: Lift the panel off its clips and stand it back in the stand, face to the arms.
metadata.fidelity: Rigid bodies, 240 Hz physics, 20 Hz control. The rack and the stand are fixed. Each post's front has real square holes (strips and bridges with gaps, holes 16 mm deep, solid behind), so a clip goes in only at a hole. The panel is one rigid body with a chamfered rigid peg on each end, a slip fit (0.75 mm play), so a panel pushed home hangs on them. Each step task code reads the panel's pose for the holes and seating, and checks the arms' collision hulls, fingers included, are 1 cm clear of it.
metadata.scores: Dream-1 run: 0.0 (both arms reached toward the stand, within about 1 cm of the panel, but the panel never moved); demo: 1.0

metadata.title: Slide a carriage onto a linear rail until it clicks
metadata.instruction: Slide the blue carriage onto the open end of the grey rail and push it along the rail until it clicks past the plunger and stops against the orange end stop.
metadata.context: Electromechanical and machine assemblers (O*NET 51-2023.00, 51-2031.00) fit carriages onto the linear guides of gantries, linear actuators and 3D printers: the carriage must be lined up with a close-fitting profile, kept square over a 10 cm slide, and pushed through a detent.
metadata.setup: Positions in cm from the midpoint between the two arm bases, on the table (x forward, y left). Rail: grey PLA, 150 g, 29 cm long, lying on the midline (y 0) from x 14.5 (open end, nearest the arms) to x 43.5.
