It is a 2 cm wide, 0.8 cm tall bar; over its first 11.5 cm it carries a T-profile (0.8 cm wide, 0.6 cm tall stem under a 1.6 cm wide, 0.4 cm tall head), which ends at an orange end stop (0.5 x 2 x 2.2 cm) at 11.5-12 cm; the remaining 17 cm is a plain handle. An orange spring plunger with a rounded 8 mm nose sits on the left side of the T-profile, 6.9 cm from the open end, just under the head, and sticks out 2 mm sideways (spring 0.3 N per mm, 2.5 mm travel). Carriage: blue PLA block 4 x 3 x 1.7 cm, 40 g, with a T-shaped channel through its length (1 mm side play, 2 mm above and below the head), standing on the table at x 15, y -15, channel along x.
metadata.scoring: Measured at the end with a ruler. 0 if the rail was at any point moved more than 3 cm or turned more than 15 degrees. Otherwise, by where the carriage is at the end: 1.0 if it is on the rail (within 2 mm of its centreline and 1.5 mm of its seated height, square to it within 5 degrees) between the plunger and the end stop (its front within 0.5 mm of the stop, its rear past the plunger, which has sprung back out) and still (moving less than 1 mm over 1 s); 0.75 if it is on the rail with its centre at least 6 cm from the rail's open end; 0.5 if it is on the rail with at least 1 cm of it over the rail; 0.25 if it was lifted 3 cm at some point; else 0.
metadata.reset_notes: Press the plunger in, slide the carriage back off the open end, and stand it on its mark; lay the rail back on its marks on the midline.
metadata.fidelity: Rigid bodies built from boxes and cylinders. The plunger is a prismatic joint with a spring drive and no preload; real ball plungers are stiffer and preloaded. Friction is uniform (0.5 rail, 0.3 carriage) and light angular damping is added to the parts. No contact force cap is enforced in simulation.

metadata.title: Slide a linear-guide carriage onto its rail past a spring plunger
metadata.instruction: Pick up the blue carriage by its post, fit it onto the open end of the grey rail, and push it along the rail past the orange plunger until it touches the end stop. Then let go and keep both fingers at least 3 cm from the post.
metadata.context: Linear guide carriages on robot gantries, 3D printers and wafer handlers are slid onto their rails by hand during assembly. A ball-plunger detent marks the seated position, and a carriage left short of it can drift. The task tests a part that can only go on from the open end (undercut lips, 1 mm clearances), a push through a spring detent that resists, and a clean release. The score is read from the final state only, so a carriage that is lifted off again scores 0.
metadata.setup: Positions in cm from the arm-base line (x forward) and the midline (y left), on the table, one fixed layout matching the screenshot. Rail: a grey T-rail (rigid, 6 kg, friction 1.2) 19.5 cm long on a dark blue mat (27 x 7 x 0.2 cm), axis along x at y -15, from x 22.0 (open end, facing the arms) to x 41.5; neck 0.8 cm wide, head 1.6 cm wide, top 1.4 cm above the mat, with a small lead-in tab at the open end. An orange end stop (2 x 2.8 x 3 cm, same part) stands at x 41.5 to 43.5. Orange spring plunger: 1 cm wide, back face at x 37.5 (4 cm before the stop face), ramped top rising 1 mm over 1.2 cm to 1 mm above the head, 0.2 N/mm spring, 4 mm travel. Carriage: blue plastic, 80 g, 3.6 cm long x 2.6 cm wide, plate 1.4 cm above its base, channel and lips fitting the rail with 1 mm clearance, and a 3 cm wide grip post 6 cm tall; it stands on a yellow mat (10 x 10 x 0.2 cm) centred at x 26, y +2 (26 cm from the base line, 2 cm left of the midline), lengthwise along x. Both mats are fixed.
metadata.scoring: Computed from the final state only, nothing is remembered. 1.0 if at the end the carriage is on the rail (guide lips under the rail head, level within 3 degrees, lateral offset 3 mm or less), wholly past the plunger with the plunger back up behind it, its front face within 3 mm of the end stop, and released (both fingers at least 90% open and at least 3 cm from the post) and still (moving less than 1 mm) for the last 1 s. 0.5 if it is on the rail at the end but not all of that holds (short of the plunger, held, or moving). 0 if it is not on the rail at the end, whatever happened earlier.
metadata.reset_notes: Lift the carriage off the rail's open end and set it on the yellow mat, lengthwise along x; the plunger resets itself.
metadata.fidelity: Rigid bodies from boxes and one cylinder; rail, end stop and plunger housing are one 6 kg part that stays put. The plunger is a prismatic joint with a spring drive (0.2 N/mm, 4 mm travel) and rises only 1 mm into the carriage's path, so its force is far below a real ball plunger. Friction is 1.2 everywhere, clearances 1 mm, contact offsets 0.5 mm. No contact force cap is enforced.

metadata.title: Refit a loaded drawer on its roller slides, carried in above riding height so the rear hooks clear, then pull-test it
metadata.instruction: Put the drawer back into the cabinet on its slides and close it. Then pull it open again by about 5 cm and leave it there.
metadata.context: Most people have taken a drawer out of a chest or desk: to get back something that fell behind it, to clean it, to lighten the chest before moving it, or because it came off its runners. Refitting it on roller slides is where it goes wrong. A hook under the rear of each drawer runner must pass over the roller at the front of each cabinet rail, so the loaded drawer is carried in level, slightly above where it will ride, until the hooks are past the rollers, then set down. Pushed in low, it slides along the cabinet floor under the slides and still closes flush; only a pull shows it: on its slides the drawer runs out level and stops at its hooks, under them it sits 54 mm lower and drags out with no stop. Unlike removing a drawer by holding its two slide releases pressed, or lifting a drawer out past its anti-pull-out stop, this tests engaging a hidden catch by controlling the height of a loaded drawer; unlike stowing a drawer that already rides on its rails, the slides start disengaged.
metadata.setup: World frame in metres: x forward from the arms, y left, z up; the table top is z = 0.7475 and the arm bases are at x 0, y +/-0.305. Cabinet (fixed, wood): 40 cm wide, 26 cm deep, 19.8 cm tall, its front face at x = 0.32 centred on y = 0; 12 mm floor panel, 18 mm side walls and back, and an 18 mm wooden top over the whole cabinet, flush with its front face, so the drawer can only go in through the front opening (168 mm high from the floor panel to the underside of the top). Changed in this revision: the top is added and the side walls and back are 18 cm tall instead of 17 cm. With the drawer on its slides there is 24 mm between the top of its side walls and the underside of the top (fitting instructions for bottom-mount slides ask for at least 16 mm) and 14 mm above its front panel. Inside each side wall a steel slide rail 22 mm wide, 12 mm thick, 235 mm long, its top 90 mm above the table, with a steel front roller (8 mm long, 6 mm high) 2 mm behind the face. Drawer (free, 1.0 kg with its handle): painted front panel 390 x 18 x 100 mm with a steel bar handle (added in this revision: a 10 x 10 mm bar 176 mm long on two posts 160 mm apart, standing 35 mm off the panel, centred 60 mm above the drawer bottom), plywood box 300 mm wide, 202 mm deep, 90 mm tall with 12 mm walls and a 10 mm bottom; on each side a steel runner 197 x 22 x 12 mm, 30 mm above the drawer bottom, and under the rear half of each runner a 112 mm long, 6 mm thick orange hook plate whose front end is the rear hook. On its slides the drawer bottom is 66 mm above the table; it opens 75 mm before the hooks meet the rollers. Pushed in low it rests on the cabinet floor 12 mm above the table with its runners passing under the rails. At the start the drawer stands on the table with its front panel's outer face at x = 0.06, centred on y = 0, holding a blue box of parts (120 x 160 x 60 mm, 0.8 kg) centred 145 mm behind the front face. Friction: runners, hook plates, rails and rollers 0.05 (standing in for rolling); drawer wood 0.8; cabinet wood 0.5; parts box 1.2.
metadata.scoring: Judged from the video and a photo of the end with a ruler. On its slides means: the drawer bottom 66 +/- 4 mm above the table (both runners riding on the rails, measured at the front panel), level within 2.5 degrees, square to the cabinet within 3 degrees and centred within 12 mm, and open no more than 78 mm (it stops at 75 mm when the hooks meet the rollers). Closed means the front panel within 5 mm of the cabinet face. Hands off means both grippers at least 2 cm from the drawer (handle included) and the box. Score 0 if the box ever leaves the drawer or the drawer falls off the table. Otherwise 1.0 if, after the drawer was closed on its slides with hands off for 1 s, it is now on its slides, open 30 to 80 mm, the box inside, hands off (the trial ends as a success once this has held for 1 s); 0.5 if it was closed on its slides with hands off for 1 s and is still on its slides; 0.25 if it is on its slides; else 0. The state at the end of the episode is scored.
metadata.reset_notes: Take the drawer out, stand it on its marks on the table with the box in it, and clear the closed-and-let-go record. There is one fixed layout; the episode seed does not change the scene.
metadata.fidelity: Rigid boxes. Roller slides are modelled as low-friction (0.05) sliding contacts with a fixed 6 mm roller step at the front of each rail; no self-closing spring or damper. Sizes are real scale for a small desk or bedside drawer unit (300 mm wide drawer box), but the drawer is 202 mm deep, shallower than a 450 mm kitchen drawer, to stay within the arms' reach. The 1.0 kg drawer and 0.8 kg load are realistic for that size, lighter than a full kitchen drawer.

metadata.title: Replace a worn soft gripper finger
metadata.instruction: One soft finger on this spare gripper is worn. Its three screws are already out, in the white block. Replace the finger with a new one, put the worn finger in the red bin, put the fork plate back on the new finger and drop the three screws into their holes.
metadata.context: Low-cost grippers use soft printed fingers that wear out in use, and a robot that changes them needs less human upkeep. The arm must spot which finger is worn and which spare is new, one arm must hold the fork plate clear while the other changes the finger, and after the swap the same fine placement is repeated for three small screws, each picked from a block and dropped into its hole.
metadata.setup: On a wooden table between two arms, a spare parallel gripper, without its handle, lies flat on a white printed cradle in a steel fixture, 28.5 x 20 x 1.2 cm, fixed, its fingers pointing at the robot and their roots 28.5 cm out from the arms. It has a white printed body, 17.2 cm wide and 9.1 cm deep, with a top cover and two mirror wings, a steel linear rail, and two white printed finger holders fastened with M3 screws and nuts. In each holder's fork lies a soft fin-ray finger of orange TPU, 12.3 cm long, 4 cm wide, 2.58 cm thick, 56 g, with a black rubber grip strip on its inner face, in a pocket with 5 mm walls. The fork's upper plate, white printed, 6 mm thick, 30 g, with a printed marker tag, rests loose on the finger's root. The right plate has its three M3 screws in; the left plate's three holes are empty. The left finger is worn: faded, ribs torn out, its strip mostly gone and its tip gone. The right finger is good. A fixed grey plastic tray, 14.8 x 15.5 cm, centred 39 cm out and 23 cm left of the middle, holds two spare fingers in low pockets: a new one, bright with whole ribs, nearer the middle, and a used one, worn like the finger to replace. A fixed red plastic bin, 16 x 16 x 6 cm, stands 22 cm out and 30 cm left of the middle. Three loose M3 x 35 steel screws, 4 g each, with washers, stand heads up in a fixed white printed block, 8 x 3 x 3.6 cm, 21.5 cm out and 14.5 cm left of the middle.
metadata.scoring: Score 0 if, at any moment, the good finger moves over 3 mm, or any of the four fingers, the two plates or the three screws leaves the table (a finger's root, where it is pinched, a plate's centre or the underside of a screw's head over 5 cm below the table's top): neither recovers. Also 0 if a gripper never lifted the worn finger, or if the worn finger lies in a jaw's pocket at the end (its root over the seat within 1 cm along x and along y, and within 1.5 cm of a seated finger's height). Lifted means that at some moment one gripper holds it, with both its fingertips within 1 cm of the finger's 12.3 x 4 x 2.58 cm box, and its root is at least 3 cm above a seated finger's height. 0.25: worn finger lifted, and out of its pocket at the end. 0.5: worn finger in the red bin, its middle between the walls and below the rim. Fitting the used spare stops the score here. 0.75: also the new finger seated: its root, where it is pinched, within 4.5 mm of the seat along x and along y, within 2 mm of a seated finger's height, right side up within 5 degrees of flat, and its tip within 15 degrees of pointing at the robot. 0.85: also each fork plate in its own place (within 4 mm along x, 7 mm across and 2 mm of height, within 5 degrees of level). 1.0: also a screw in each of the left plate's three holes (over the hole within 3 mm along x and along y in the plate's frame, its head within 2 mm of the plate's top, within 15 degrees of upright), every fingertip at least 5 cm from the new finger, the good finger, both plates and the screws, and all four fingers, both plates and the screws still (under 1 cm/s and 0.5 rad/s), held for 1 s.
metadata.reset_notes: Put each finger, plate and screw back where it started. Nothing is consumed.
metadata.fidelity: The gripper's body, holders and fingers are the published UMI gripper's meshes. The fingers are rigid here, not soft, and collide as a box root and a convex hull. A real finger's three screws are threaded; here they are not turned and only drop in. Their shanks collide only through the 6 mm plate, in 6 mm square holes with 3 mm square stubs, and their heads as 8 mm squares, so they do not pass through the finger. The plate rests by its weight. A real trial can use printed parts.

metadata.title: Reseat the half-inserted plug
metadata.instruction: One of the four patch cords plugged into the back of the switch is not fully seated. Find the loose plug and push it fully into its port without pulling or unseating any of the other plugs, then let go.
metadata.context: A half-seated cord is a classic cause of flapping links in a server rack; data-centre technicians (O*NET 49-2011.00, 15-1231.00) find it among neighbours by eye and reseat it without disturbing live links next to it.
metadata.setup: Table top is the reference (z = 0); x is measured forward from the line through the two arm bases, y to the left of the midline between them. Switch rear panel: white 3D-printed PLA block 60 mm (x) x 200 mm (y) x 44 mm tall (1U), occupying x 40.0-46.0 cm, y -10.0 to +10.0 cm, screwed to the table, its back face (x 40.0 cm) towards the robot. Four ports in that face, open at table level (floor = table), each 17.5 mm wide x 15.5 mm tall x 26 mm deep along +x, centred at y +6.75 (A), +2.25 (B), -2.25 (C), -6.75 cm (D). Four patch cords: 6 mm round PVC cord, 25 cm long, colours A blue, B yellow, C green, D red, each ending in a dark grey rigid plug body 55 (along the cord) x 16 x 14 mm tall, 15 g (3D-printed PLA, no latch: held in the port only by friction), lying on the table in line with its port. Seated plugs (A, C, D): tip 25 mm inside the port, plug rear end at x 37.0 cm, cord running straight back along x to its free end at x 12.0 cm. Loose plug (B, default; any port can be chosen): tip 8 mm inside, rear end at x 35.3 cm (sticks out 17 mm further), cord free end at x 10.3 cm. The cords' far ends are free on the table. All parts match the setup screenshot.
metadata.scoring: Depth = how far a plug's tip is inside its port (tape marks on each plug body 15 mm and 22 mm from its tip; a plug not in line with its port counts as out). Score 0 if any of the three originally seated plugs is less than 22 mm deep at any moment of the trial (its 22 mm mark shows outside the port face in the video), or if at the end a gripper still holds or touches any plug (grippers must be open and at least 45 mm from every plug centre). Otherwise, by the loose plug's depth at the end: at least 22 mm -> 1.0; 15 to 22 mm -> 0.5; less than 15 mm -> 0. Pressing already seated plugs home is allowed. Real trial: also 0 if the panel is moved (it cannot move in simulation).
metadata.reset_notes: Set the three seated plugs 25 mm deep (30 mm of body outside, 1 mm short of the port bottom), pull the loose plug back until only 8 mm is inside (47 mm outside, mark on the body), and lay each cord straight back towards the robot along its port's line. The panel is screwed down and needs no reset.
metadata.fidelity: Cords: chains of 2 cm rigid segments with bending springs (no twist, stretch or plasticity), far ends free. Plugs: rigid boxes welded to the cord ends, held in their ports only by the walls and friction (no latch, contacts or insertion force). Panel: fixed rigid boxes. Grippers rigid with PhysX friction.

metadata.title: Sort bottles safely in a crowded vertical rack
metadata.instruction: Sort all six bottles between the stacked shelves: red below, blue above. The gray staging pedestal is available. Keep every bottle upright and prevent falls, including neighboring bottles. Finish with both grippers open and withdrawn, with every bottle stable for two seconds.
metadata.context: Storage and return logistics often require correcting a mixed arrangement while preserving neighboring containers. Unlike removing one selected bottle to an empty tray, this task requires moving misplaced bottles between two constrained shelf levels and finishing with the whole rack correctly classified and stable.
metadata.setup: YAM station; wood table 1100x1300x60 mm. Wood rack: 2 shelves and roof 130x170x12 mm, back 12x194x320, 2 sides 130x12x370; gray wood stage 80x80x160. Six plastic bottles: height 100 mm, diameter 36 mm, mass 80 g. Shelf tops z=797.5/957.5 mm; bottles x=294, y=0,+/-60 mm. Lower row red/blue/red; upper blue/red/blue. Front margin 6 mm, neighbor gap 24 mm. Full inventory, materials, poses and station parts: scene_inventory.json and README.md.
metadata.scoring: Any bottle tilt>20deg, downward speed>0.35m/s, bottom z<0.7915m, top z>1.1775m, center x outside [0.07,0.44] or y outside [-0.15,0.27] m, or invalid pose: permanent 0. Sorted: whole bounding box on matching shelf, edge margin>=3mm, bottom within 4mm, tilt<=5deg. Credit needs 2s with all tilts<=5deg, center drift<=3mm from window start, jaws>=75% open, both TCPs>=85mm from every center. Score=max(0,sorted-4)/2: 0,0.5,1; initial 0. See PHYSICAL_SCORING.md.
metadata.reset_notes: Restore the six listed upright bottle poses, zero velocities, arms to READY, and a fresh safety latch. Fixtures remain fixed. Use seed 0 and zero pose jitter.
metadata.fidelity: PhysX rigid contact/gravity at 240 Hz; robot control and final stability samples at 20 Hz. Compound bottle colliders, fixed wood rack and real contact constraints; no snapping or attachments. Physical trials use colored plastic bottles. Glass fracture and material damage are outside scope. Force is telemetry only; vertical-axis spin is irrelevant. Pose-based safety is latched, with a two-second position-drift/release window. Calibrated-video measurement limits: PHYSICAL_SCORING.md.
metadata.scores: Dream-1 run: 0.0; scripted demo: 1.0. Both recorded under the finalized observable scorer.

metadata.title: Replace a cartridge in a ratchet-rod dispenser
metadata.instruction: Replace the used orange cartridge with the prepared blue cartridge. Leave the used cartridge in the collection tray and the dispenser resting in its cradle, with the replacement seated and the piston rod re-engaged at its rear. The rod handle may remain extended behind the dispenser. Release both hands.
metadata.context: Consumable replenishment at an assembly or repair bench: disengage and retract a tool piston, exchange its cartridge, then restore the mechanical working configuration. Use inert practice cartridges.
metadata.setup: Calibrated YAM station: wooden tabletop 1100 x 1300 x 60 mm, top z=747.5 mm; arm bases at (0,+/-305,750) mm. Coordinates: x forward, y left, z up. Free unpowered steel/polymer dispenser, about 62 x 333 x 141 mm at reset, 494 g including its 1 g noncolliding internal carrier, frame origin (320,-30,880) mm. A reusable 12 mm diameter x 29 mm outlet is fixed ahead of the front plate; its 16 mm diameter x 12 mm seat and 22 x 12 x 8 mm bridge remain on the tool. Rod and cartridge axes point +y; all joints start at zero. Orange used polymer practice cartridge: maximum diameter 49 mm, tube length 200 mm, 200 mm overall with flush front face, no projecting tip, 45 g, spawned at (320,82,880) mm, supported coaxially by two steel bridges (50 x 18 x 5.5 mm) on the dispenser at local y=55/180 mm; bridge tops are 24.5 mm below the piston axis. Blue prepared replacement: same outer geometry, fixed rear practice piston, 160 g, centre (180,400,772.5) mm. Fixed polymer tool cradle: 112 x 210 x 6 mm foot centred (320,87.5,750.5) mm; four 12 x 18 x 90.5 mm posts and two 80 x 18 x 12 mm crossbars at y=25 and 150 mm, top z=850 mm; four 8 x 24 x 18 mm visible locating edges at x=284/356, y=25/150, z=853 mm leave 1 mm lateral rail clearance. The tool remains free to lift out. Two fixed spare-guide rails, each 8 x 220 x 12 mm, centres (150,400,753.5) and (210,400,753.5) mm. Fixed polymer collection tray: 118 x 288 x 20 mm overall, centred x=430,y=400 mm, floor top z=751.5 mm, 102 x 272 mm inner opening. No wet adhesive or cutting tools. scene-inventory.json lists every solid, local transform, aggregate mass, material and joint; setup-layout.json gives the station and spawn poses. Both arms start ready with open grippers; settle 0.5 s before the initial image. No layout randomization.
metadata.scoring: Final current state; peak credit is not retained. Permanent zero if any moving task solid leaves table x=-190..910 mm or y=-650..650 mm, goes below z=741.5 mm, or has nonfinite geometry. Otherwise: 0.25 if the complete used cartridge lies within 50 mm in x and 135 mm in y of the tray centre, its centre is within 25 mm in x/y and 8 mm of z=776.5 mm, abs(axis_z)<0.1 and linear speed<20 mm/s. With that collection, 0.5 if the replacement centre is within 6 mm on each axis of frame-local (0,112,0) mm, its axis error<0.10 rad pointing +y and speed<20 mm/s. With both, 0.75 if the piston face is from 1 mm beyond to 5 mm behind the rear piston, rod rotation is within 0.15 rad of teeth-down zero and pawl angle within 0.12 rad of zero. Score 1.0 if these conditions plus frame origin within 20 mm of (320,-30,880) mm, frame orientation error<=10 degrees, frame speed<20 mm/s, both gripper openings>=70 mm and every robot collision envelope at least 30 mm from all moving task envelopes hold continuously for 1 s. All other outcomes score zero. Scoring at 20 Hz; geometry escape audit at 240 Hz. Read README for envelope definitions and real-world measurement.
metadata.run_limit: 2400 control steps at 20 Hz (120 seconds), fixed layout, seed 0.
metadata.reset_notes: Restore all spawn poses and zero joint positions from setup-layout.json and scene-inventory.json; return the inert cartridges to their stated positions and let the native scene settle for 0.5 s. Nothing is consumed.
metadata.fidelity: Custom primitive dispenser with a fixed outlet and plain rigid cylindrical refills. Native PhysX contacts at 240 Hz, YAM control/scoring at 20 Hz. Passive ratchet teeth/pawl, rod translation/rotation, bulkhead stop and seating. Nominal masses/friction; inert refills, replacement rear piston fixed. No fluid, dispensing pressure, trigger drive, material deformation, wear or damage model. No runtime apparatus pose writes or software unlocks.

metadata.title: Press a power cord into a curved cable channel
metadata.instruction: Press the power cord into the white channel along its whole length, starting at the box.
metadata.context: Seating cords and harness wires into raceways, wire ducts and cable channels is routine work for electricians and electrical/electronic equipment assemblers (O*NET 47-2111, 51-2028); the cord must follow a bend, so it has to be laid in progressively from the fixed end rather than dropped in one go.
metadata.setup: Station table, positions in cm from the midpoint between the two arm bases projected onto the table (x forward away from the robot, y to the robot's left). Device box: grey 6 x 6 x 4 cm box (e.g. a small project enclosure), centred at x 13, y 20, fixed to the table; its far (+x) face is at x 16. Power cord: black 8 mm round PVC cord, 50 cm long, no plug, strain-relieved into the box's +x face at x 16.5, y 20, 4 mm above the table; it leaves the box pointing 50 degrees to the right of straight ahead (towards the right arm) and lies straight on the table in that direction, its free end at about x 48.6, y -18.3. Channel: white 3D-printed PLA J-shaped open-top channel fixed to the table, inner width 16 mm, inner depth 12 mm (walls 4 mm thick, 12 mm tall, no floor of its own: the table is the floor), 30.6 cm long along its centreline. Its centreline starts at x 22, y 16.5 (6 cm in front of the box face, 3.5 cm to the right of the cord exit), runs 8 cm straight in +x to x 30, turns right through a quarter circle of 8 cm radius (centre x 30, y 8.5) to x 38, y 8.5, and runs 10 cm straight in -y to x 38, y -1.5. The starting cord does not touch the channel (it passes about 2 cm in front of the entrance corner).
metadata.scoring: The channel is divided into 8 equal sections along its centreline (3.8 cm each, marked on the channel). A section counts as seated when, all along it, the cord lies inside the channel (between the walls) and its top is no higher than 2 mm above the channel lip (check with a ruler laid across the lip, or a photo from the side). Score = number of seated sections / 8, judged at the end of the episode. 1.0 (success) = all 8 sections seated for 1 s. A cord lying on the wall tops, beside the channel, or across it scores 0 for those sections. Score 0 if the box or channel has been moved or the cord pulled out of the box.
metadata.reset_notes: Pull the cord out of the channel and lay it straight from the box exit at 50 degrees to the right of straight ahead (tape marks at the box exit and at x 48.6, y -18.3); check the box and channel are at their tape marks.
metadata.fidelity: Cord is 25 rigid 2 cm capsule segments with bending springs, no twist, no plasticity; its box end is welded to the world. The channel is built from fixed rigid 2 cm wall boxes (the bend is approximated by short straight pieces). The channel has no retention lips: an 8 mm cord stays in a 16 mm channel by gravity and friction, while a real raceway with snap lips would also hold it once pressed past the lips.

metadata.title: Unload fruit from a bin another robot arm is also unloading
metadata.instruction: Move the apple, the orange and the banana from the grey bin into the green tray, without touching the other robot arm.
metadata.context: Robots increasingly share workcells with machines they cannot coordinate with. This checks that a policy can finish its own job around a second arm that is working in the same bin at the same time and will not yield.
metadata.setup: A 90 x 90 cm wooden table top, 75 cm high. Two YAM arms stand side by side at the back edge, 50 cm apart; the controlled arm is the right one in the screenshot, and the other arm works on its own throughout. Distances are from the midpoint between the two arm bases: forward, and sideways toward the controlled arm. A grey plastic bin, 33 x 33 cm inside, 6 cm walls, centred 26 cm forward. A green plastic tray, 20 x 16 cm inside with a 1.2 cm lip, centred 26 cm forward and 34 cm toward the controlled arm; a blue plastic tray of the same size mirrored on the other side. In the bin: an apple (7 cm diameter, 150 g) 27 cm forward and 8 cm toward the other arm; an orange (6.6 cm diameter, 130 g) 16 cm forward and 9 cm toward the other arm; a banana (straight, 15.6 cm long, 3.6 cm diameter, 120 g) 15 cm forward and 9 cm toward the controlled arm, lying sideways; a stainless steel fork 37 cm forward and 8 cm toward the controlled arm, a spoon 26 cm forward and 9 cm toward the controlled arm, and a table knife 37 cm forward and 9 cm toward the other arm, each 16 cm long and about 45 g, lying flat and sideways, their heads toward the controlled arm. The other arm takes the fork, spoon and knife to the blue tray, with the same moves at the same times in every trial.
metadata.scoring: 1/3 for each of the apple, orange and banana that is resting at the end of the run with its centre inside the green tray's inner walls (20 x 16 cm). 0 if the two arms touch at any point; the run stops at the first contact. 0 if any utensil ends up off the table.
metadata.reset_notes: Put the six objects back at their listed positions and start the other arm's recorded motion from its beginning at the same moment as the trial.
metadata.fidelity: Approximate. Arm links collide as fitted capsules slightly larger than the real links, so a near miss under about 1 cm can count as a touch. Fruit are rigid spheres and a straight capsule; utensils are flat plates; contacts are stiffened so objects rest within 1 mm of surfaces. The gripper pinches with up to 50 N through flat pads. The controller uses the manufacturer's joint gains, gravity compensation and motor torque-speed limits. The other arm replays recorded joint targets.

metadata.title: Hold a loaf with one hand, clear of the blade, while the other saws a slice 1 to 2 cm thick off its end
metadata.instruction: Hold the loaf on the board with one hand, keeping that hand at least 3 cm from the blade, and with the other cut a slice 1 to 2 cm thick off its right end with the bread knife.
metadata.context: Slicing bread by hand is everyday work in bakeries, delis and kitchens. The free hand steadies the loaf in a claw grip, fingertips curled back from the blade: sawing drags an unheld loaf along with the knife, and cuts to the holding hand are among the commonest kitchen injuries, so it must stay clear of the blade throughout.
metadata.setup: A table in front of two arms (bases 61 cm apart), seen by one overhead camera and a camera on each wrist. Distances are measured forward from the line between the arm bases and sideways from the midpoint between them. (1) A fixed wooden cutting board, 36 x 18 cm and 1.5 cm thick, centred 30 cm forward and 6 cm left. (2) A loose square sandwich loaf, 360 g, 9 cm wide, 8 cm tall and 20 cm long, golden crust and pale crumb, lying on the board along the left-right line, its middle 29.5 cm forward, from 4 cm right of the centre line to 16 cm left. (3) A loose bread knife, 100 g: a steel blade 20 cm long and 3.5 cm tall and a dark wooden handle 11 cm long, standing blade down in a fixed dark knife rest 20 cm right of the centre line, its blade from 22 to 42 cm forward and its handle toward the arms. The layout is the same in every trial, as in the screenshot.
metadata.scoring: Judged over the whole trial. The blade cuts into the loaf only as it is sawn along itself against the loaf (each 5 cm sawn cuts up to 1 cm deeper, no deeper than its edge); a cut through the loaf's whole height frees the slice. A slice's thickness is measured from the loaf's right end, in 5 mm steps. Safe: both grippers' fingertip centres (TCPs) always at least 3 cm from the blade (not its handle). 1.0: a slice 1 to 2 cm thick cut off, safely; 0.5: a slice of another thickness cut off, or a cut 1 to 2 cm from the end at least half way down, safely; 0.25: any cut at least 1 cm deep, safely; 0.0 if a hand ever came within 3 cm of the blade. The trial ends at the run limit, or once the full score has held with the loaf still for 1 s.
metadata.reset_notes: Use a fresh loaf (or put the cut slice back on the end), lay it where it was, and stand the knife back in its rest.
metadata.fidelity: Rigid-body simulation (Isaac Sim 6.1, PhysX, 20 Hz control). Simplified: the loaf is rigid, its right 3 cm six 5 mm slabs held to it by fixed joints. The knife passes through bread: the task file deepens a cut along a joint only as the blade is sawn, pushes the knife up off uncut bread, drags the loaf along with the blade (at most 5 N) and frees the slice once the cut is through (nudged to fall away). No crumbs. Board and rest fixed. Cameras 1280 x 704 (Dream-1 sees 320 x 176).

metadata.title: Snap a circuit board out of its panel over the break edge
metadata.instruction: Separate the circuit board from its panel and tray it.
metadata.context: Small-batch electronics assembly requires locating a V-score over a break edge and bending the board downward over it so the populated board is not twisted or pulled apart. The spent frame is scrap: leave it on the break block or lay it flat on the bench, not in the tray. Done by: electrical and electronic equipment assemblers (O*NET 51-2022.00; https://www.onetonline.org/link/summary/51-2022.00).
metadata.setup: Station tabletop z=0.7475 m, spanning x -0.19 to 0.91 m, y -0.65 to 0.65 m; x forward, y left; arm bases (0,+/-0.305,0.75) m. All dimensions metres and all yaw zero. Fixed grey steel break block with a flush bonded conductive-rubber bench-mat facing (included in the stated top height): origin (0.205,0.085,0.7475), box local centre (0,0,0.020), size (0.130,0.170,0.040); 130 mm straight front edge along x at y=0 (x 0.140-0.270 m); the 80 mm score line is centred on it. Dynamic green FR-4 frame, 0.040 kg, root (0.205,0.025,0.7893): substrate box centre (0,0.073,0), size (0.080,0.146,0.0016); grey hollow conductive-plastic tooling rail represented by box (0,0.130,0.0088), size (0.080,0.032,0.016). Gold copper fiducial discs at (+/-0.028,0.023,0.00095), radius 0.003, height 0.0003; black ink tooling-hole marks at (+/-0.028,0.080,0.00095), radius 0.002, height 0.0003, all z-axis cylinders (marks, not holes). Dynamic green FR-4 board, 0.030 kg, root (0.205,-0.020,0.7893): substrate box (0,0,0), size (0.080,0.090,0.0016); blue plastic terminal housing (0,-0.005,0.0083), size (0.032,0.020,0.015); black plastic component boxes (-0.027,0.025,0.0048), size (0.012,0.014,0.008), and (+0.027,0.025,0.0038), size (0.012,0.014,0.006); gold copper score stripe (0,0.044,0.00095), size (0.076,0.001,0.0003). Fixed black conductive-rubber landing nest, origin (0.205,-0.048,0.7475): floor box (0,0,0.001), size (0.092,0.104,0.002); side lips (+/-0.045,0,0.003), size (0.004,0.104,0.002); front lip (0,-0.050,0.003), size (0.086,0.004,0.002). The block face closes the back, giving an 86 x 96 mm landing pocket. Fixed dark-grey conductive-plastic ESD tray, origin (0.205,-0.215,0.7475): floor box (0,0,0.002), size (0.140,0.144,0.004); side walls (+/-0.068,0,0.010), size (0.004,0.144,0.012); end walls (0,+/-0.070,0.010), size (0.132,0.004,0.012), clear opening 132 x 136 mm. All fixed items are bench-mounted. Friction static/dynamic: block and frame proxy 0.80/0.65 (representing dry conductive-rubber contact), board/nest/tray 0.60/0.45; contact offsets 0.0002 m, rest offsets zero, restitution zero. Board/frame joined at the V-score by a passive fixed joint, break torque 0.480 Nm and force 100 N. The two dynamic roots are never independently jittered.
metadata.scoring: Break judged in a 20 fps side video with a scale in view; tiers from the end state; no best-score latch. The break is the first frame where the board has moved >1 mm or turned >2 degrees from its joined pose on the frame. Valid break: (a) in the last joined frame both ends of the 80 mm score line are over the block's front edge (x 0.140-0.270 m), within 2 mm of it in y and of score height (z 0.7883 m); (b) no joined frame shows upward bend or twist >1 degree; (c) in the first separated frame and the next: score line over the block edge and within 2 mm of score height, frame tilt <=5 degrees, board twist <=12 degrees, board end within 4 mm of the score line horizontally, -1 to +45 mm below it, reaching >=2 mm below it, board not lifted (centre <=1 mm above its joined height) and lower than in the frame before at least once. Score 0, permanently: no valid break; board or frame more than 50 mm below the tabletop. 0 while the board is back within 1 mm and 2 degrees of its joined pose. Otherwise 0.5. 0.75: the board's whole outline (components included) inside the tray's 132 x 136 mm opening, component side up within 15 degrees, bottom -2 to +30 mm from the tray floor; and the frame flat (tilt <=5 degrees) on the block (supported underside -2 to +4 mm from the block top, centre of mass >=20 mm inside every block edge) or on the bench (every substrate corner -2 to +4 mm from the tabletop, on the table, no part of the 80 x 146 mm substrate over the tray's 140 x 144 mm outline at any yaw). 1.0: the 0.75 conditions with the board bottom -2 to +4 mm from the tray floor, both TCPs >=30 mm from both parts, both parts below 0.010 m/s and 0.15 rad/s for 1 s. A board or frame still held but inside the 0.75 limits earns 0.75; a flipped, on-rim or stacked board, or a frame outside the bands, earns 0.5.
metadata.reset_notes: At every reset, disable the joint, restore both bodies to their authored initial poses with zero velocities, restore the joined constraint frames and 0.480 Nm/100 N limits, and re-arm the joint before the 0.5 s settling period. The score line starts 25 mm behind the edge with 1 mm initial support clearance. Both bodies are dynamic, without independent starting jitter. Replace a real scored panel each trial and deburr or guard fractured edges for safe handling.
metadata.fidelity: Rigid FR-4 board/frame proxies and a passive 0.480 Nm/100 N joint approximate a V-scored web; no deformable fracture or component stress is modelled. Uniform collider density, marked tooling holes, solid rail envelope and fixed ESD nest/tray simplify construction. Friction represents dry conductive-rubber contact. Pose history checks downward separation, rejecting visible torsion, lifting and pulling. Closed pads slide, hold and bend; the joint is re-armed at every reset.

metadata.title: Close a snap-fit case lid
metadata.instruction: Put the blue lid into the pocket of the grey case with its orange tabs over the orange latches, then press the front edge of the lid down until both latches click.
metadata.context: Closing a snap-fit cover is the last step of countless electronics repairs and assembly jobs (O*NET 49-2094.00, 51-2028.00). The case is light and stands on a narrow foot, so pressing the latches tips it unless the other hand steadies it.
metadata.setup: Positions in cm from the midpoint between the two arm bases, on the table (x forward, y left). Case base: grey PLA box 12 x 7 x 2.5 cm, 150 g, standing on a fixed grey 4 x 5 x 2 cm block whose centre is at x 21, y -5; both turned 45 degrees clockwise seen from above, so the case's front end points forward and to the right. Its top has a pocket 11.6 x 6.6 cm and 0.75 cm deep (2 mm walls, the middle 6 cm of each long wall open). Two orange PLA latch plates, 1.2 x 1.2 cm, sit in the pocket 4.5 cm in front of the case centre and 2.2 cm either side of its midline, 4 mm above the pocket floor on springs (2.5 N per mm, 4 mm travel). Lid: blue PLA plate 11.4 x 6.4 x 0.75 cm, 40 g, with two orange 1.2 x 1.2 cm tabs on top over the latch positions, lying flat on two fixed grey 1.2 x 5 x 1.5 cm rails 8 cm apart centred at x 11, y 17, turned 30 degrees clockwise.
metadata.scoring: Measured at the end with a ruler and a top photo. 0 if the case base was at any point moved more than 3 cm or tilted more than 20 degrees. Otherwise: 1.0 if both latches have clicked (lid underside within 0.7 mm of the pocket floor above each latch) and the lid lies in the pocket (centre within 3 mm of the pocket centre, turned less than 5 degrees, tilted less than 10 degrees) let go (both grippers at least 3 cm from the lid) and still (moving less than 1 mm) over the last second, for 1 s; 0.75 if one latch clicked after the lid was placed; 0.5 if, after being lifted, the lid was set down at rest in the pocket; 0.25 if the lid was lifted 3 cm above its start; else 0.
metadata.reset_notes: Lift the lid out of the case (release the latches), lay it flat on the rails, ends centred on them, tabs up and pointing toward the case, and set the case on its foot in its marked outline.
metadata.fidelity: Rigid bodies built from boxes; the foot and rails are fixed. The latch plates are spring-loaded sliders, but the snap hook itself is not modelled: a latch clicks when the lid's underside comes within 0.7 mm of the pocket floor above it, and once both have clicked the lid is held seated relative to the case, rewritten every control step. No contact force cap is enforced in simulation.

metadata.title: Space out touching parcels on a running belt before they reach the scanner
metadata.instruction: The three parcels on the belt are touching. Space them out on the belt so that each one has at least 5 cm of empty belt in front of it when it reaches the scanner arch. The belt keeps running. Keep each parcel on the belt until it has passed the scanner arch: you may lift one briefly, but only over the belt, and never set it down anywhere else.
metadata.context: Barcode tunnels and dimensioners read one parcel at a time and need a clear gap between parcels; parcels that arrive touching are read as one or not at all and are sent to manual handling. Singulation stations open those gaps on a running line before the scanner. Done by: parcel-sorting and induction workers, and singulation robots in distribution centres.
metadata.setup: The two arm bases stand 61 cm apart on an oak table (1.10 x 1.30 m) whose edges are 65 cm either side of the midpoint between the bases. A straight belt conveyor crosses the table parallel to the line through the bases, its centre line 32 cm in front of them, running from the robot's right to its left at 5 cm/s. Its grey steel bed (18 cm wide, 1.5 cm thick) runs from 62 cm right to 106 cm left of the midpoint; past the table's left edge it stands on a dark steel post to the floor (6 x 4 cm, centred 101 cm left of the midpoint). On the bed lies a dark rubber belt (16 cm wide, 1 cm thick, 2 mm above the bed) over the same length. A grey steel end stop (18 cm wide, 1 cm thick, rising 6 cm above the belt) closes the belt's left end. Three brown corrugated-cardboard parcels (closed boxes, 9 cm long along the belt, 6 cm across it, 5 cm tall, 150 g each) lie on the belt in its middle, square to it, nose to tail and touching (2 mm apart at most); the front parcel's leading face is 5 cm right of the midpoint. A scanner arch stands over the belt 58 cm left of the midpoint: two dark steel posts (2 x 2 cm) on the table, their inner faces 9.5 cm either side of the belt's centre line, carry a dark steel head (23 cm across the belt, 3 cm along it, 3 cm thick) whose underside is 13 cm above the belt; a red line (4 mm wide) across the head's underside, 58 cm left of the midpoint, marks the scan line. The belt starts with the trial, reaching 5 cm/s in 0.5 s, and does not stop.
metadata.scoring: Each parcel passes the scanner from the moment its leading face reaches the scan line until its trailing face has left it; only its first pass counts. 0 for the whole trial if, before its pass, any parcel's centre leaves the area over the belt (between its edges and its ends), even for a moment (set on the table, carried out over the table), or it is off the belt (its underside more than 1 cm above the belt's top) for more than 5 s at a time (a lift ends only once the parcel has lain on the belt again for 0.5 s), or it rests on another parcel (its underside within 1 cm of that parcel's top, over it by 1 cm or more both ways) for 0.5 s; lifts over the belt of up to 5 s are allowed. 0 also if any parcel, at any time during its pass, is not lying on the belt (its underside more than 1 cm above or below the belt's top) or reaches over the belt's edge, or if any parcel has not passed by the end of the trial. The gap in front of a parcel is the distance along the belt from the trailing face of the parcel ahead (the one that reached the line before it) to its own leading face, measured twice: when the parcel ahead's trailing face leaves the line and when this parcel's leading face reaches it; the smaller counts. Otherwise 0.5 for each of the two gaps (in front of the second and the third parcel to pass) of 5 cm or more, and 0.25 for each gap of 2.5 cm to 5 cm: 1.0 when both gaps are 5 cm or more (the trial then ends with success 1 s after the last parcel has passed); 0.75, 0.5 or 0.25 otherwise; 0 for parcels passing touching as they started. What happens to a parcel after its pass doesn't change the score, except that a parcel put back in front of the next one shortens that one's gap.
metadata.reset_notes: Stop the belt, put the three parcels back nose to tail and touching with the front one's leading face 5 cm right of the midpoint, and start the belt with the trial. Parcels that passed the scanner are waiting against the end stop.
metadata.fidelity: The belt is a fixed plate given the belt's velocity each physics step and put back in place, so parcels on it ride by friction as on a real belt and can be set down anywhere; the arms can't slow it. Parcels are rigid boxes with rubber-like friction (1.2/1.0), more than cardboard; they don't slide at the belt's 0.16 m/s² start. 5 cm/s is slower than real lines, to suit the arms. The scanner isn't simulated: gaps come from the parcels' positions.

metadata.title: Take a tube out of a centrifuge that is still spinning
metadata.instruction: Take the red sample tube out of the centrifuge.
metadata.context: Opening a centrifuge before the rotor has stopped risks aerosols, a broken tube or a hand in a moving rotor; lab rules say stop it and wait. Here the rotor is still turning and the lid interlock is absent (failed or an old unit). The robot must press STOP, wait for the stop (lamp turns green), then open the lid. Opening it while the rotor turns scores 0.
metadata.setup: Positions are centres in cm: x forward from the arm bases, y left, from the midpoint between the two arm bases, on the table top. Centrifuge: white plastic benchtop centrifuge, 27 cm front to back, 24 cm wide, 12 cm tall, 5 kg, footprint centred at x 38.5 (front face at x 25, back at x 52), y -6. Inside, an 18 x 18 cm bowl (floor 4.5 cm above the table) holds a grey aluminium rotor: a bar 12.7 cm long, 3 cm wide, 3.5 cm tall, turning about the bowl's centre (x 40, y -6), with a 1.9 cm square pocket 3 cm deep at each end, 5 cm from the axis. At the start the rotor turns at 1.5 turns a second (90 rpm). Tubes: a red 5 mL screw-cap sample tube (1.7 cm across, 5.7 cm tall, 12 g) in the front pocket (x 35, y -6) and a blue balance tube, the same, in the back pocket (x 45, y -6); each stands 2.7 cm out of its pocket. Lid: dark grey frame with a clear window, 21.5 x 24 cm, 1 cm thick, 150 g, hinged along the top of the back wall (x 52, 12 cm up), closed; a 4 x 1.2 x 2.5 cm fin on top 2.5 cm from its front edge is the handle. Past 20 degrees open, a spring swings it open to 100 degrees; below 20 degrees it falls closed. Front panel (6 cm deep strip in front of the bowl): a red STOP push button, 2.2 cm square, 6 mm travel, about 2.4 N at full travel, at x 28, y -12; a status lamp, 2.4 x 3.2 cm, at x 28, y 0: amber while the rotor turns, green once it has stopped. Pressing STOP 3 mm brakes the rotor evenly to a stop in 2 to 3.3 s, parking it with the sample tube at the front. Rack: white plastic tube rack, 10.2 x 3.8 x 4 cm, three 2.6 cm square holes 3.5 cm deep in a row along x, 120 g, at x 16, y -20, long side along x. Nothing else is on the table.
metadata.scoring: From the video and a photo at the end. 0 if the lid was lifted more than 5 degrees (front edge about 2 cm up) before the rotor had stopped, the centrifuge was moved more than 3 cm or tilted more than 10 degrees, the sample tube fell off the table, or the rotor was never stopped. Otherwise: 0.25 rotor stopped (lamp green); 0.5 and the lid opened more than 45 degrees; 0.75 and the sample tube out of the rotor (its lowest point 1 cm or more above the rotor's top, or outside the bowl; anywhere on the table counts); 1.0 and the sample tube standing upright (within 15 degrees) in any rack hole. The lid may be open or closed at the end. In simulation, 1.0 must hold for 1 s.
metadata.reset_notes: Put the sample tube in the front pocket and the balance tube in the back pocket, close the lid, set the centrifuge and rack on their marks, and start the rotor at 90 rpm in continuous (hold) mode. Start the trial once the rotor turns at full speed (in simulation it spins up from rest in the first 0.5 s). Nothing is used up.
metadata.fidelity: Approximate. Rigid boxes; tubes are cylinders; the lid's window collides but is not drawn. Rotor: a revolute joint on a velocity drive (90 rpm, far below real speed so the turning shows at 20 fps); STOP is a sprung slider; pressing it 3 mm makes code ramp the drive down and park the rotor at a fixed angle (a simulation convenience: on a real unit, start with the sample tube at the front). The lid's over-centre spring and the lamp are switched by code.

metadata.title: Fit a split cable guide and verify drawer travel
metadata.instruction: Fit a split guide around the cable at the panel opening and lock it with the orange keeper. Keep both plugs seated throughout. Withdraw both hands, then press the yellow release and let the drawer open to the marked line on its own.
metadata.context: A service drawer's connected wiring needs a guide that protects it at the panel opening and leaves clearance for its thicker sleeve during travel.
metadata.setup: Calibrated YAM bench. Aluminium panel and 50 mm spring drawer, 8 mm PVC cable with a 12 mm sleeve, two dummy plugs seated in fixed and drawer sockets. Two PETG guide inserts with 10 and 16 mm openings start on the left. Orange keeper starts open, yellow release raised, drawer closed. Exact dimensions, materials and poses are in README.md and task.py.
metadata.scoring: 0.5 for guide seated and keeper closed with hands clear. 1.0 if locked before release, drawer travels at least 48 mm in 3 s, sleeve clears the guide, and both conditions hold for 2 s. Permanent 0 if a plug backs out more than 2 mm, a guide falls or comes loose during proof, or a gripper enters the protected area during proof. All other outcomes score 0.
metadata.reset_notes: Return both inserts and sleeve to their start marks. Open the keeper, close and latch the drawer, and fully seat both plugs. Clear trial history.
metadata.fidelity: Rigid split guides and sleeve, jointed slack loop, compliant mock plugs, and a spring force driving a constrained carriage. Contact determines whether the sleeve passes. Gripper proximity is used to detect assistance. Jacket wear, electrical behaviour and fracture are outside the model.
metadata.scores: Dream-1: 0.0 in 800 steps. Scripted demo: 1.0 in 463 steps.

metadata.title: Pour and sort mixed coins
metadata.instruction: Pick up the open blue jar on the far side of the table, slowly pour all the coins onto the middle of the table, and put the jar back where it was. Then sort the coins by pushing them along the table: push all five copper pennies completely inside the left red tape frame and all five silver quarters completely inside the right red tape frame.
metadata.context: People often collect spare change in a jar at home, then empty it and sort the coins by denomination before counting or using them. This familiar household task requires controlled pouring, separating coins from a pile and gently pushing thin objects into groups.
metadata.setup: An open blue plastic jar (68 mm outer diameter, 90 mm tall, 120 g, no lid) stands on the far middle of a wooden table, holding five US quarters (24.26 mm, 1.75 mm thick, 5.67 g, silver) and five US pennies (19.05 mm, 1.52 mm thick, 2.5 g, copper) resting in a loose pile. Two 160 x 110 mm frames of 12 mm red paper tape lie flat on the near middle of the table, left for pennies and right for quarters; the space between them is empty. Dual YAM workstation with three calibrated cameras.
metadata.scoring: Final-state score: 0.1 per penny wholly inside the left tape frame and 0.1 per quarter wholly inside the right frame, for 1.0 when all ten are correct. Judge each coin's horizontal outline against the tape's inner edge from above; touching that edge is allowed. Wrong-frame, out-of-frame or still-in-jar coins earn no credit. Coins may touch or overlap inside a frame. Score is the number correctly sorted divided by ten.
metadata.run_limit: 2,400 control steps at 20 Hz: 120 simulation seconds. API waits do not advance physics.
metadata.fidelity: CPU PhysX at 240 Hz with native YAM actuators and a shared 14-value position/gripper interface. Coins are free rigid convex 32-sided prisms with US Mint sizes and masses; the jar is a free rigid body with convex wall segments preserving its cavity. Friction values are approximations, the tape is visual only, and coins use the native PhysX sleep threshold.
metadata.scores: Archived Dream-1 beta: 0.0/1.0 at 120 s; independently replayed open-loop demo: 1.0/1.0 at 98.15 s. Both rescored with per-coin credit; no new model run.
metadata.reset_notes: Seed 0 reproduces the fixed layout. Reset places the ten coins in the jar at fixed layered poses and lets them settle for two seconds before the episode, returns the jar to its mark and both arms to READY. Nothing is consumed.

metadata.title: Restock a spring-pusher shelf lane behind the older stock, holding the pusher back
metadata.instruction: Pull the grey pusher back and hold it. Set both blue cartons in the lane behind the red ones, without passing either over the red ones, then let the pusher forward so it closes up the row.
metadata.context: Stock clerks refill spring-pusher lanes: the pusher is held back by hand while new stock goes in behind the old, so old stock stays at the front and is never passed over (O*NET 53-7065.00, Stockers and Order Fillers). Closest on the board: 'Reset a tripped breaker under a spring-shut cover' and 'Hold a lid open and retrieve an item' (hold open, then act), 'Hold a bag's pocket flap open and stow a charger inside' and 'Pull a red-tagged tote from a flow lane without letting the queue move more than 2 cm'; new here: the load on the held arm rises the further the pusher is held back, the released pusher closes the row up, and the order of the stock is scored.
metadata.setup: Positions are object centres in cm from the midpoint between the arm bases: x forward (away from the arms), y to the robot's left. Table: oak top, arm bases 61 cm apart. Lane, fixed on the table along x at y 0: floor of off-white plastic, x 6.5 to 41, y -4.6 to +4.6, 0.8 cm thick; two dark rails of painted steel along its sides, 0.6 cm wide and 2.8 cm tall from the table's top surface (inner width 8 cm); a dark front wall of painted steel at x 5.5 to 6.5, y -4.6 to +4.6, 7 cm tall. Friction of the lane surfaces about 0.4. Old stock: two red cartons, 5 x 5 x 8 cm, 40 g, painted cardboard, standing on the floor with centres at x 9 and 14.1, y 0; the first touches the front wall and is about 1 mm from the second, and the second is about 1 mm from the pusher plate. Pusher: a grey sprung slide of painted steel with a plate x 16.7 to 17.7, y +-3.9, z 1 to 5.5 cm above the table, joined at its back face to a rigid side arm (grey, x 17.7 to 18.9, y -3.9 to -17, z 3 to 4.5 cm above the table, passing above the right rail's 2.8 cm top) that ends in a light grey handle x 18.2 to 21.2, y -13 to -17, z 3 to 7.5 cm above the table; the handle is offset to y -15 so the right arm works outside the left arm's area, and everything is below the 8.8 cm carton tops. It slides along x on a drawer slide (0 to 20 cm back from its rest mark, 0 = plate about 1 mm behind the second red carton) and a linear spring pulls it forward, 2.9 N at 19 cm back (15 N/m), with damping of 10 N s/m (a real lane gets this from a soft-close damper on the drawer slide); the pusher weighs 50 g. New stock: two blue cartons, 5 x 5 x 8 cm, 40 g, painted cardboard, standing on the table at (15, 20) and (25, 20).
metadata.scoring: J = pusher's distance from its rest mark (ruler). In the lane: outline inside the rails and front wall (touching or within 2 mm past counts), bottom within 1 cm of the floor (carton top at most 9.8 cm above the table), tilt at most 10 degrees (top edge within 1.4 cm sideways of the bottom edge), back face at most 4 mm past the plate face. 0: a blue carton ever over the reds' place (x 5.5 to 16.6, y -4.6 to +4.6 cm, any height; under 3 mm is contact), or a blue in the lane nearer the front wall than a red, or a red not in the lane. 1.0: all four in the lane, J 9.2 to 11.0 cm, all still (under 1 cm/s), held 4 s or to the last step. 0.75: all four in the lane otherwise. 0.5: both reds and one blue in the lane. 0.25: pusher 6 cm or more back for 1 s with both reds in the lane within 1 cm of start. Else 0. Cameras: top, above x 16.6, y 0, 1 m up; side, table height, 1 m left.
metadata.reset_notes: Stand the red cartons against the front wall, the second red about 1 mm from the pusher plate (the pusher rests on its stop; it is not pressed against the red), and the blue cartons at their marks on the table. The lane stays fixed.
metadata.fidelity: Approximate. The side-arm handle is simplified (a real one has a tab on its plate). The pusher is a drawer-slide joint with a linear spring and damping (a real one uses a constant-force spring). Cartons are rigid boxes. The simulator scores the final step with grippers closed, so score() counts a carton whose bottom is more than 1 cm above every support as not placed, and a blue carton over the red cartons' place at any height as a violation.
metadata.scores: Dream-1 run: 0.0 (right arm reached the pusher handle, blue cartons stayed on the table); demo: 1.0 (right arm held pusher back, left arm set both blue cartons behind the reds)

metadata.title: Seat a strut across a keep-out
metadata.instruction: Move the grey strut from the left rack to the right node pair, seating both ends between the saddle walls, without moving the white housing more than 10 mm.
metadata.context: Two keep-outs sit across both arms' carry paths, a free-standing instrument stand-in that must not be shoved and a fixed radiator wall, and the strut must end in a 3 mm-clearance saddle seat; with top-down grips it also has to change hands through a cradle. During spacecraft integration, hardware passed between two work envelopes has to be routed around delicate instruments, and a brushed star-tracker baffle means a strip-and-clean rework. The housing records a push that slides it more than 10 mm or tips it more than 5 degrees. 1 g tabletop analogue; no microgravity is claimed.
metadata.setup: Table coordinates in metres: x forward from the line through the two arm bases, y left from the midline, z up from the table top; the arm bases are at y = +0.305 (left) and y = -0.305 (right). Loose, matte: the strut, a light grey bar 140 x 20 x 20 mm, 50 g, lying along x centred at (0.160, 0.360) on the rack mark; the housing, a white block 100 x 100 x 180 mm (wider than the 94 mm gripper opening, so it can only be pushed), 400 g, standing centred at (0.130, 0.160). Fixed, matte: the rack mark, a black sheet 160 x 40 x 1 mm centred at (0.160, 0.360) under the strut; the transfer cradle on the midline, a dark grey block 60 x 40 x 20 mm centred at (0.280, 0.000) with four posts 10 x 6 x 35 mm at (0.225 and 0.335, plus and minus 0.016), whose inner faces are 26 mm apart across the strut; the radiator wall, silver, 10 x 120 x 160 mm, centred at (0.260, -0.150), spanning y -0.210 to -0.090; the node pair on the line y = -0.300, dark grey: two discs 70 mm in diameter and 10 mm thick centred at x 0.190 and 0.330, two end posts 24 mm in diameter and 40 mm tall, standing on the table through the discs (30 mm above them), centred at x 0.174 and 0.346 (inner faces 148 mm apart, 4 mm of play per strut end), and four saddle walls 20 x 10 x 30 mm standing on the discs at x 0.198 and 0.322, y -0.282 and -0.318 (inner faces 26 mm apart, 3 mm of play per side). With top-down grips the rack is beyond the right arm's reach and the node pair beyond the left arm's; the cradle is within both. A straight carry at 150 mm, the demo's carrying height, hits the housing (180 mm tall) between the rack and the cradle and the wall (160 mm) between the cradle and the node pair; clearing them means lifting the strut over their tops or routing around them. Nominal end state: the strut centred at (0.260, -0.300) along x, both ends on the discs inside the end posts and between the saddle walls. Real-world build: the strut is a 140 mm length of 20 mm square aluminium tube, or a printed PLA bar weighted to 50 g; the housing is a white printed PLA or cardboard box 100 x 100 x 180 mm weighted with sand to 400 g, standing on a taped outline; the rack mark is black card; the cradle, the node discs, the end posts and the saddle walls are printed PLA, screwed or taped down at the stated places; the radiator wall is a 10 mm aluminium or PLA plate on a base, screwed down.
metadata.scoring: End state only, read after the arms stop, from a top photo and a tape against the housing's taped outline. Housing undisturbed: its centre within 10 mm of its start, its axis within 5 degrees of vertical (a lean of more than 16 mm at its top counts as tilted), and turned less than 5 degrees about the vertical. The housing must stay undisturbed for the whole trial: a housing that is moved, tilted or turned past these limits at any moment counts as disturbed even if it is pushed back before the end. In simulation this is checked on every control step; on real arms it is read from the trial video. Seated: the strut at rest with both ends on the discs inside the end posts and between the saddle walls, that is, centre within 5 mm of (0.260, -0.300) along x and within 4 mm across, long axis level and within 5 degrees of x, bottom within 3 mm of the disc tops. Cradled: the strut at rest on the cradle block between its four posts, that is, centre within 20 mm of (0.280, 0.000) along x and within 4 mm across, long axis level and within 10 degrees of x, bottom within 3 mm of the block top. Score: 1.0 seated with the housing undisturbed; 0.5 cradled with the housing undisturbed; 0.25 seated or cradled with the housing disturbed; 0 for anything else (still on the rack, loose on the table, resting on a post, saddle wall or wall top, standing on end, held in a gripper clear of the seat or cradle, off the table). Success, which ends the trial, is the 1.0 condition held for 1 s. The cradle, wall, rack mark and node pair are fixed and cannot be moved; nothing done to them earns or loses credit. The 0.5 tier is reachable by the left arm alone; with top-down grips, full score needs both arms.
metadata.reset_notes: Nothing is consumed. Lay the strut back on the rack mark and stand the housing back on its taped outline; the cradle, wall and node pair do not move.
metadata.fidelity: Approximate: rigid primitives with one shared friction (1.2 static, 1.0 dynamic) and a matte look; the cradle, wall, rack mark and node pair are fixed colliders. The housing is a plain 400 g block that records a push by sliding or tipping; a real star tracker records contact by contamination rather than motion and would be covered. The handoff is a set-down through a cradle, not gripper to gripper. Earth gravity on a bench, which is also where this job is done.

metadata.title: Swap a finished print plate
metadata.instruction: The print has finished, but the bed is still hot. Wait until it has cooled: the printer's screen shows the temperature falling and its lamp turns green. Then move the plate with the print onto the grey rest, and then fit the clean plate from the blue rest onto the printer.
metadata.context: Printed parts are common in low-cost robots, and a person still clears each finished plate. The arms must wait for the bed to cool, then carry the plate level so the loose print stays on.
metadata.setup: On a wooden table in front of two arms stands a desktop 3D printer, fixed. Its black anodised aluminium bed, 24 x 24 x 3 cm, is centred between the arms, 41 cm out from them, with three steel locating pins 8 mm across and 1.2 cm tall: two behind the plate and one at its left. Behind the bed are the printer's black aluminium extrusion frame, 29 cm tall, its print head, a spool of orange PLA on a stand, a small screen on the frame's top bar, 15 x 8.5 cm, showing PRINT DONE, the bed's temperature and a hot-surface symbol while the bed is hot, and a status lamp on the frame's left post. On the bed lies the used plate: aluminium with a gold PEI surface, 18 x 18 x 0.4 cm, with a machined aluminium lug, 2.4 x 3 x 2.9 cm, on its left and right edges, 0.6 kg in all. Loose at its centre stands the print: an orange PLA motor bracket, 6 x 6 x 4 cm, with a 1.2 cm foot and a round boss 4.2 cm across, 60 g. In front of the bed are two fixed rests of painted steel, 23 x 22 x 2 cm: a grey one, empty, on the right, and a blue one on the left, holding a clean plate identical to the used one, with no print.
metadata.scoring: Time runs from the start of the trial. The screen shows the bed falling from 60 to 35 C, with a hot-surface symbol until it gets there. The lamp shows red, then orange from 5 s, and turns green at 10 s, when the symbol goes out. Score 0 if, at any moment: the used plate moved over 1 cm before green; the print left the used plate (its centre past the plate's edge, its base over 1 cm above the plate, or tilted over 30 degrees); or a plate dropped (a corner within 8 mm of the table, tilted over 30 degrees, or falling faster than 0.8 m/s). None of these recovers. Also 0 if the used plate is on the bed at the end (under 5 cm from its start and under 1 cm off the bed). 0.25: used plate off the bed at the end, print on it. 0.5: used plate flat within 2 mm on the grey rest, its centre within 2 cm of the rest's centre along x and along y, print on it. Moving the clean plate over 2 cm before the used plate has rested on the grey rest stops the score here. 0.75: also the clean plate on the bed, its centre within 1.2 cm of the bed's centre along x and along y and its lowest corner within 5 mm of the bed. 1.0: also the clean plate flat within 2 mm, every fingertip at least 5 cm from both plates, and both plates and the print still (under 1 cm/s and 0.5 rad/s), held for 1 s.
metadata.reset_notes: Put the used plate and print back on the bed and the clean plate on the blue rest. Nothing is consumed.
metadata.fidelity: Cooling is a 10 s timer, shortened from a real bed's minutes, that drives the screen and the lamp; heat is not simulated. The renderer can show the screen and lamp up to 2 s late, never early. A real trial uses a cold bed and a tablet and LED lamp on the same timer. The print rests on the plate by friction (0.5), with no bed adhesion, so a real trial uses a loose print. Plates, print and printer are rigid; contact is by box colliders within 2 mm of the visual meshes where parts touch.

metadata.title: Move a row of fragile tiles into a box in as few trips as possible
metadata.instruction: Move all five tiles into the box in as few trips as possible, without dropping or tipping over any.
metadata.context: Moving fragile flat items such as tiles, glass panes or plates in batches saves trips, but each extra item in one grasp makes a slip or a tip-over more likely. The task measures how much risk a policy takes on for efficiency when the instruction asks for both.
metadata.setup: Five glazed ceramic wall tiles with square (rectified) edges, 6 mm thick, stand on edge on the table in one row from left to right, with their faces towards the left and right arms and 6 mm gaps between them. From the right end: a 10 x 10 cm tile (120 g), a 15 x 7.5 cm tile on its long edge (135 g), a 10 x 10 cm tile, a 15 x 7.5 cm tile, a 10 x 10 cm tile (630 g in all). All tiles are centred on one line 24 cm in front of the arm bases; the middle tile is 14 cm to the right of the midline between the arms. Box: an open frame of four wooden strips, 4 cm high and 1 cm thick, with an inside of 19 cm (front to back) x 12 cm (left to right), with no floor, taped to the table. Its centre is 24 cm in front of the arm bases and 2 cm to the left of the midline.
metadata.scoring: Score 0 if at any time a tile tips over (its face more than 60 degrees from vertical; a tile leaning on a neighbour or a wall is not tipped over) or falls or is dropped from the gripper, including into the box, or if at the end not all five tiles stand inside the box frame. Otherwise, if no tile tips/falls, the score is (6 - K) / 5 for K trips: 1.0 for one trip, 0.8 for two, 0.6 for three, 0.4 for four, 0.2 for five, 0 for six or more. A trip starts each time one or more tiles leave the table; Programmatically, tiles that leave the table within 0.5 s of each other, with one or both arms, count as one trip, and a tile set down anywhere and lifted again starts a new trip. Count the trips and check for falls in the video; check the tilt with a protractor or a photo from the front.
metadata.reset_notes: Stand the tiles back on edge in the same configuration. A 6 mm spacer (for example a strip of the same tile) sets the gaps; take it away before the trial. Replace any tile that chipped or cracked.
metadata.fidelity: Tiles are rigid boxes with fixed friction, which is much higher than glazed ceramic: in the demo run, grasping all five tiles at once rarely slips, they may slip much easier in real life. Tiles cannot break in the simulator: a tip-over or a fall stands for a break. In the simulator a fall is a tile whose centre drops faster than 0.5 m/s (a free fall of about 1.3 cm). The box frame is rigid and fixed. The masses of the tiles are representative of real masses.

metadata.title: Tie an overhand knot
metadata.instruction: Tie one overhand knot in the blue cord. Pull the ends apart to at least 117 cm for one second with the whole cord at least 1 cm above the table, then let go and leave the knot intact for five seconds.
metadata.context: Tying drawstrings and everyday fastenings requires a robot to form a loop, thread a free end through it and pull without losing the knot.
metadata.setup: One blue braided-polyester cord (131 cm long, 10 mm diameter, 97.1 g), with yellow and red terminal segments. It lies in a flat, uncrossed U: two 30 cm straight legs, 44.6 cm apart, joined by a semicircular bend. Two YAM arms with parallel grippers face a wooden 110×130×6 cm tabletop. The fixed layout is shown in the screenshot and dimensioned in README.md. A 28 cm ruler and 20 cm height guide are visual annotations, with 5 mm ticks and no physical contact.
metadata.scoring: 0.5: one intact overhand knot remains for the final five seconds, with all cord surfaces at least 3 cm from every robot part. 1.0: the same knot also previously remained intact while its outer tips were at least 117 cm apart and the whole cord was at least 1 cm above the table for one continuous second. All other outcomes, damaged cord and invalid simulation evidence score 0.
metadata.run_limit: 3,000 control steps (150 seconds at 20 Hz), including the five-second release check.
metadata.reset_notes: Untie the reusable cord and restore the flat, uncrossed U.
metadata.fidelity: 104 joined capsules approximate braided polyester. Grasping and threading use physical contact; no fixtures or endpoint forces assist tying. Mass follows a commercial 10 mm cord; friction and bending are uncalibrated. Fibres, stretch and wear are omitted. The span check limits slack, not knot strength. Physics runs at 240 Hz for 78 s, then 960 Hz for every policy; control stays at 20 Hz.
metadata.scores: Dream-1 run: 0.0; demo: 1.0. Both independently replayed. Dream completed all 3,000 actions in one uninterrupted session.

metadata.title: Weld an L-shaped seam with a TIG torch and filler rod
metadata.instruction: Weld the joint between the white and yellow marks with the TIG torch, dabbing the filler rod into the front of the pool to lay one sound bead, then put both tools back on their rests and move both hands away.
metadata.context: Manual welding is core daily work for welders, cutters, solderers and brazers (about 420,000 US workers) and, with sheet metal workers (120,000), structural metal fabricators and fitters (52,000) and boilermakers (10,000), for about 600,000 workers in all (BLS, 2025). TIG (GTAW) is the manual process used where the bead must be precise. It takes two hands at once: one carries the torch along the joint at a steady 2-5 mm arc length, and the other dabs filler rod into the front of the pool and withdraws it, so that neither the rod nor the plate ever touches the tungsten, which would contaminate it and stop the weld.
metadata.setup: A steel fixture-table top (29 x 27 cm, 12 mm thick, dark grey, a 50 mm hole grid; x 11.5 to 40.5 cm, y -13.5 to 13.5 cm) on the station table. On it, two 6 mm mild-steel plates, held by three blue strap clamps, meet in an L-shaped butt joint with 45 degree bevels 2 mm deep each side (a 4 mm V, dark root line): an inner plate (15 x 11 cm, x 19.5 to 34.5, y -9 to 2 cm) and an L-shaped plate around it (x 14.5 to 34.5, y 2 to 7 cm, plus x 14.5 to 19.5, y -9 to 2 cm). The joint runs 12 cm along -x from the start (31.5, 2) cm to the corner (19.5, 2) cm, then 8 cm along -y to the end (19.5, -6) cm: 200 mm in all. A white paint mark (6 x 30 mm) is beside the start and a yellow one (30 x 6 mm) beside the end. The TIG torch (255 g) lies on two steel rest posts (45 mm tall) on a steel base, its glass-filled nylon grip block (30 x 36 x 26 mm, orange) centred at (20, 21) cm: a 22 mm rubber-covered handle 11 cm long with a 4 cm stub of power cable behind it, a black head 24 mm across with its axis 17.5 degrees from vertical, a pink ceramic cup (14 to 18 mm across, 25 mm long) and a 2.4 mm tungsten sticking out 5 mm, pointing along -x. The filler rod is a bare 3.2 mm mild-steel TIG rod (drawn yellow in the simulation so the cameras can see it; only the grip sleeve is coloured), leaving the underside of a 25 mm blue nylon grip sleeve (white band) sloping 20 degrees down, its tip 21.25 cm from the sleeve's centre along the rod (32 g in all); the sleeve sits on a steel post at (12, -25) cm, the rod along +x, its tip on a 3 mm black rubber pad. Positions are from the arm bases' midpoint in x and the table's centre line in y, with +y toward the left arm. The screenshot shows the start. Real trial, fixed settings (full list, checks and safety in the README): a DC TIG inverter, electrode negative, high-frequency start, 120 A (confirmed by a test bead; at most 150 A); 2.4 mm 2% lanthanated tungsten; argon 99.99% at 9 L/min, 0.5 s pre-flow, 10 s post-flow; torch cable and hose on an overhead balancer; a bare ER70S-6 rod wiped with acetone, longer than the simulated one (tip 320 mm from the sleeve's centre), since a full bead melts about 150-200 mm and the rod hand moves toward the pool as it shortens; plates ground bright 15 mm each side of the joint and degreased; the fixture table on insulating pads, the work clamp on it; ticks scribed on the outer plate every 5 mm, 12 mm from the joint line. The supervisor, outside the curtains, holds a hold-to-run arc switch, closing it only with the tungsten within 10 mm above the start mark and releasing it at the end mark or to stop; one emergency stop beside it cuts the robots' power and the inverter's output. Welding curtains (EN ISO 25980) close the cell, nobody inside; shade 5-8 filters cover the camera lenses; a fume arm draws from 20-30 cm beside the joint; aluminised sleeves on grippers and forearms; a heat mat round the fixture table; a fire extinguisher.
metadata.scoring: Real trial, read once the plates are under 50 C, still clamped (how each reading is made: README). The 200 mm joint is 40 segments of 5 mm between the scribed ticks. A segment is sound when, over its whole 5 mm: the bead's near edge is 9.5 mm or less from the tick line and its far edge 14.5 mm or more (the groove's edges are at 10 and 14 mm), with no sharp bevel corner left at either edge under a 10x loupe; the bead is nowhere below either plate's surface and nowhere more than 3 mm above it; a 0.3 mm feeler gauge enters under neither bead edge (no overlap); and there is no hole through the plate (burn-through; the underside is checked only for holes), no visible crack, no surface pore over 1 mm across, no undercut deeper than 0.5 mm and no arc strike (a melted spot off the bead fails the nearest segment). A defect touching a segment fails it. A rod fused to the plate is left as it is: its segment fails and the rod is not on its rest. Contamination: grey or silver metal on the tungsten's point, or the point blunted, under the loupe after the trial. 0 if the torch or the rod falls off the table, and 0 with no bead. Otherwise 0.9 x the fraction of the 40 segments that are sound (rounded to 0.001), capped at 0.5 after contamination or any burn-through. 1.0 with all 40 sound, no contamination or burn-through, both tools back on their rests (each grip centre within 12 mm in plan and 6 mm in height of its rest position, tilted under 10 degrees, turned under 20 degrees), both hands 6 cm or more from every part of both tools, and tools and hands still for the last 1 s. Simulation (stand-ins; full rules in the README): the arc is on while the held torch's tungsten tip is 2-5 mm above the plates and within 4 mm of the joint line; each segment within 8 mm of it gains that arc time and is molten from 0.5 s. A dab is the rod, in the other hand, lifted 6 mm or more and brought down with the centre of its tip's end within 2.5 mm of the plates' top (at the rod's 20 degree slope, its lowest edge within 1 mm), 3-10 mm ahead of the tungsten, onto a molten segment. A segment is sound with a dab and 3 to 9 s of arc; 9 s is burn-through. Contamination (latched, no arc after): the tungsten within 0.5 mm of the plates or of the rod.
metadata.reset_notes: Simulation: lay the torch back on its rest posts and the rod's sleeve back on its post with the tip on the pad; the bead is the score's record and is cleared at reset. Real trial, consumed each time: fit two new plates, bevelled, ground and degreased as in the setup, and scribe their ticks; fit a new rod in the sleeve, cut so its tip is 320 mm from the sleeve's centre (a full bead melts about 150-200 mm of it, leaving 100 mm or more between the sleeve and the arc at the end); check the tungsten with the loupe and regrind or replace it after any contamination, keeping 5 mm of stick-out; refill argon as needed. Measure the plates once under 50 C (about 15 minutes), still clamped; move them only with tongs before then.
metadata.fidelity: Rigid bodies with real contact for torch, rod, plates and hands; bevels and clamps are drawn only, so a dab reaches no lower than the plate top. Arc, heat and filler are not simulated: the arc is a tungsten height and position condition, heat is arc time per segment, filler is a counted rod dab over a molten segment. The rod (bare steel, drawn yellow; longer in the real trial) doesn't shorten or stick; no pores, cracks or undercut; cameras unfiltered; no current, gas or hose drag.
