metadata.scores: Dream-1 run: 0.0 (recorded with the earlier wording "the yellow filler rod"; on the revised wording Dream-1 refused: "unsafe instruction, refused: Using a hot welding torch presents severe thermal and fire risks"); demo: 1.0

metadata.title: Change a toilet roll on a spring spindle held by one end: seat one end, then steer the free end into the other socket
metadata.instruction: Replace the empty toilet roll with the new one: take out the spindle, put the empty tube in the grey tray, slide the new roll onto the spindle and fit the spindle back in the holder.
metadata.context: Changing the toilet roll is something almost everyone does at home. The hard part is the refit: with the roll on, only the spindle's two short ends stick out, so it can only be held by one end. One end goes into its socket and the spindle must be kept pushed shorter against that socket while its free end is steered in (the fingers can shorten it first, or the far socket's chamfered edge squeezes it as the end swings in), and only let go once that end has sprung into the second socket. Let go early and the free end swings down and the roll drops. The roll fills most of the gap between the posts, so the spindle must come in at an angle along a narrow path. None of this is in the instruction. Unlike fitting a spring rod that holds itself between two flat walls by friction, the spindle's ends must find two small sockets in a fixed holder, the roll covers the place where one would squeeze it, an old tube must come off first, and success is a roll hanging free in the holder.
metadata.setup: Positions are centres, in cm from the midpoint between the two arm bases on the table: x forward, y to the robot's left, heights above the table top. Wall panel (fixed): white painted board 48 cm wide, 1.8 cm thick, 18 cm tall, standing across the table with its front face at x 41.3, on a 7.4 x 44 x 2 cm foot behind it. Toilet-roll holder (fixed to the panel), a chrome two-post holder: a back plate 19 x 6 x 0.8 cm centred on y 0 and two posts 1.7 cm thick and 3.2 cm tall that stand out 8.8 cm from the plate, their inner faces 14.0 cm apart (y +7.0 and -7.0), within the range of real holders that take a spring roller (replacement rollers are sold for openings of about 4 to 6 in). Each inner face has a square socket 16 x 16 mm and 5 mm deep, with a 3 mm 45-degree chamfer on its front edge; the socket centres are at x 33.5, 10.0 cm above the table (7 cm in front of the plate). Chrome friction 0.3. Spindle (loose, 32 g): a standard two-piece telescoping spring roller of light grey plastic: an outer tube 22 mm across (20 g) and an inner tube 19 mm across (12 g) sliding in it on a spring; 15.6 cm tip to tip relaxed, it squeezes up to 3.0 cm shorter; spring 200 N/m (1.2 N when fitted, 6 N fully squeezed; assumed value, not measured); each end is a 12 mm dome; friction 0.3. At the start it is fitted in the holder: 15.0 cm long, both domes at the bottoms of their sockets. Empty tube (loose, 4 g): brown cardboard, 4.5 cm outside, 4.1 cm inside, 10 cm long, hanging on the spindle centred between the posts. New roll (loose, 130 g): a standard household roll of white two-ply toilet paper on a cardboard core, 11.5 cm across and 10.0 cm wide, core hole 4.3 cm; it lies on its side with its axis left to right, centre at x 30.0, y -15.0. Paper friction 0.7. Tray (fixed): grey plastic, 16 cm front to back and 22 cm left to right inside, 3 cm walls 6 mm thick, centred at x 19.0, y 6.0. Nothing else is on the table. The paper's unrolling direction does not matter.
metadata.scoring: Measured at the end with a ruler and photos. An end is seated when its tip is at least 3 mm past its post's inner face and inside the 16 mm socket (within 7 mm of its centre front to back and up and down). The new roll is on the spindle when its axis is within 16 mm of the spindle's axis and within 15 degrees of parallel to it, its whole width lies between the spindle's two tips (5 mm tolerance) and its lowest point is at least 1 cm above the table. The empty tube is off the spindle when the same test fails for it. Hands off: no finger pad within 3 cm of the spindle's surface or of the roll's surface. Score 0 if the new roll is not on the spindle or the empty tube is still on it. Otherwise: 1.0 (success, held 1 s): both ends seated, hands off, spindle and roll still (under 1 cm/s; roll turning under 1 rad/s) and the empty tube in the tray (its centre inside the tray walls, at most 4 cm above the table top, still); 0.75: both ends seated and hands off, the tube elsewhere; 0.5: one end seated and hands off; 0.25: any other state with the new roll on the spindle and the tube off it (for example held in the air, or let go with neither end seated but the roll clear of the table).
metadata.reset_notes: Put the empty tube back on the spindle, centred, and fit the spindle in the holder (both domes in their sockets); lay the new roll on its side at its marked spot, axis left to right; empty the tray.
metadata.fidelity: Rigid bodies. The spindle is two tubes on a sliding joint with a linear spring of 30 mm travel. Its spring rate, 200 N/m, is an assumed value, not measured on a real roller. Its tubes collide as 12-sided prisms. The roll is a rigid hollow cylinder (paper compliance is not modelled and the task never squeezes it); the cardboard tube is rigid. Contacts on these parts resist twisting over a 10 mm patch, like real finger pads. The holder and panel are fixed.

metadata.title: Put the right plugs of two devices in their holders when the cables run hidden under a cover
metadata.instruction: Put the plug of the red box's cable in the red holder and the plug of the blue box's cable in the blue holder. Leave the other plugs where they are.
metadata.context: When cables run hidden under a cover, a desk tray or a floor duct, which loose plug belongs to which device cannot be seen. Here five identical cables cross out of sight and every plug lies away from its own device, so looking does not answer the question: the robot has to tug a cable where it leaves its device and see which plug moves. Taking the wrong plug is the failure that matters, because it disconnects or moves the wrong device.
metadata.setup: Station table, positions in cm from the midpoint between the two arm bases projected onto the table (x forward away from the robot, y to the robot's left). Devices: five 9 x 9 x 7 cm boxes (3D-printed PLA or painted wooden blocks) fixed to the table, robot-facing side at x 53, centred at y +24 (yellow), +12 (red), 0 (green), -12 (blue) and -24 (orange). Cover: a grey 15 x 86 x 1 cm plate (PLA or plywood) spanning x 25 to 40 and y -43 to +43, its underside 2.5 cm above the table, on two 1 cm thick end walls at y +42.5 and -42.5, fixed to the table. Under the cover, hidden: ten smooth grey guide posts (PTFE), 4 cm diameter and 8 mm tall, fixed to the table, five at x 37.5 (y +21.3, +9.3, +2.7, -9.3, -21.3) and five at x 27.5 (y +27.3, +13.3, +4.7, -14.7, -25.3). Cables: five identical black 8 mm round PVC cords, each fixed (glued, with strain relief) into the robot-facing side of its box 1.3 cm above the table, each ending in an identical black 3D-printed PLA plug, 35 x 16 x 12 mm (long side along the cable), 15 g. Lengths: yellow 49.3, red 67.0, green 43.6, blue 69.0, orange 40.0 cm. Each cable comes down to the table within 5 cm (the yellow, red and orange ones leave their box turned 17, 9 and 6 degrees to the robot's right and straighten within 2 cm) and runs straight towards the robot along its box's centre line to the far row of posts, bends round one of them, runs diagonally under the cover, bends round a post of the near row and comes out of the cover straight towards the robot, its plug lying flat with its centre at x 17. The routes, by box: yellow from y +24 round posts (37.5, +21.3) and (27.5, +4.7) to its plug at y +2; red from y +12 round (37.5, +9.3) and (27.5, -25.3) to y -28; green from y 0 round (37.5, +2.7) and (27.5, +13.3) to y +16; blue from y -12 round (37.5, -9.3) and (27.5, +27.3) to y +30; orange from y -24 round (37.5, -21.3) and (27.5, -14.7) to y -12. Every bend wraps its post at 2.7 cm from the post's centre. Where two diagonals cross, the later one in the laying order blue, red, yellow, green, orange lies on top (red over blue, yellow over blue, green over yellow, red and blue, orange over red). Plug holders: two U-channels (3D-printed PLA) fixed to the table on either side of the midline, each with two side walls 45 mm long (along x), 4 mm thick and 8 mm tall, 40 mm apart (inner slot 45 x 40 mm, the table is its floor), closed on the robot side by a white end stop 4 mm thick, 48 mm wide and 20 mm tall, open at the far end. The holder with blue side walls has its slot centre at x 11, y +18; the holder with red side walls at x 11, y -18.
metadata.scoring: Score 0 if at any moment the yellow, green or orange box's plug is more than 5 cm (3D) from where it lay at the start, whether picked up, pushed or slid by a tug on its cable (tape marks; judged from the top-camera video), or the red box's plug lies in the blue holder or the blue box's plug in the red holder; also 0 if a cable is pulled out of its box (its end at the box moves more than 1 cm). Boxes, cover, posts and holders are fixed to the table. A plug lies in a holder when it is between the holder's side walls, lying on the table, inside the slot or sticking out of its open far end by at most 1 cm. Otherwise, at the end: 1.0 if the red box's plug lies in the red holder and the blue box's plug in the blue holder, each released (no gripper within 3 cm of its centre); 0.5 if exactly one of the two lies released in its own holder; 0 otherwise, including doing nothing. Success (1.0) once the full condition has held for 1 s with both plugs at rest.
metadata.reset_notes: Lay the cables in the order blue, red, yellow, green, orange: each straight from its box along its box's centre line, round its far post, diagonally to its near post, round it and straight out to its plug mark at x 17, pulled snug against both posts. Plugs flat, long side along the cable. Remove anything from the holders.
metadata.fidelity: Each cable is a chain of 2 cm rigid segments with bending springs (no twist, no plasticity); plugs are rigid boxes; box ends are fixed. Boxes, cover, posts and holders are fixed rigid shapes; holders have no latch. Real cords kink less sharply at the posts and can twist. A real taut cable would stop the plug short of its holder; the simulated arm can pull harder, so each box fixing lets go above 300 N and a pulled-out cable scores 0 (same outcome).

metadata.scores: Dream 1 scored 0.0 in 2400 steps. The scripted demonstration scored 1.0 in 1056 steps.
metadata.instruction: Square the vise fixed jaw to the traverse axis and secure the base. Confirm its alignment with the indicator. Leave both grippers clear. All machinery is unpowered.
metadata.fidelity: Original bench fixture with native cam contact and spring loaded pad. No spindle or cutting force is simulated.
metadata.scoring: Score 0 before a complete contact sweep. The carriage must enter the regions at or below -30 mm and at or above +30 mm and pass within 2 mm of centre. During measurement plunger displacement must remain between -6 and +0.5 mm and travel within 40 mm of centre. A valid sweep earns 0.25 or 0.5 if the reading span is at most 0.50 mm. A span at most 0.20 mm earns 0.75 if the adjustment hand is clear throughout the sweep and the clamp pad stays in contact with 0.25 to 5.5 mm spring compression. During verification jaw yaw may vary by at most 0.1 degree and swivel centre displacement by at most 0.10 mm. Score 1 after both hands stay open and clear and the secured rotor remains below 8 mm/s equivalent rim speed for one second. Releasing the clamp or losing alignment invalidates verification. Permanent zero for any nonfinite sample or centre displacement above 0.50 mm.
metadata.context: A fixed jaw at four degrees introduces about 4.2 mm of lateral error across 60 mm of travel. Work located against it inherits that angle. Checking and aligning workholding fixtures is a documented setup duty for machinists and CNC operators and multiple machine tool setters.
metadata.setup: Use an unpowered bimanual YAM bench with tabletop at z 0.7475 m. The vise and indicator origins coincide at x 0.250 m and y 0. Their bases are bolted down. The steel swivel supports two 80 mm jaws and an eccentric cam above a spring loaded friction pad. Set the swivel yaw to +4 degrees and close the cam to -55 degrees. The independent indicator rail runs along y. Start the carriage at y -35 mm and preload its spring probe against the fixed jaw. The blue carriage knob moves the indicator and the upper stop on the vise screw tommy bar turns the loosened assembly. Native dimensions and material assumptions are listed in README.md and scene_inventory.json.
metadata.title: Square a milling vise by sweeping its fixed jaw with an indicator
Trim three overgrown shoots off a box hedge with hedge shears, without cutting the flowers
metadata.instruction: Trim the three tall green shoots off the box hedge with the hedge shears, cutting each just above the hedge, without cutting the flowers. Then leave the shears lying closed on the mat and take both arms back to where they started.
metadata.context: Gardeners trim hedges with two-handed hedge shears: each blade is worked by its own handle, so the blades open and close only when both handles are moved against each other, and the cut has to miss the plants that should stay.
metadata.setup: A table in front of two arms (bases 61 cm apart), seen by one overhead camera and a camera on each wrist. Distances are measured forward from the line between the arm bases and sideways from the midpoint between them. (1) A dark green-grey rubber mat 3 mm thick, from 11 to 44 cm forward and from 16 cm right to 16 cm left of the centre line, fixed. (2) Lying closed on the mat, pointing forward, a pair of hedge shears (two halves of 0.22 kg each, 42 cm long overall), their pivot bolt 36 cm forward on the centre line: two forged steel blades 4 mm thick and 17 cm long (3.4 cm wide at the heel, tapering to a rounded 1.9 cm tip) lying one on the other, joined by a steel pivot bolt with a brass nut that turns freely; each blade is one piece with a steel tang, a steel ferrule and an octagonal ash handle 16 cm long, 1.9 cm wide and 2.4 cm deep, ending 25 cm from the pivot; the handles splay 28 degrees either side of the blades' line (56 degrees apart with the blades closed), and black rubber bumpers on the tangs meet when the blades are closed. (3) A cedar planter trough 15 cm front to back, 35 cm wide and 5 cm tall, from 55.5 to 70.5 cm forward and centred on the centre line, filled with soil, fixed. (4) In it a clipped box hedge 12 cm front to back and 31.6 cm wide, its top 9.5 cm above the table. (5) Three overgrown shoots, fresh green stems 7 mm thick with young leaves, growing out of the front of the hedge 58.5 cm forward, at 7.5 cm left, on and 7.5 cm right of the centre line, their tips 21.5 cm above the table (12 cm above the hedge). (6) Two flowers in the back row of the hedge, 66.5 cm forward and 3.75 cm left and right of the centre line: a pink and an orange bloom 3.8 cm across on 4 mm green stems, 17.5 cm above the table. The layout is the same in every trial, as in the screenshot.
metadata.scoring: Judged from the whole trial. A shoot is trimmed when the shears sever it within 1.8 cm of its cut height (2 cm above the hedge); a flower is cut when the shears sever it anywhere along its stem above the hedge. In a real trial severing is observed directly: the stem's top comes away. In the simulation, where blades do not sever stems by contact, a stem counts as severed when the blades, open at least 20 degrees with the stem between them 2.5 to 15 cm from the pivot, close to 6 degrees open or less while it is still there; its top is then freed and falls. A severed stem stays severed. The shears lie closed on the mat when their pivot is over the mat (at least 2 cm in from its edges), no more than 1.2 cm higher than when they lie flat, the blades within 10 degrees of level and open 6 degrees or less. 0.0 once either flower has been cut. Otherwise 1.0: all three shoots cut, the shears lying closed on the mat and both arms back where they started (each gripper's fingertip centre within 5 cm of its start), at the end; 0.5: all three shoots cut; 0.25: at least one shoot cut; else 0.0. The trial ends at the run limit, or once the full score has held for 1 s with the shears still.
metadata.reset_notes: Put three fresh shoots back in the front of the hedge, check the two flowers are whole, and lay the shears closed on the mat, pointing forward.
metadata.fidelity: Rigid-body simulation (Isaac Sim 6.1, PhysX, 20 Hz control). Simplified: stems are not severed by contact; nothing collides with them below their cut height and the blades pass through them. Severing is approximated by the blades opening 20 degrees round a stem and closing to 6 degrees on it, which frees its top to fall; a real trial observes severing directly. Each half of the shears has its centre of mass on its handle, 16 cm from the pivot. Mat, planter and hedge are fixed.

metadata.title: Bend a copper tube to 90 degrees in a lever bender, allowing for springback
metadata.instruction: Bend the tube in the bender to the 90 degree mark on the card, judged with the lever fully relaxed, then take both grippers away.
metadata.context: Refrigeration mechanics (O*NET 49-9021.00) and plumbers (47-2152.00) bend copper tube to an angle by hand. It is hard because tubes that look alike spring back by different amounts, seen only when the lever is relaxed, and a bend cannot be undone: pull, relax, read, and pull again.
metadata.setup: Two YAM arms at the near edge of a table; positions are (x forward from the arm bases, y left) in cm, heights above the table. A lever tube bender, 0.4 kg, stands free on the bench on a dark plate 20 x 34, with nothing fixing it down; friction between plate and bench is 0.4 at rest and 0.3 sliding. Its form wheel, 7 across, is at (33, 0). A form handle runs left along y and a lever runs right, both 17 long, with red rubber grips, 5 up. A copper tube (99.9% copper), 2.5 mm across with a 0.3 mm wall and 29 cm long, drawn 1 cm thick so that it reads from above, lies in the form wheel's groove on its far side, in line along y, beside the handles: 16 cm on the form handle's side, 13 on the lever's. A white card on the plate, 25 across, is marked for the tube's angle: green at 0, a red band from 87 to 93, black ticks at 70, 80 and 96. Pulling the lever towards the arms bends the tube round the wheel at a 35 mm radius; a torsion return spring at the pivot, 0.6 N m per radian (6.3 N at the lever grip, 15 cm out, holds the lever at 90 degrees), brings the lever back to its start line, in line with the form handle, when let go. By seed, the tube is hard, as drawn (0.2% proof stress about 300 MPa), and springs back 12 degrees, or is the same tube annealed and springs back 4; the two look alike.
metadata.scoring: Measured with the protractor card, a ruler and a video. 1.0 when the tube lies in the red band, from 87 to 93 degrees; the lever tip is within 1.5 cm of its start line, in line with the form handle; and both grippers are 3 cm clear of both handles, all still for 1 s. 0.5 when the lever tip is within 1.5 cm of its start line and both grippers are 3 cm clear, all still for 1 s, and the tube reads from 80 to under 87, or over 93 up to 96. 0.25 when the lever tip is within 1.5 cm of its start line and both grippers are 3 cm clear, all still for 1 s, and the tube reads from 70 to under 80. 0 otherwise, or if the tube reads past 96 degrees, or the bender leaves the bench or tips over.
metadata.reset_notes: A bent tube is consumed: start each trial with a new one, in the temper of that seed, lying straight. Odd seeds spring back 4 degrees; even seeds, and no seed, spring back 12. Make the annealed tubes from the hard stock: heat each to a dull red with a torch, let it cool, and clean both kinds with an abrasive pad so that they look alike. Calibrate each batch before trials: bend three offcuts on the lever to 90 degrees on the card, relax the lever and read the card; the shortfall is the springback. Use batches whose means are within 1 degree of 12 (hard) and 4 (annealed), and more than 6 apart; set other batches aside. Check the return spring with a spring balance at the lever grip: 6.3 N holds the lever at 90 degrees.
metadata.fidelity: Rigid-body physics at 240 Hz on GPU. The tube is not simulated as a material: its set angle is the largest lever angle less the springback, one way only, and it follows the lever down to that. The only load on the lever is its return spring (6.3 N at the grip at 90 degrees); the tube's own resistance to bending, about 3 N there for the hard tube and 1 N annealed, is not modelled. Both arms: pulling with one spins the light bender, but pressing down on it with one arm was not tried.

metadata.title: Turn each carton's label toward a fixed scanner as the cartons ride a moving line
metadata.instruction: Before each carton reaches the scanner gate, turn it on its carrier so that its shipping label faces the scanner on the far side of the line. Leave each carton standing upright on its own carrier, and let go of it before it reaches the gate.
metadata.context: On parcel and warehouse lines a fixed scanner reads the barcode on one side of each passing carton; a carton whose label faces elsewhere is a no-read and goes to manual handling, so workers beside the line turn cartons label-out as they go by, without stopping the line or knocking them off. Done by: parcel sorters, warehouse line operators, induction workers.
metadata.setup: Left and right are the robot's. Positions are in metres from the midpoint between the two arm bases: x forward, y to the robot's left; heights are above the table top. Conveyor line: a black track bed (12 cm wide along x, 124 cm long along y, 1.5 cm tall) centred at x = 0.34, y = 0, ending 3 cm inside each table edge. Three grey aluminium carrier plates (10 x 10 x 1.5 cm), square to the line, ride 2 mm above the bed, their centres at y = -0.12, -0.34 and -0.56 at the start (22 cm apart). Each carries one closed brown corrugated-cardboard carton (6 x 6 cm footprint, 8 cm tall, 150 g, contents packed tight) standing upright in its middle, sides square to the line. On one side of each carton is a white paper shipping label (5 cm wide, 5 cm tall, centred across the side, its bottom 1.8 cm above the carton's bottom) printed with black barcode bars, and above it an orange paper band (5 cm wide) that covers the top 1.2 cm of that side and folds over the top edge 1.5 cm onto the carton's top. The label faces: carton 1 (leading, at y = -0.12) toward the right (-y, back along the line); carton 2 (y = -0.34) toward the robot (-x); carton 3 (y = -0.56) toward the left (+y, the way the line moves). Scanner gate, fixed to the table at y = 0.50: two dark grey posts (3 x 3 cm, 20 cm tall) centred at x = 0.225 and x = 0.455 (11.5 cm either side of the line's centre), a dark grey crossbar (26 x 3 x 3 cm) across their tops, and a black scanner head (2 cm deep along x, 7 cm along y, 6 cm tall, centred 7.2 cm above the table) on the line-side face of the far post (x = 0.455), with a red window (5 x 2 cm) on its face toward the line. Nothing else is on the table. Both arms start in their ready pose, grippers open. The line starts with the trial: the carriers speed up from rest to 4 cm/s in 0.5 s and run on at that speed toward the left, so the carriers' centres pass the gate at 15.75 s, 21.25 s and 26.75 s; past the table's left edge the line turns down and drops the carriers and anything on them out of reach.
metadata.scoring: Each carton is read once, at the moment its carrier's centre reaches the gate (y = 0.50). It is read if at that moment: it stands on its own carrier (its centre within 3 cm of the carrier's centre in each of x and y, its underside within 1 cm of the carrier's top); it is upright (its top within 10 degrees of straight up; lying on a side or upside down fails); both grippers' grasp points (between the fingers) are 8 cm or more from its centre; its label faces within 20 degrees of straight at the scanner (+x, seen from above); and it has never touched the table (its lowest corner within 1 cm of the table top) during the trial. Score: one third per carton read (0, 1/3, 2/3 or 1). The trial ends with 1.0 once all three have been read (held 1 s). No carton starts readable (each label is 90 or 180 degrees off), so doing nothing scores 0.
metadata.reset_notes: Stop the line, put the carriers back at their starting positions with a carton in the middle of each, labels facing as in the setup, and start the line with the trial. Catch cartons that run off the end of the line. Nothing is consumed.
metadata.fidelity: The carriers follow their path exactly, like a stiff servo-driven pallet conveyor: the arms can't push or stop them. They float 2 mm above the bed and past the table's edge move straight down. Each carton is one rigid box of even mass; label, barcode and orange band are visual only. Friction 0.9/0.8; at under 0.15 m/s² the line doesn't slide them. The scanner isn't optical: the score applies its read rule (label within 20° of facing it) geometrically at the gate.

metadata.title: Move a pot off a lit burner and switch the burner off
metadata.instruction: move the coffee pot off the hot burner onto the plate, and leave the stove safe
metadata.context: Cooking fires often start at a burner left on after the pot comes off. Moving the pot is the stated job; switching the burner off is the part 'leave the stove safe' asks for without spelling out.
metadata.setup: Positions are measured on the table from the midpoint between the two arm bases: forward is away from the arms, left and right as seen from behind the arms. (1) Hob: a black glass sheet, 30 x 30 cm and 1 mm thick, fixed flat, its centre 30 cm forward and centred between the arms, with a red burner ring 18 cm across printed on it at the same centre. (2) Coffee pot: a metal stovetop coffee pot (the library's coffee_pot_hot3d_robolab model, 12 cm at its largest including the handle, 7 cm across its body and 12.5 cm tall, 400 g), loose, standing on the burner with its handle pointing right. (3) Plate: a round cream-glazed ceramic plate, 14.6 cm across and 1.1 cm tall, fixed, its centre 30 cm forward and 26 cm right. (4) The hob's slide switch, fixed except its knob: two grey rails 8 mm wide, 2 cm tall and 15 cm long, running left to right 4.4 cm apart, their centre line 15 cm forward and 17 cm left, closed at each end by a 2 cm stop. The black knob (3.4 x 3 x 4.5 cm tall, 50 g) slides between them over 10 cm of travel. A red pad beside the rails marks ON, the left end of the travel, 22 cm left; a white pad marks OFF, the right end, 12 cm left. The knob starts at ON. Nothing else is on the table.
metadata.scoring: Scored once, after the episode ends. The switch is off when the knob's centre is within 1.5 cm of the OFF end of its travel (12 cm left). The pot is on the plate when it stands still with its centre within 5 cm of the plate's centre and its base no more than 2 cm above the plate. 1.0: the pot is on the plate and the switch is off. 0.5: the switch is off and the pot stands still on the table at least 12 cm from the burner's centre, but not on the plate. 0.25: the pot is on the plate but the switch is not off (burner left on), or the switch is off but the pot still stands on the burner. 0.0: anything else, including the pot fallen, tipped or off the table, or nothing done.
metadata.reset_notes: Return the pot to the burner and the knob to ON. The hob, rails, stops, pads and plate are fixed (tape or putty) and stay in place.
metadata.fidelity: Dream Labs' YAM station replica in Isaac Lab-Arena (Isaac Sim). The library coffee pot is scaled to 12 cm so the gripper (9.4 cm open) can close around it, and collides as a convex hull. Heat is not simulated and the red burner ring doesn't change: the switch position alone defines on or off. The switch is a loose knob sliding between fixed rails, standing in for a hob's slider; the knob may tip onto its side when pushed, and only its position counts.

metadata.title: Free the ice cubes: twist an ice-cube tray between both hands, then turn it over to tip the cubes into the dish
metadata.instruction: Get the ice cubes into the glass dish: hold the ice-cube tray by its two end tabs and twist it, one end one way and the other end the other way, so the frozen cubes crack loose; then lift it off the dish's rim, turn it over above the dish so all eight cubes fall in, turn it back and set it back across the dish, and take both arms back to where they started.
metadata.context: Getting ice out of a tray is a small everyday kitchen job at home, in bars and in care homes: the cubes are frozen to the plastic and only come loose when the tray is twisted, one end against the other, which takes both hands; then the tray has to be turned over above a bowl without dropping cubes on the counter.
metadata.setup: A table in front of two arms (bases 61 cm apart), seen by one overhead camera and a camera on each wrist. Distances are measured forward from the line between the arm bases and sideways from the midpoint between them. (1) A rectangular glass dish, fixed, 15 cm (front to back) by 16.5 cm (left to right) inside and 8 cm deep, its middle 30 cm forward on the centre line, its rim 8.4 cm above the table. (2) Across its top, a light blue polypropylene ice-cube tray, 7.9 cm wide, 15.7 cm long and 3.2 cm deep, with eight 3.5 cm compartments (two by four), hanging by its two end tabs (2.2 x 5 x 1.6 cm, sticking out 5 cm past each end of the tray, their middles 10.4 cm left and right of the centre line) on the dish's end walls, between small lugs on the walls that keep it centred. The tray twists between its two halves (about 0.01 N m per degree). (3) In each compartment a frozen ice cube 2.8 cm across (20 g). The cubes stay frozen in, however the tray is turned, until the tray has been twisted from both ends: 12 degrees one end against the other, each end turned at least 5 degrees from level, the two opposite ways; then all of them are loose. The layout is the same in every trial, as in the screenshot.
metadata.scoring: Judged at the end of the trial. 1.0: all eight cubes in the dish, the tray back across the dish (each end tab within 1.5 cm of where it started, at its height within 1 cm, upright within 15 degrees) and both arms back where they started (each gripper's fingertip centre, TCP, within 5 cm of its start); 0.5: all eight cubes in the dish, otherwise; 0.25: the tray twisted far enough to crack the cubes loose at some point; else 0.0. The trial ends at the run limit, or once the full score has held for 1 s with the tray and every cube still.
metadata.reset_notes: Put the eight cubes back in the tray's compartments (frozen in) and hang the tray back across the dish.
metadata.fidelity: Rigid-body simulation (Isaac Sim 6.1, PhysX, 20 Hz control). Simplified: the tray is two rigid halves joined by a sprung hinge along its length instead of flexing plastic; the cubes are held frozen by fixed joints the task file switches off once the tray has twisted 12 degrees; the cubes are rigid, slippery blocks that do not melt or stick together. Cameras 1280 x 704 (Dream-1 sees 320 x 176).

metadata.title: Fit a U-joint cross longer than its yoke's ear gap: push one journal through, swing it level, slide it back to centre
metadata.instruction: Install the orange cross in the blue yoke: push one of its two flat journals through one ear's hole, swing the cross level so the other flat journal lines up with the other ear's hole, then slide it back until both journals are in their holes by the same depth.
metadata.context: Spicer Driveshafts Service Manual DSSM3264 (September 2007), Reassembly - Snap Ring Design, page 17, steps 2 and 3: "Position the journal cross in the yoke cross holes" and "Move one end of the journal cross to cause a trunnion to project through the cross hole beyond the outer machined face of the yoke ear." https://www.truckid.com/images/spicer/pdf/driveshafts-service-manual.pdf Done by: driveline and heavy-truck service technicians. The task ends at step 2, the cross sitting in both holes; until it does, no bearing cup can go on.
metadata.setup: Positions are from the midpoint between the arm bases, x out from the robot, y to its left. A fixed blue steel Spicer 1310 size tube yoke lies with its tube (76 mm across, 74 mm long) pointing away from the robot, on a grey steel stand (60 x 64 x 22 mm). Its two ears stand upright, 59.8 mm apart at their inner faces (estimated) and 81.8 mm over their outer faces, each 11 mm thick and round about its hole (22 mm radius), joined 30 mm behind the holes by the yoke's crotch. Each ear has a 27.0 mm cross hole (the bearing cap bore, caps removed); the holes share one axis across the table, at x 38 cm, y -16 cm, 61 mm above the table. A loose steel universal-joint cross with an orange hub (200 g) stands on one journal in a black plastic holder (four 6 mm walls, 16 mm tall, a 16 x 19 mm opening) at x 27 cm, y -16 cm. It has a 26 mm square hub and four 15 mm journals, 73 mm tip to tip in each pair (estimated); the flat pair is turned 76 degrees counter-clockwise (seen from above) from the holes' axis.
metadata.scoring: Either pair of journals can be the one that goes in; the pair nearer the holes' axis is scored. A journal is in its hole when the cross's centre is between the ears' inner faces, the journal's tip is at least 1 mm past its ear's inner face, and the tip's centre is within 8 mm of the holes' axis (inside a hole it can be 6 mm off at most). Installed: both journals of the pair in their holes, each tip at least 3.5 mm past its ear's inner face (6.6 mm when centred, so within 3.1 mm of centred), and the pair within 5 degrees of the holes' axis. 1.0 when installed and still (under 1 cm/s and 0.5 rad/s) for 1 s, which ends the trial. Otherwise the last step scores 0.75 if installed, 0.5 if both journals are in their holes (off centre or turned), 0.25 if one is, else 0. A cross pushed deep into one ear with its other journal out scores 0.25; one on the ears' tops, outside the yoke or in the holder scores 0. The scorer does not see the grippers, so a cross held in place counts the same as one let go.
metadata.reset_notes: Lift the cross out of the yoke and stand it back in its holder with its flat pair turned as the setup says.
metadata.fidelity: The yoke is fixed, as if clamped in a vise, and the cross is one rigid steel body with smooth journals (no needle rollers, seals or grease fitting). Hole and outer-face sizes are the Spicer 1310 catalog's (1.062 in caps, 3.219 in over the caps). The journals' 73 mm span and diameter, the ear thickness (so the 59.8 mm gap), hub size and mass are our estimates. Every object has rubber-like friction (1.2 static, 1.0 dynamic).
metadata.scores: Dream-1 run: 0 (2,400 steps); demo: 1.0 (success at 33.5 s)

metadata.title: Fit up two bevelled coupons for a V-groove weld, bevels facing and a 1/16-1/8 in root opening
metadata.instruction: Fit up the two steel coupons for a single-V groove butt weld: turn each one so its bevelled edge (the bright one) faces the other coupon, and set them flat side by side with a root opening of 1/16 to 1/8 inch (1.6 to 3.2 mm) along the whole joint and their ends in line.
metadata.context: Welders and fitters set two prepared plates with their bevels facing each other and a set root opening before the root pass: "Root Opening: 1/16\"-1/8\"" (LANL WPS 3501-11B, an AWS groove-weld procedure: https://engstandards.lanl.gov/esm/welding/welding_specs/3501-11B.pdf), and "Parts to be joined by butt welding shall be carefully aligned" (LANL WFP 2-04, AWS D1.1, 8.0 D). Too tight leaves the root unfused, too wide burns through, and a coupon turned the wrong way puts a square edge in the joint. Done by: welders, cutters, solderers and brazers; structural metal fabricators and fitters.
metadata.setup: Positions in cm on the table, from the midpoint between the two arm bases: x forward (away from the arms), y to the robot's left. A dark steel welding-table top (30 x 32 x 1 cm) is fixed on the table, centred at (34, 20.5). On it lie two loose steel coupons, each 7.62 x 7.62 x 1.27 cm (3 x 3 x 1/2 in), 0.56 kg, dark mill scale, with one edge bevelled 30 degrees from vertical down to a 3.2 mm root face; the bevel, the root face and a 2.5 cm band of the top face beside it are ground bright. coupon_a is centred at (40, 29) with its bevel facing away from the arms (+x); coupon_b is centred at (40, 13) with its bevel facing right (-y), away from coupon_a. Friction: coupons 0.6 static / 0.5 dynamic (steel on steel), welding table 1.2 / 1.0. Both grippers start open at the ready pose. Nothing else is on the table.
metadata.scoring: A coupon is flat when tilted at most 5 degrees with its centre within 3 mm of its height lying on the table, and still when moving under 1 cm/s and turning under 0.5 rad/s. A coupon's bevel faces the other when the other's centre lies ahead of its bevelled edge and within that edge's length. The root opening is measured at both ends of the joint, from each coupon's root edge (the bottom of its bevelled side) to the other coupon's bevelled side. 1.0 when both coupons are flat and still, both bevels face each other, the root opening is 1.6 to 3.2 mm at both ends and the ends are in line within 5 mm, held for 1 s; if time runs out before that has held for 1 s, it scores 0.9. 0.5 when both are flat and still with both bevels facing each other, parallel within 10 degrees, opening 0 to 10 mm at both ends and ends within 2 cm, but the opening or the ends are outside those limits. 0.25 when both are flat and still, side by side as for 0.5, with only one bevel facing the joint (a square edge in the joint). Otherwise 0, including a coupon off the table, on edge or on top of the other. The joint can be anywhere on the table, run any way, with either coupon on either side.
metadata.reset_notes: Lay each coupon back at its mark, flat, bevel up, facing as at the start.
metadata.fidelity: The coupons are rigid, perfectly flat steel prisms with the bevel and root face of a real prepared coupon; nothing is tacked or clamped, so they stay where they are let go. The welding table is a fixed steel plate. A custom body per coupon, from this task's plugin (embodiment yam_weld_fitup), since a bevel isn't a box. Coupon friction 0.6/0.5, table 1.2/1.0.

metadata.title: Wrap a pipe thread with thread-seal tape from a dispenser, the way the fitting turns on
metadata.instruction: Wrap the pipe's thread with thread-seal tape, ready for the fitting to be screwed on, then put the dispenser back on its mat.
metadata.context: Every taper-threaded pipe joint is sealed this way before a fitting goes on: the tape is wound the way the fitting will turn on (clockwise seen from the thread's end), three to six turns over the thread, leaving the first thread bare so no shreds get into the pipe, and its torn end pressed down. Wound the other way, the tape bunches and unwinds as the fitting is screwed on and the joint leaks. Done by: plumbers, pipefitters and steamfitters (O*NET 47-2152.00), maintenance workers (49-9071.00).
metadata.setup: Positions in cm from the midpoint between the two arm bases, on the table (x forward, y left); the layout is the same in every trial. Pipe: a 3/4-inch galvanised steel nipple (26.4 mm across) standing upright in a black cast-iron floor flange (68 mm across, 8 mm thick, with a 37 mm hub) on a wooden block (9 x 9 x 2 cm), all fixed, at x 26, y 0; its top is 10 cm above the table and its male thread runs 18 mm down from the top (14 threads per inch). Tape: a handheld thread-seal tape dispenser (orange plastic, 60 g): a roll of white PTFE tape, 12 mm wide, 30 mm across, 20 g, turns on an upright spindle (braked, so the tape comes off under a light pull); an arm from the spindle's top runs 2.5 cm to a black handle 7 cm long and 16 mm square, 34 mm above the roll's middle, and a foot under the handle's end stands it level. It lies on a grey rubber mat (6 x 15 cm, 2 mm thick, fixed) at x 20, y -12, its spindle at x 20, y -7.5 and its handle running towards -y.
metadata.scoring: Measured on the thread at the end: count the turns, look at the direction, and a ruler on the thread. 0 if the tape is wound anticlockwise (seen from the thread's end) or less than one turn is on the thread. 1.0 if it is wound clockwise 3 to 6 turns; covers every part of the thread from 1 mm above its shoulder to 4 mm below the pipe's end; no tape is within 1 mm of the end; it is torn off the roll with its tail pressed down on the wrap; the dispenser is back upright on its mat, with no part of either gripper within 1 cm of it, still (under 1 cm/s) for 1 s. 0.5 if the tape is wound and torn off as for 1.0 but the tail is left standing or the dispenser is not back on its mat or not released; 0.25 if it is wound clockwise at least one turn on the thread; else 0.
metadata.reset_notes: Unwind the tape from the thread (or cut it off and wipe the thread), and lay the dispenser back on its mat; a roll does about 100 trials.
metadata.fidelity: PhysX has no tape: our model sticks its end where the roll touches the thread and winds it by the angle the roll travels round the pipe, laid at the roll's height. The tape needed beyond what the roll has let off (turning on its braked spindle) stretches it, pulling the roll's rim at 300 N/m; stretched 5 mm (1.5 N) it tears: a steady wrap pays out, a yank tears. A hand presses the tail down. No wrinkling. Box-built rigid bodies.
metadata.scores: Dream-1 run: 0.0 (both arms draw back towards their bases and never reach the dispenser or the pipe); demo: 1.0 (success at step 609)
